course_1_la_naissance_de_l_islam_622|The.explanation: The two powers surrounding the Arabian Peninsula in the 7th century. Byzantium (Eastern Roman Empire) and the Sassanids (Zoroastrian Persian Empire) were exhausting themselves in an endless war, clearing the way for Arab conquests.
Community of Muslim believers, transcending tribal boundaries. All Muslims form a single body regardless of their origin.

course_1_la_naissance_de_l_islam_622|Jih.explanation: Arabic term literally meaning "effort". Refers to the inner effort for self-improvement and the armed defense of the community.

course_1_la_naissance_de_l_islam_622|Bed.explanation: Arab nomads living in the desert, organized into tribes bonded by kinship ties.

course_1_la_naissance_de_l_islam_622|raz.explanation: Rapid attacks led by tribes against caravans or enemy camps to seize livestock or goods.

course_1_la_naissance_de_l_islam_622|Dhi.explanation: Legal status of 'protected' granted to monotheistic non-Muslims living under Islamic authority.

course_1_la_naissance_de_l_islam_622|jiz.explanation: Annual tax paid by non-Muslim populations (subject to the Dhimma) in exchange for the protection of the state.

course_1_la_naissance_de_l_islam_622|Con.explanation: Edict issued by Muhammad shortly after the Hegira, governing the relations between monotheists (Muslims and Jews) and the clans of the Medina oasis.

course_1_la_naissance_de_l_islam_622|Qur.explanation: Powerful merchant tribe that controlled Mecca and the Kaaba at the time of Muhammad.

course_1_la_naissance_de_l_islam_622|Cal.explanation: Successor to Muhammad as head of the Muslim community and the Islamic empire (caliphate).

course_1_la_naissance_de_l_islam_622|Byz.explanation: The two powers surrounding the Arabian Peninsula in the 7th century. Byzantium (Eastern Roman Empire) and the Sassanids (Zoroastrian Persian Empire) were exhausting themselves in an endless war, clearing the way for Arab conquests.

course_2_l_appel_d_urbain_ii_et_la_1re_c.explanation: Definitive break between the Roman Catholic Church and the Orthodox Church, over papal authority and the Filioque question. This schism made relations between Byzantium and Rome complex at the time when Alexios I was requesting military aid.
Byzantine Emperor who sent an embassy to Pope Urban II to request mercenaries against the Seljuk Turks. His modest request unintentionally triggered the massive mobilization of the first crusade.
Full remission of the earthly punishment owed for one's sins, granted by the Pope. Urban II promised it to everyone who joined the crusade, a powerful reason to sign up in a deeply religious society.
Major defeat of the Byzantine Empire against the Seljuk Turks in 1071, causing the loss of Anatolia and the military decline of Byzantium.
Spiritual and social movement initiated by the Church in the 10th and 11th centuries to limit feudal violence and protect non-combatants.
Ecclesiastical assembly of 1095 during which Urban II launched his call to the crusade.
Popular preacher who led the 'Crusade of the Poor', a disorganized wave preceding that of the barons.
Norman prince from Southern Italy and one of the primary military leaders of the first crusade, founder of the Principality of Antioch.
Title held by Godfrey of Bouillon, who refused the title of King of Jerusalem out of religious humility.
Religious and military order founded in 1119 to protect pilgrims in the Holy Land, becoming a major financial power.
Sultan of Kurdish origin who unified the Muslim world and retook Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187.
Four Christian states (County of Edessa, Principality of Antioch, County of Tripoli, Kingdom of Jerusalem) created by the crusaders in the Near East at the end of the 11th century.

course_3_la_prise_de_rome_par_les_wisigo.explanation: Nomadic people from Central Asia who swept into Europe around 370, pushing the Goths and other Germanic peoples to cross Roman borders to flee. Their leader Attila would ravage Europe in the 450s.

Treaty by which Rome authorized a Barbarian people to settle on its territory in exchange for military service. The Visigoths obtained a foedus in 382, but Rome did not respect it, which explains Alaric's revolt.

course_3_la_prise_de_rome_par_les_wisigo.displayTerm: The division of the Empire in 395
course_3_la_prise_de_rome_par_les_wisigo.explanation: Upon the death of Theodosius I, the Empire was shared between his two sons: Honorius in the West (capital Ravenna) and Arcadius in the East (Constantinople). This permanent division weakened the response to invasions.
A branch of early Christianity, deemed heretical by the Council of Nicaea, which considered that Christ was not equal to God the Father.
Church Father and translator of the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate), witness to the psychological shock caused by the fall of Rome.
Germanic people who seized Roman North Africa and sacked Rome in turn in 455 in a much more devastating manner than Alaric.
Federation of Germanic peoples settled on the lower Rhine, which eventually conquered Gaul under Clovis after the collapse of the Empire.
Germanic people from whom came Odoacer, the military leader who deposed the last Western Emperor.
King of the Visigoths and former officer in the Roman army, he led his people to the capture of Rome in 410 after the failure of negotiations with the Empire.
Western Roman Emperor (395-423) who moved the capital to Ravenna and was unable to prevent the sack of Rome.
Italian city that became the capital of the Western Empire in 402 due to its strategic position protected by marshes.
Theological and philosophical treatise by Saint Augustine written following the sack of Rome to justify Christianity against pagan criticism.
Last Western Roman emperor, deposed at about 15 years of age by the leader Odoacer in 476.
Heruli military leader who overthrew the Western Empire in 476 and established himself as King of Italy under the nominal suzerainty of Constantinople.

course_4_le_couronnement_de_charlemagne_.explanation: Politics entity born from The Coronation of Charlemagne (800), claiming to embody the continuity of the Roman Empire in the West under Christian authority. It lasted until 1806 and structured the Germanic space for a thousand years.

Carolingian "envoys of the master": royal inspectors sent in pairs (one bishop, one layman) to control local administration and render justice in the name of the emperor. Key instrument of Carolingian government over an immense territory.

English scholar brought in by Charlemagne to lead the Palatine School in Aachen. He oversaw the reform of writing and education, training a generation of literate administrators who maintained the empire.
Germanic people established in Northern Italy from the 6th century onwards, whose kingdom was conquered by Charlemagne in 774.
Nomadic horse-riding people originally from Central Asia, settled in the Danube plain, whose empire was destroyed by Carolingian armies.
Pyrenean pass where the rear-guard of Charlemagne's army was massacred in 778 by the Vascons, an event which inspired the famous 'Song of Roland'.
High local dignitaries appointed by the sovereign to administer a province (the county) in his name, possessing military and judicial powers.
Reference currency imposed by Charlemagne's monetary reform, replacing gold with silver as the basis of the European economic system for several centuries.
High local dignitary appointed by the sovereign to administer a province (the county) in his name, holding military and judicial powers.

course_5_la_magna_carta_1215|The feudal.explanation: Medieval organization based on personal ties: the suzerain grants land (fief) in exchange for military service and loyalty. The Magna Carta (1215) was extracted within this contractual framework: the barons reminded the king of his obligations.

course_5_la_magna_carta_1215|The loss of.explanation: Major event where John Lackland lost his possessions to Philip II Augustus, provoking the fiscal crisis at the origin of the Magna Carta (1215).

course_5_la_magna_carta_1215|Habeas corp.explanation: Legal principle protecting against arbitrary arrest: any person arrested must be brought before a judge. A direct legacy of clause 39 of the Magna Carta, it became a pillar of Anglo-Saxon law.

course_5_la_magna_carta_1215|Philip II A.explanation: King of France (1180-1223) who dismantled the Plantagenet empire by taking Normandy and Maine back from John Lackland.

course_5_la_magna_carta_1215|Bouvines.explanation: Decisive battle of 1214 where Philip II Augustus defeated a coalition including England, sealing the fate of John Lackland.

course_5_la_magna_carta_1215|Bill of Rig.explanation: The first ten amendments to the United States Constitution, guaranteeing individual liberties and limiting federal power.

course_5_la_magna_carta_1215|Eleanor Roo.explanation: First Lady of the United States and a key figure in the drafting of the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

course_5_la_magna_carta_1215|Innocent II.explanation: Extremely powerful Pope (1198-1216) who excommunicated John Lackland before becoming his ally and annulling the Magna Carta at his request.

course_5_la_magna_carta_1215|Stephen Lan.explanation: Archbishop of Canterbury whose appointment was at the origin of the conflict between John Lackland and the Pope. He played the role of mediator and intellectual architect of the Charter.

course_5_la_magna_carta_1215|Edward Coke.explanation: 17th-century English jurist who reactivated the use of the Magna Carta to oppose the royal absolutism of the Stuarts.

course_6_la_peste_noire_en_europe_1347_1.explanation: Medieval medical belief that diseases were caused by impure vapors emanating from stagnant waters and corpses. It explains the total helplessness of medicine against the Plague - one could not treat what one did not understand.

Genoa and Venice, whose commercial ships linked the Black Sea to Europe, were the vectors of the epidemic. Genoese ships introduced the plague to Sicily in 1347, spreading the bacteria through their Mediterranean trade networks.

Accused of poisoning wells, tens of thousands of Jews were massacred in Germany and France during the Plague. Pope Clement VI defended them but was little heard in devastated cities looking for scapegoats.
A period of relative economic and politics stability in Eurasia under the Mongol Empire during the 13th and 14th centuries, which unintentionally facilitated the spread of the plague.
A network of trade routes connecting Asia to Europe, the primary vector for the spread of the plague from the East to the Black Sea trading posts.
A Genoese trading post in Crimea (modern-day Feodosia). The siege of the city by the Mongols in 1346 is considered the gateway for the plague into the Mediterranean.
Ancient Greek physician whose theories (notably the theory of humors) dominated medieval medicine, preventing an understanding of the bacterial origin of the plague.
The scientific name for the rat flea, the actual vector of transmission for the Yersinia pestis bacterium from animals to humans.
A fanatical religious movement whose members publicly flogged themselves as a sign of penance to end the epidemic, which was seen as divine punishment.
Pope residing in Avignon during the Black Death. He distinguished himself by protecting Jews from pogroms and by commissioning medical reports on the scourge.
Italian writer who witnessed the plague in Florence. His masterpiece, the Decameron, accurately describes the social and psychological impact of the epidemic on his contemporaries.
Period of climatic cooling beginning in the 14th century, responsible for poor harvests and famines that weakened the immune resistance of Europeans before the plague.
Mongol empire established on the Russian and Central Asian steppes, whose armies besieged Caffa and introduced the plague to European trading posts.

course_7_jeanne_d_arc_et_la_guerre_de_ce.explanation: Agreement by which Charles VI of France disinherits his son, the Dauphin Charles, in favor of the King of England Henry V, creating a Franco-English dynastic union.

Ceremony by which the King of France was anointed with holy oil, conferring upon him a quasi-sacred character. Only a king crowned in Reims was fully legitimate in the eyes of the Church and the people - hence the urgency for Joan to lead Charles VII there.
French faction allied with the English, led by the Duke of Burgundy (Philip the Good in 1429). Their alliance with England was broken by the Treaty of Arras in 1435.
Belief according to which God intervenes directly in human history and politics to fulfill his will.
Bishop of Beauvais and supporter of the English, he was the architect of the trial sentencing Joan of Arc in Rouen.
Decisive battle of 1453 which marks the effective end of the Hundred Years' War and the near-total expulsion of the English from the kingdom of France.
Faction of the French nobility faithful to the House of Orléans and to the legitimacy of the Valois (Charles VII) during the civil war against the Burgundians.

course_8_la_chute_de_constantinople_1453.displayTerm: The sack of Constantinople by the 4th Crusade (1204)
course_8_la_chute_de_constantinople_1453.explanation: The crusaders, diverted by Venice, looted Christian Constantinople for three days in 1204. This trauma permanently weakened Byzantium and explains Byzantine mistrust of the West during the siege of 1453.

course_8_la_chute_de_constantinople_1453.displayTerm: The Greek diaspora and the Renaissance
course_8_la_chute_de_constantinople_1453.explanation: Greek scholars fleeing Constantinople brought their manuscripts to Italy, contributing decisively to the Renaissance. The fall of Byzantium paradoxically accelerated the intellectual revival of the West.

Constantinople had preserved and transmitted Roman law, Greek philosophy, and Christian theology for a thousand years. Its fall put an end to this living continuity between Antiquity and the modern world.
Last Byzantine emperor (1449-1453), he died in combat during the final assault on Constantinople.
Elite corps of the Ottoman infantry, originally composed of converted Christian prisoners, renowned for their discipline and loyalty to the Sultan.
Name given to Constantinople after the Ottoman conquest, although the official name did not become Istanbul until the 20th century.
Estuary flowing into the Bosphorus, forming a protected natural harbor that separated the city of Constantinople from its suburb of Galata.
System of land fortifications of Constantinople erected in the 5th century, famous for its complexity and historical invincibility until 1453.

course_9_l_empire_azteque|The Five Suns.explanation: Aztec myth: the universe has already been created and destroyed four times. The current fifth sun is only kept alive through human sacrifices. This cosmology made sacrifices cosmically necessary - without them, the sun would stop.

course_9_l_empire_azteque|The chinampas.explanation: "Floating gardens" created in Lake Texcoco: artificial islands of mud and vegetation allowing for highly productive agriculture. Tenochtitlán was surrounded by a network of canals and cultivated lands that fed 200,000 inhabitants.

course_9_l_empire_azteque|Tenochtitlán a.explanation: Aztec capital founded in 1325 on an islet in Lake Texcoco, where Mexico City is located today. It was one of the largest cities in the world in 1519, with a sophisticated network of aqueducts and canals.

course_9_l_empire_azteque|Aztlán.explanation: Mythical place of origin of the Aztec peoples, often located in northern present-day Mexico or the southwestern United States.

course_9_l_empire_azteque|Tlaxcaltecs.explanation: Fierce enemy people of the Aztecs who became the main military ally of Hernán Cortés during the conquest.

course_9_l_empire_azteque|Smallpox.explanation: Infectious disease of European origin which was the main agent of mortality during the fall of the Aztec empire.

course_9_l_empire_azteque|Nahuatl.explanation: Language spoken by the Aztecs and still practiced by many communities in Mexico today.

course_9_l_empire_azteque|New Spain.explanation: Name given to the Spanish colony established on the ruins of the Aztec empire after 1521.

course_9_l_empire_azteque|Huitzilopochtl.explanation: God of the sun and war among the Aztecs, spiritual guide of the Mexica migration and main beneficiary of human sacrifices.

course_9_l_empire_azteque|Moctezuma II.explanation: Last great Aztec ruler reigning during the arrival of Cortés. His hesitant management of the invasion facilitated the capture of Tenochtitlán.

course_9_l_empire_azteque|Templo Mayor.explanation: Double pyramid in the center of Tenochtitlán dedicated to Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc (god of rain), the religious and political heart of the empire.

course_10_la_decouverte_de_l_amerique_14.explanation: The triumph of the capture of Granada released resources and created a momentum of national ambition that explains Isabella of Castile's support for Columbus.
Florentine navigator who understood that the discovered lands were an unknown continent. The continent was named in his honor in 1507.
Agreement arbitrated by the Pope dividing the world into two spheres of influence between Spain (west) and Portugal (east).
Greek scholar from the 3rd century BC who was the first to calculate the circumference of the Earth with remarkable precision thanks to the shadow cast by the sun.
Contract signed in April 1492 between Christopher Columbus and the Catholic Monarchs, setting the financial conditions and honorary titles of the navigator in case of success.
A family of wealthy Spanish shipowners, including the brothers Martín Alonso and Vicente Yáñez, who were the true technical and financial supporters of the 1492 expedition.
Indigenous people inhabiting the Greater Antilles at the time of Columbus's arrival; they were the first to suffer the consequences of Spanish colonization.

Even before anesthesia, infections after surgery were killing patients. Semmelweis (1847) and then Lister (1867) imposed hygiene: hand washing and sterilized instruments. Together, anesthesia and antisepsis transformed surgery.

course_11_la_prise_de_la_bastille_1789|T.displayTerm: The Ancien Régime and the three estates
course_11_la_prise_de_la_bastille_1789|T.explanation: French society divided into three estates: Clergy (1st), Nobility (2nd), and Third Estate (97% of the population, 3rd). At the Estates General, each estate had only one vote out of three, despite the overwhelming demographic representativeness of the Third Estate.

Royal order of imprisonment without trial or explanation, signed by the king. The Bastille symbolized this royal arbitrariness, even though in July 1789 it contained only 7 prisoners - its value was purely symbolic.

course_11_la_prise_de_la_bastille_1789|A.explanation: Conflict (1775-1783) during which France helped the American colonies free themselves from British rule. The financial cost of this support was one of the major causes of the French monarchy's bankruptcy.

course_11_la_prise_de_la_bastille_1789|T.explanation: A wave of panic and peasant revolt that spread across the French countryside between July and August 1789, leading to the destruction of manorial records.

course_11_la_prise_de_la_bastille_1789|A.displayTerm: Ancien Régime and the three estates
course_11_la_prise_de_la_bastille_1789|A.explanation: French society divided into three estates: Clergy (1st), Nobility (2nd), and Third Estate (97% of the population, 3rd). At the Estates General, each order had only one out of three votes, despite the overwhelming demographic representativeness of the Third Estate.

course_12_la_strategie_de_napoleon_a_ulm.explanation: An autonomous military unit of 15,000 to 30,000 men including all arms, capable of fighting alone for several days. This organizational innovation allowed for the speed of maneuver that was Napoleon's strength.
Nelson's decisive naval victory over the Franco-Spanish fleet, the same week as Ulm. It put an end to the plans to invade England and explains why Napoleon could never defeat British maritime power.
Napoleonic economic politics (1806) forbidding all European trade with England, to ruin it economically. Its imperfect application forced Napoleon to invade the Iberian Peninsula and then Russia.
Mountain range in southwestern Germany from where Mack expected to see Napoleon arrive.
Name given by Napoleon to the French military forces he personally commanded between 1805 and 1814.

course_13_la_bataille_de_waterloo_1815|T.explanation: Meeting of European powers to rebuild the post-Napoleonic order. It redrew the map of Europe, restored monarchies, and created the "European Concert" which maintained a relative peace for almost a century.
Pact signed in 1815 between Russia, Austria, and Prussia to defend monarchical principles against revolutionary ideas. It was the instrument for suppressing liberal uprisings of the 1820s-1830s.

course_13_la_bataille_de_waterloo_1815|M.explanation: Nicknamed "the bravest of the brave," he led the French cavalry at Waterloo. His disastrous charge against the British squares, launched too early without artillery support, was one of the fatal tactical mistakes of the day.

course_13_la_bataille_de_waterloo_1815|C.explanation: Napoleon's tactical maneuver consisting of positioning himself between two enemy armies to face them separately, thus avoiding being overwhelmed by their combined strength.

course_13_la_bataille_de_waterloo_1815|G.explanation: Massive concentration of cannons advocated by Napoleon to break through enemy lines through intensive bombardment on a specific point.

course_13_la_bataille_de_waterloo_1815|L.explanation: Post-1815 diplomatic principle aimed at restoring royal dynasties to their thrones at the expense of regimes resulting from the Revolution or the Empire.

course_13_la_bataille_de_waterloo_1815|S.explanation: Infantry defensive formation composed of several ranks of soldiers forming a rectangle, with bayonnets facing outward to break cavalry charges.

course_14_la_commune_de_paris_1871|The F.explanation: Conflict triggered by Napoleon III, ending with the crushing defeat at Sedan and the capture of the Emperor. The humiliating capitulation and the siege of Paris created the breeding ground for the Commune.

course_14_la_commune_de_paris_1871|Adolp.explanation: Head of the provisional government in Versailles who ordered the crushing of the Commune during the "Bloody Week" (May 21-28, 1871). A former journalist and historian, he was the first president of the Third Republic.

course_14_la_commune_de_paris_1871|The I.explanation: Organization founded in London in 1864, bringing together trade unions and workers' parties from several countries. Although the Commune was not its direct work, Marx celebrated it as the first experience of workers' power.

course_14_la_commune_de_paris_1871|Natio.explanation: Citizen militia composed mainly of Parisians, with its own weapons and elected leaders. In 1871, it becomes the armed wing of the Commune.

course_14_la_commune_de_paris_1871|Fédér.explanation: Name given to the supporters of the Paris Commune, as they claimed to belong to a federation of autonomous communes.

course_14_la_commune_de_paris_1871|Louis.explanation: Nicknamed the 'Red Virgin', she is one of the major figures of the Commune, an anarchist activist and ambulance driver on the barricades.

course_14_la_commune_de_paris_1871|Inter.explanation: Organization founded in London in 1864, bringing together trade unions and workers' parties from several countries. Although the Commune was not its direct work, Marx celebrated it as the first experience of workers' power.

course_15_la_belle_epoque_1871_1914|The.explanation: A Jewish officer, Alfred Dreyfus, was wrongly convicted of espionage by an anti-Semitic general staff. The affair tore France apart between Dreyfusards and anti-Dreyfusards, revealing deep tensions within French society.

Meeting of European powers to settle the partition of Africa without war among themselves. In a few decades, Europe colonized 90% of the African continent, drawing arbitrary borders that still cause conflicts today.

course_15_la_belle_epoque_1871_1914|Augu.explanation: Philosophy according to which science will solve all human problems. The dominant doctrine of the Belle Époque, it explains the optimism of this period and its brutal shattering by the war of 1914.

course_15_la_belle_epoque_1871_1914|Fran.explanation: Conflict of 1870-1871 which led to the fall of Napoleon III and the unification of Germany, creating lasting French resentment (the loss of Alsace-Lorraine).

course_15_la_belle_epoque_1871_1914|Firs.explanation: Global conflict from 1914 to 1918 that ended European hegemony and radically transformed borders and national societies.

course_15_la_belle_epoque_1871_1914|Sigm.explanation: Austrian physician, founder of psychoanalysis. His work 'The Interpretation of Dreams' (1900) marks a major breakthrough in the understanding of the human psyche.

course_15_la_belle_epoque_1871_1914|Rela.explanation: Physical theory published by Albert Einstein in 1905, overturning the concepts of space and time inherited from classical physics.

course_15_la_belle_epoque_1871_1914|Art.explanation: Artistic style of the late 19th century characterized by curved lines and patterns inspired by nature, affecting architecture and decoration.

course_15_la_belle_epoque_1871_1914|Fauv.explanation: French pictorial movement of the early 20th century favoring bright and arbitrary colors to express emotions rather than reality.

course_15_la_belle_epoque_1871_1914|Cubi.explanation: Artistic avant-garde movement initiated by Picasso and Braque, breaking down objects into simple geometric shapes.

course_15_la_belle_epoque_1871_1914|Drey.explanation: A Jewish officer, Alfred Dreyfus, was wrongly convicted of espionage by an anti-Semitic general staff. The affair tore France apart between Dreyfusards and anti-Dreyfusards, revealing the deep tensions in French society.

course_16_la_bataille_de_verdun_1916|The.explanation: Franco-British offensive launched on July 1, 1916, to relieve Verdun. It caused 60,000 British casualties on the first day alone, the deadliest day in British military history.

course_16_la_bataille_de_verdun_1916|Tre.explanation: Since 1914, the Western Front had stabilized into a network of trenches from the North Sea to Switzerland. This positional warfare explains why battles like Verdun were fought over a few square kilometers for months.

course_16_la_bataille_de_verdun_1916|The.displayTerm: The heavy artillery of the Great War
course_16_la_bataille_de_verdun_1916|The.explanation: Artillery accounted for 60-70% of First World War casualties. Technical progress since 1870 had made offensive weapons far more powerful than defenses, creating the trench impasse.

course_16_la_bataille_de_verdun_1916|Ger.explanation: Codename of the German operation on Verdun, meaning "court" or "judgment" in German, illustrating Falkenhayn's will to judge and annihilate the French army.

course_16_la_bataille_de_verdun_1916|Bar.explanation: Town located behind the Verdun front, starting point of the Sacred Way through which supply trucks passed.

course_16_la_bataille_de_verdun_1916|Nor.explanation: System of troop rotation established by Pétain at Verdun, consisting of rotating divisions to the front for a short period to maintain their combat effectiveness.

course_16_la_bataille_de_verdun_1916|Red.explanation: Land so torn up by the fighting and so full of unexploded shells that after the war the French state banned all farming and rebuilding there.

course_16_la_bataille_de_verdun_1916|Hea.displayTerm: Heavy artillery of the Great War
course_16_la_bataille_de_verdun_1916|Hea.explanation: Artillery accounted for 60-70% of casualties in the First World War. Technical progress since 1870 had made offensive weapons far more powerful than defenses, creating the stalemate of the trenches.

course_17_la_revolution_russe_1917|Raspu.explanation: A Siberian healer monk who gained the influence of Tsarina Alexandra by relieving the hemophilic crises of Tsarevich Alexei. His alleged political interference and scandalous image deeply discredited the imperial court.

course_17_la_revolution_russe_1917|Marxi.explanation: An ideology combining Marx's economic theories (class struggle, exploitation of the proletariat) and Lenin's tactical innovations (disciplined avant-garde party, organized revolution). This was the ideology of the Bolsheviks who took power in October 1917.

course_17_la_revolution_russe_1917|The P.explanation: A council of workers' and soldiers' delegates, elected in factories and barracks. In 1917, it effectively controlled the streets and the army, creating an unstable "double power" in the face of the legal provisional government.

course_17_la_revolution_russe_1917|First.explanation: Global conflict (1914-1918) that caused the collapse of several empires, including the Russian Empire, which was unable to keep up with the industrial pace of the conflict.

course_17_la_revolution_russe_1917|Douma.explanation: The Russian parliament created after the 1905 revolution. In 1917, it was largely ignored by Tsar Nicholas II.

course_17_la_revolution_russe_1917|Duma.explanation: The Russian parliament created after the 1905 revolution. In 1917, it was largely ignored by Tsar Nicholas II.

course_17_la_revolution_russe_1917|Julia.explanation: Calendar used in Russia until 1918, which was 13 days behind the Western Gregorian calendar (hence the discrepancy between February/March and October/November).

course_17_la_revolution_russe_1917|April.explanation: Political program presented by Lenin upon his return from exile, advocating for the immediate transition from the bourgeois revolution to the socialist revolution.

course_17_la_revolution_russe_1917|Leon.explanation: Marxist revolutionary and organizer of the Red Army. He was the technical mastermind of the October 1917 insurrection.

course_17_la_revolution_russe_1917|Brest.explanation: Peace treaty signed in March 1918 between Bolshevik Russia and Germany, formalizing the Russian withdrawal from the war at the cost of heavy territorial losses.

course_18_la_grande_depression_1929|The.explanation: A monetary system where currencies were convertible into gold at a fixed rate, limiting the ability of states to create money. It mechanically spread the American crisis to the entire world: when the United States reduced their money supply, all countries linked to gold suffered.

course_18_la_grande_depression_1929|Roos.explanation: A set of American programs combining economic stimulus (large public works), financial reform (FDIC, SEC), and social protection. It did not end the crisis, but it laid the foundations of the American welfare state.

course_18_la_grande_depression_1929|Purc.explanation: The practice of borrowing from one's bank to buy shares, betting on their rise. Very widespread in the 1920s, it amplified the bubble and, during the crash, forced millions of Americans to sell urgently to repay their loans.

course_18_la_grande_depression_1929|over.explanation: A situation where the supply of goods exceeds consumer demand, leading to a drop in prices and an accumulation of useless stock.
Refers to a financial asset (stock or real estate) whose market price is significantly higher than its actual economic value.

course_18_la_grande_depression_1929|bank.explanation: When many of a bank's customers pull out their deposits at the same time for fear it will fail, and in doing so actually cause it to fail.

course_18_la_grande_depression_1929|Herb.explanation: 31st President of the United States (1929-1933), often criticized for his inability to act effectively at the onset of the crisis.

course_18_la_grande_depression_1929|defl.explanation: A generalized and lasting fall in prices and wages, which often worsens the crisis by increasing the real burden of debt.

course_18_la_grande_depression_1929|Weim.explanation: Republican regime in place in Germany between 1919 and 1933, destabilized by economic instability and the rise of extremes.

course_18_la_grande_depression_1929|lais.explanation: Liberal economic principle advocating for the absence of state intervention in market mechanisms.

course_18_la_grande_depression_1929|reco.explanation: Economic policy that tries to lift demand and production by increasing public spending.

course_18_la_grande_depression_1929|Gold.explanation: Monetary system where currencies were convertible into gold at a fixed rate, limiting the ability of states to create money. It mechanically spread the American crisis to the entire world: when the United States reduced its money supply, all countries linked to gold suffered.

course_18_la_grande_depression_1929|Buyi.explanation: Practice of borrowing from one's bank to buy shares betting on their rise. Very widespread in the 1920s, it amplified the bubble and, during the crash, forced millions of Americans to sell urgently to repay their loans.

course_19_la_bataille_de_stalingrad_1942.explanation: The German invasion of the USSR: 3 million soldiers on a 3,000 km front, the largest military operation in history. Failing to take Moscow in 1941 pushed Hitler to shift his effort south in 1942, toward the oil of the Caucasus.

Commander of the surrounded German 6th Army. Hitler made him Field Marshal on January 30, 1943, to encourage him to die rather than surrender. Paulus capitulated the following day, becoming the first German Field Marshal to be captured alive.

Soviet counter-offensive (November 19 operations, 1942) which encircled the 300,000 soldiers of the 6th Army in a giant pincer movement. Planned by Zhukov and Vasilevsky, it transformed the fierce defense of Stalingrad into a decisive strategic victory.
The codename for the German army's summer offensive in 1942, aimed at the oil fields of the Caucasus.
The German air force, which played a crucial role in the initial bombings of Stalingrad.
Head of the Luftwaffe, he wrongly promised Hitler that his aircraft could resupply the encircled 6th Army by air.

course_20_hiroshima_et_nagasaki_1945|Nuc.explanation: A reaction in which the nucleus of a heavy atom (uranium 235, plutonium 239) splits, releasing colossal energy and new neutrons that trigger a chain reaction. This is the principle of the atomic bomb.

course_20_hiroshima_et_nagasaki_1945|The.explanation: Stalin declared war on Japan exactly on the day of the Nagasaki bomb, invading Manchuria. Some historians believe that this Soviet threat was as decisive as the bombs in the Japanese decision to surrender.

course_20_hiroshima_et_nagasaki_1945|Rad.explanation: A syndrome caused by exposure to radiation: nausea, hair loss, internal hemorrhaging, immune failure. Tens of thousands of survivors died in the following weeks from this disease, which was then unknown to doctors.

course_20_hiroshima_et_nagasaki_1945|Leó.explanation: Hungarian-born physicist who conceived the idea of a nuclear chain reaction and convinced Einstein to write to Roosevelt to launch the American atomic program.

course_20_hiroshima_et_nagasaki_1945|Jor.explanation: New Mexico desert where the Trinity test was conducted, chosen for its geographical isolation.

course_20_hiroshima_et_nagasaki_1945|Kam.explanation: Suicide attack units of the Imperial Japanese Army that crashed their planes into Allied ships to cause as much damage as possible.

course_20_hiroshima_et_nagasaki_1945|Pot.explanation: Conference held in July 1945 where the Allies (Truman, Stalin, Churchill/Attlee) discussed the fate of Japan and postwar Europe.

course_20_hiroshima_et_nagasaki_1945|Boc.explanation: Name of the B-29 bomber that dropped the 'Fat Man' atomic bomb on Nagasaki on August 9, 1945.

course_20_hiroshima_et_nagasaki_1945|Kok.explanation: The first target chosen for the second atomic bombing, spared by the weather, which forced the pilot to head for Nagasaki instead.

course_20_hiroshima_et_nagasaki_1945|Gyo.explanation: Radio address recorded by Emperor Hirohito and broadcast on August 15, 1945, announcing the unconditional surrender of Japan.

course_20_hiroshima_et_nagasaki_1945|Hib.explanation: Japanese term referring to the survivors of the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, victims of physical after-effects and discrimination.

course_20_hiroshima_et_nagasaki_1945|Nuc.explanation: Strategic doctrine based on the threat of using nuclear weapons to prevent an adversary from launching an attack.

course_20_hiroshima_et_nagasaki_1945|Sov.explanation: Stalin declared war on Japan exactly on the day of the Nagasaki bombing, invading Manchuria. Some historians believe that this Soviet threat was as decisive as the bombs in the Japanese decision to surrender.

course_21_rosa_parks_et_montgomery_1955|.explanation: National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, founded in 1909 to defend civil rights through legal means. Rosa Parks was an active member and had undergone civil disobedience training long before her famous gesture.

State laws that set up racial segregation in the American South after 1877. The name comes from a stock character in minstrel shows. They separated Black and white people completely in schools, transportation, hospitals, and every public space.

US Supreme Court ruling declaring segregation in public schools unconstitutional. This decision gave legal momentum to the Civil Rights Movement and explains why Montgomery was then also challenged in the courts.
1896 Supreme Court ruling that validated segregationist laws under the 'separate but equal' principle.
Socialist training and civil rights education center in Tennessee where Rosa Parks learned methods of non-violent resistance.
Historic federal law that ended all forms of racial segregation in public places and banned employment discrimination.

course_22_la_crise_des_missiles_de_cuba_.explanation: Nuclear doctrine stating that neither the United States nor the USSR could survive a nuclear war. This logic of balanced terror deterred everyone from attacking and structures the entire dynamic of the Cuban crisis.

Failed invasion attempt of Cuba by Cuban exiles trained by the CIA. The humiliating failure weakened Kennedy, encouraged Khrushchev to take risks and strengthened Castro, creating the conditions for the 1962 crisis.

American nuclear missiles installed in Turkey in 1961, within reach of the USSR. The final secret agreement included their discreet withdrawal - a concession that Kennedy kept secret for decades so as not to appear to be yielding to Soviet blackmail.
Codename for the secret Soviet operation to deploy troops, aircraft, and nuclear missiles to Cuba in 1962.
Period of the Cold War (1962-1979) characterized by a desire for dialogue, peaceful coexistence and nuclear arms limitation treaties.
NATO member country where the United States had installed Jupiter missiles, constituting one of the reasons for the Soviet response in Cuba.
Soviet intermediate-range ballistic missiles deployed in Cuba, capable of reaching most of the American territory.

course_23_la_guerre_d_algerie_1954_1962|.explanation: Unlike the protectorates (Morocco, Tunisia), Algeria had been three French departments since 1848. Any independence therefore legally amounted to an amputation of national territory - hence the intensity of the politics conflict in the metropole.

Coup d'état attempt by four generals opposed to independence. De Gaulle crushed it in four days thanks to a radio speech. It was followed by the creation of the OAS, a pro-French Algeria terrorist organization.

Nickname for settlers of European origin living in Algeria. Nearly a million of them had to leave the country in 1962 under traumatic conditions, abandoning their homes under the threat 'the suitcase or the coffin'.

Unlike the protectorates (Morocco, Tunisia), Algeria had been divided since 1848 into three French departments attached to the Ministry of the Interior. Any independence was therefore legally considered a secession from the national territory.
Law passed in 1956 by the French Parliament entrusting the army with full police powers in Algeria to fight against the nationalist insurrection.
Asymmetric combat technique practiced by the FLN, based on ambushes, attacks and the use of the population as a refuge, faced with a more powerful conventional army.
Failed coup attempt in Algiers in April 1961 by four generals (Challe, Jouhaud, Zeller, Salan) opposed to Charles de Gaulle's politics of self-determination.
Organisation de l'Armée Secrète. Clandestine terrorist organization supporting French Algeria which increased the number of attacks to prevent independence between 1961 and 1962.
Official end of military hostilities between two warring forces.
Muslim fighters recruited as auxiliaries in the French army. Abandoned by France in 1962, thousands were massacred in Algeria or confined to camps in mainland France.

Unlike the protectorates (Morocco, Tunisia), Algeria had been divided since 1848 into three French departments attached to the Ministry of the Interior. Any independence was therefore legally considered a secession from the national territory.

course_24_la_bataille_de_dien_bien_phu_1.explanation: Strategy of weak forces against a technically superior army: avoid pitched battles, harass the enemy, use the terrain and popular support, exhaust the opponent over the long term. The Viet-Minh excelled at it throughout the Indochina War.
Accords ending the Indochina War: Vietnam was divided at the 17th parallel. Reunification elections scheduled for 1956 were never held, sowing the seeds of the American war that was to follow.

General-in-chief of the Viet-Minh, former self-taught history teacher in strategy. His genius was to have dozens of heavy cannons transported by hand and bicycle up the hills overlooking Dien Bien Phu - a logistical feat considered impossible.
Founder of the Vietnamese Communist Party and the Viet Minh league. A leading figure in Vietnam's independence, he became the president of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam.
Northern part of present-day Vietnam, centered around Hanoi. It was the historical heart of the Viet Minh resistance during the Indochina War.
System of seasonal winds in Southeast Asia causing torrential rainfall from May to October, turning the Dien Bien Phu terrain into an impassable swamp.
Conflict (1955-1975) pitting North Vietnam (communist) against South Vietnam (supported by the United States), prolonging the tensions born from the 1954 division.

course_25_le_genocide_armenien_1915_1916.displayTerm: The Young Turks (Committee of Union and Progress)
course_25_le_genocide_armenien_1915_1916.explanation: Turkish nationalist movement that overthrew Sultan Abdul Hamid II in 1908. The Enver-Talaat-Cemal triumvirate, extremist nationalists, organized the genocide in the context of the war, in a project for an "ethnically pure Turkey".

First wave of Armenian massacres under Sultan Abdul Hamid II, causing between 100,000 and 300,000 deaths. This unsanctioned precedent showed future Ottoman authorities that such crimes could go unpunished.

The term "genocide" was coined by legal scholar Raphael Lemkin in 1944 specifically with Armenians in mind. The UN Convention (1948) defines it as the intent to destroy "in whole or in part" a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.
Ottoman administrative system organizing populations by religious denominations, offering a certain autonomy to minorities protected by the sultan.
Nationalist political party (the Committee of Union and Progress) that took power in 1908 and pushed its program toward a Pan-Turkism that shut out Christian minorities.
Dispersion of a people across the world after exile from their homeland. The Armenian diaspora was born from the flight of genocide survivors.
Physical, intentional, systematic, and programmed extermination of a human group because of its ethnic, religious, or social origins.

course_26_la_creation_de_l_onu_1945|The.explanation: Meeting between Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin laying the foundations of the post-war world order: division of Europe into zones of influence, conditions for Soviet entry against Japan, structure of the UN to be created.

course_26_la_creation_de_l_onu_1945|Veto.displayTerm: Veto power in the Security Council
course_26_la_creation_de_l_onu_1945|Veto.explanation: Each of the 5 permanent members can block any Council resolution with a single "no" vote. This mechanism paralyzed the Council during the Cold War and continues with Russia and China on many contemporary crises.

course_26_la_creation_de_l_onu_1945|The.explanation: The UN's judicial organ based in The Hague, which settles disputes between states. Unlike the ICC (which judges individuals), it judges states. Its decisions are binding but it has no enforcement mechanism.

course_26_la_creation_de_l_onu_1945|Glob.explanation: Attempt to regulate international relations through common rules and shared institutions to solve problems that cross the borders of a single state.

course_26_la_creation_de_l_onu_1945|Blue.explanation: Military personnel made available to the UN by member states to conduct peacekeeping operations in conflict zones.

course_26_la_creation_de_l_onu_1945|Isol.explanation: Foreign policy doctrine in which a state stays out of other countries' affairs in order to protect its independence and its immediate interests.

course_27_la_naissance_de_l_ue_de_la_cec.explanation: After three wars in 70 years, France and Germany had made their rivalry the main driver of European conflicts. The ECSC and then the Élysée Treaty (1963) sealed a friendship that became the engine of all European integration.

Founding treaty of the European Union creating European citizenship, launching the single currency process (the euro in 2002), establishing a common foreign policy and strict economic convergence criteria.

course_27_la_naissance_de_l_ue_de_la_cec.displayTerm: The four freedoms of the single market
course_27_la_naissance_de_l_ue_de_la_cec.explanation: Free movement of goods, people, services, and capital - foundations of the common market of the Treaty of Rome. They represent the deepest economic integration ever achieved between sovereign states.
Speech delivered on May 9, 1950, by Robert Schuman, considered the birth certificate of European construction.
Common Agricultural Policy, set up in 1962 to ensure Europe's food self-sufficiency and modernize its agriculture.
Supranational executive body of the ECSC, ancestor of the current European Commission, independent of national governments.
Economic area without customs borders where the four freedoms of movement (goods, people, services, capital) apply.

course_28_le_genocide_rwandais_1994|The.explanation: Peace agreement between the Hutu government and the RPF (Rwandan Patriotic Front). Hutu extremists, refusing any power-sharing, organized the genocide to prevent it from being implemented.

course_28_le_genocide_rwandais_1994|UNAM.explanation: The UN peacekeeping mission in Rwanda, commanded by the Canadian general Roméo Dallaire, had 2,500 soldiers on the ground. Dallaire warned the UN in January 1994 that a genocide was being prepared, but he was ordered not to act. That refusal is now seen as a historic failure of the UN.

course_28_le_genocide_rwandais_1994|Radi.displayTerm: Radio Télévision Libre des Mille Collines (RTLM)
course_28_le_genocide_rwandais_1994|Radi.explanation: Hutu extremist radio station that, during the genocide, broadcast live lists of people to be killed and called for the extermination of Tutsis, described as "cockroaches." It constituted a major tool for coordinating the massacres.

course_28_le_genocide_rwandais_1994|Rwan.explanation: Political and military movement formed by Tutsi exiles in Uganda. Led by Paul Kagame, it launched the offensive that ended the genocide in July 1994.

course_28_le_genocide_rwandais_1994|Hutu.explanation: Extremist ideology advocating Hutu supremacy and the physical elimination of Tutsis, considered foreign invaders.

course_28_le_genocide_rwandais_1994|Soma.explanation: Reference to the Battle of Mogadishu (1993) where American soldiers were killed, which cooled any willingness for American military intervention in Africa.

course_28_le_genocide_rwandais_1994|Turq.explanation: French military operation launched in June 1994 under a UN mandate, officially humanitarian, but whose role regarding fleeing perpetrators of the genocide remains controversial.

course_28_le_genocide_rwandais_1994|Zair.explanation: Former name of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), where millions of Hutus (refugees and perpetrators of the genocide) fled after the victory of the RPF.

course_28_le_genocide_rwandais_1994|Gaca.explanation: Rwandan community courts established to judge the perpetrators of the genocide and promote national reconciliation.

course_28_le_genocide_rwandais_1994|Inte.explanation: Jurisdiction established by the UN based in Arusha (Tanzania) to try the high-ranking officials responsible for the genocide.

course_29_la_chute_du_mur_de_berlin_1989.explanation: Gorbachev's reforms starting from 1986: glasnost (transparency) allowed criticism of the Soviet regime, while perestroika (restructuring) attempted to reform the economy. They unintentionally destabilized the entire Soviet bloc.
Liberal reform of communism in Czechoslovakia, crushed by the invasion of Soviet tanks. Gorbachev's decision not to repeat this intervention in 1989 was therefore historically revolutionary.

General Secretary of the GDR since 1971, he had declared that the Wall would last "another 50 or 100 years." Replaced on October 18, 1989, just before the fall of the Wall, he died in exile in Chile in 1994.
German Democratic Republic, a socialist state created in 1949 in the Soviet occupation zone, with East Berlin as its capital.
Expression popularized by Winston Churchill referring to the physical and ideological border separating Europe under Soviet influence from Western Europe.
Peaceful protest movement in Czechoslovakia (November-December 1989) which led to the end of the communist regime without major violence.

course_30_la_blitzkrieg_1940|The Maginot.explanation: Line of fortifications built by France in the 1930s along the Franco-German border. The Blitzkrieg bypassed it through the Belgian Ardennes, supposed to be impassable for tanks - making the Maginot Line totally useless.

course_30_la_blitzkrieg_1940|The Sichels.explanation: General von Manstein's plan: concentrate armored units in the Ardennes to break through the center and reach the English Channel, encircling the Franco-British armies engaged in Belgium. Bold and risky, this plan was a total success.

course_30_la_blitzkrieg_1940|Operation D.explanation: Maritime evacuation of 338,000 French and British soldiers surrounded at Dunkirk by an improvised flotilla of military and civilian vessels. This "miracle" allowed Great Britain to continue the war, but left France without an army.

course_30_la_blitzkrieg_1940|Wehrmacht.explanation: Name of the German army between 1935 and 1945, including the land army, the navy, and the air force.

course_30_la_blitzkrieg_1940|Schwerpunkt.explanation: Main application point of military effort during an offensive, aiming to concentrate force on a narrow area to break the front.

course_31_le_plan_marshall_1947_1952|The.explanation: Truman's speech (March 1947) asserting that the United States would support any people resisting "subjugation by outside pressures." It marked the official beginning of the Cold War and the politics of containment of communism.

International communist organization created by Stalin in response to the Marshall Plan, to coordinate European communist parties. It forced Czechoslovakia and Poland, which had accepted Marshall aid, to refuse it.

"Economic miracle" of West Germany: between 1950 and 1960, its GDP tripled, moving from an economy in ruins to the leading European economic power. Partly funded by the Marshall Plan and favored by the 1948 monetary reform.

course_31_le_plan_marshall_1947_1952|ERP.explanation: European Recovery Program, official name of the reconstruction program better known as the Marshall Plan.

course_31_le_plan_marshall_1947_1952|OEE.explanation: Organization for European Economic Cooperation, created in 1948 to coordinate how Marshall Plan aid was shared out among the countries receiving it.

course_31_le_plan_marshall_1947_1952|EEC.explanation: European Economic Community, the predecessor of the European Union, whose beginnings of economic cooperation date back to the collective management of the Marshall Plan.

course_32_la_guerre_du_vietnam_1955_1975.explanation: American foreign politics theory according to which if one country became communist, its neighbors would fall one after another. It justified the commitment in Vietnam to "stop communist progression in Southeast Asia."

Simultaneous attack by the Viet Cong on more than 100 American cities during the Vietnamese New Year. Militarily a failure for Hanoi, it destroyed the credibility of the Johnson administration in the United States.

Nationalist and communist leader, founder of the Viet-Minh (1941), first president of North Vietnam. His popular legitimacy as a liberator against the Japanese then the French gave him a politics advantage that the United States could never match.
Conflict (1946-1954) pitting France against the communist Viet Minh, resulting in French defeat and the independence of its former colonies.
Massive aerial bombardment campaign conducted by the US Air Force against North Vietnam between 1965 and 1968.
Military strategy aiming to flush out insurgents in the jungle to eliminate them through firepower rather than holding territorial positions.
Headquarters of the United States Department of Defense, by extension the American military command.
Massacre of hundreds of Vietnamese civilians by American soldiers in 1968, the revelation of which shocked world opinion.

Simultaneous Viet Cong attack on more than 100 American-held cities during the Vietnamese New Year. Militarily a failure for Hanoi, it destroyed the credibility of the Johnson administration in the United States.

course_33_le_proces_de_nuremberg_1945_19.explanation: Legal category invented at Nuremberg to designate the persecution and extermination of civilians. Unlike war crimes, they apply even in times of peace and have no statute of limitations. Nuremberg distinguished them for the first time.

Principle established at Nuremberg: individuals can be judged for international crimes even if they were acting on behalf of a state. "Obeying orders" is not an admissible defense - a founding principle of international criminal law.

Heir to the Nuremberg Principles, created in 2002 by the Rome Statute to judge genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. 124 countries have ratified it, but not the United States, Russia or China.
Body of rules governing relations between states and, since Nuremberg, defining individual responsibilities before the international community.
Name of the German air force under the Third Reich, led by Hermann Göring.
Agreement signed on August 8, 1945, establishing the procedural rules for the International Military Tribunal in Nuremberg.
Legal principle according to which someone cannot be condemned for an act that was not illegal at the time it was committed.
Massacre of Polish officers by the Soviets in 1940, which the USSR attempted to blame on the Germans during the Nuremberg trials.
Set of guidelines codified by the UN in 1950, notably asserting that no one is above international law, even a head of state.

course_34_la_decolonisation_panorama_194.explanation: Joint Roosevelt-Churchill declaration affirming the right of peoples to self-determination. Used by independence movements as an argument against their colonizers, it created an ideological contradiction that empires could not resolve.

First meeting of the independent countries of Asia and Africa (29 nations), which affirmed non-alignment and anti-colonialism. It marked the birth of the "Third World" as a force in international politics.
Term describing the forms of economic and politics domination exercised by former colonial powers over their formally independent ex-colonies, via multinationals, debt, and military bases.
Intergovernmental organization composed mainly of former territories of the British Empire, facilitating economic and politics cooperation.
Independence leader of Ghana and leading figure of Pan-Africanism, he became the country's first president in 1957.
French political regime (1946-1958) that collapsed under the pressure of the Algerian War.
Hero of the independence of the Belgian Congo, assassinated in 1961 with the alleged complicity of Western secret services.
Created in 1963 to promote the unity of African countries, it was replaced by the African Union in 2002.
Created in 1963 to promote the unity of African countries, it was replaced by the African Union in 2002.

course_35_l_apartheid_et_mandela_1948_19.explanation: "Homelands" to which Black people were assigned according to their ethnic group under apartheid. These non-viable territories represented 13% of South African territory for 80% of the population - a total geographical segregation.
Police opened fire on a peaceful demonstration against pass laws, killing 69 people. The global shock led to the banning of the ANC and pushed Mandela to create the armed wing of the resistance.

Instituted after 1994, it allowed perpetrators of apartheid crimes to obtain amnesty in exchange for a full public confession. Presided over by Desmond Tutu, it chose national reconciliation rather than trials.
Afrikaans term meaning 'separateness'. Political regime in force in South Africa from 1948 to 1994, based on systematic segregation and the domination of the white minority.
African National Congress. South African political movement founded in 1912 to defend the rights of Black people, which became a political party after 1994.
A set of judicial or non-judicial measures (such as the TRC) implemented to remedy mass human rights violations during a regime change or after a conflict.

course_36_la_revolution_culturelle_en_ch.explanation: Program of forced collectivization launched by Mao which caused the greatest famine in human history: between 15 and 55 million deaths. Its failure explains Mao's political sidelining and his need to regain control via the Cultural Revolution.

Young revolutionaries mobilized by Mao to attack the "four olds". They humiliated millions of teachers, doctors, intellectuals, and Party officials in public sessions of criticism and forced confession.
Twice purged during the Cultural Revolution, he became the de facto leader of China after Mao's death (1976) and the father of economic reforms. His pragmatism transformed China into a global power.
Handwritten wall poster in large characters, used in China for propaganda, political attacks, or public denunciation.
President of the People's Republic of China and number 2 of the regime, he was Mao's main target during the Cultural Revolution. Humiliated and tortured, he died in prison in 1969.
Armed forces of the People's Republic of China (PLA). It intervened starting in 1968 to end the chaos created by the Red Guards.
Last wife of Mao Zedong and influential member of the Gang of Four. She was the architect of the radical cultural politics during the Revolution.
Group of radical leaders who directed the purges of the Cultural Revolution. Their arrest in 1976 marks the end of the Maoist era.

course_37_la_shoah_mecanismes_d_un_genoc.explanation: A meeting of 15 high-ranking Nazi officials where the "Final Solution" was planned and coordinated: the systematic extermination of Europe's Jews through death camps. It showed that the genocide was a bureaucratically organized state decision.

SS mobile extermination units that followed the army during the invasion of the USSR. They shot approximately 1.5 million Soviet Jews. The Babi Yar massacre (33,771 deaths in two days) is the most famous example.

A philosophical concept developed during the Eichmann trial: the worst crimes can be committed by ordinary, bureaucratic individuals who "do their job" without reflecting on the moral consequences of their actions.
Term of Russian origin designating a violent, often deadly, attack led by a population against a Jewish community, with the tacit or active complicity of the authorities.
Forced process of isolation and grouping of a population in a closed and guarded neighborhood. Under the Nazis, ghettos served to isolate Jews before their deportation.
Generic term (grouping Roma and Sinti) designating populations persecuted by the Nazis on a racial basis. Between 250,000 and 500,000 of them were exterminated.
International institute for the memory of the Holocaust located in Jerusalem, dedicated to the study of the genocide and to honoring the victims as well as the Righteous Among the Nations.

course_38_le_11_septembre_2001|The Sovie.explanation: The United States armed the Afghan mujahideen to fight the Soviets. These Islamist networks, particularly Bin Laden's, trained and financed during the Cold War, subsequently became Al-Qaeda.

course_38_le_11_septembre_2001|Al-Qaeda.explanation: A terrorist organization founded by Osama bin Laden in 1988 to fight the Soviets in Afghanistan. Its vision: a global war against the West and the corrupt Arab regimes supported by it. September 11 was its largest operation.

course_38_le_11_septembre_2001|The Iraq.explanation: American invasion based on false information about weapons of mass destruction. It destabilized the Middle East, dismantled Iraqi state structures, and created the vacuum in which the Islamic State (ISIS) emerged.

course_38_le_11_septembre_2001|Saudi Ara.explanation: Kingdom that holds Islam's holy sites, Mecca and Medina. Bin Laden saw the stationing of American troops there in 1990 as a sacrilege, and it turned him into an outright enemy of the United States.

course_38_le_11_septembre_2001|Taliban.explanation: Islamist fundamentalist movement that ruled Afghanistan from 1996 to 2001. They provided refuge and training bases to Al-Qaeda before being overthrown by the coalition led by the United States.

course_38_le_11_septembre_2001|Enduring.explanation: Name of the military operation launched by the United States in October 2001 in response to the September 11 attacks, aiming to dismantle Al-Qaeda in Afghanistan.

course_38_le_11_septembre_2001|Guantanam.explanation: Military prison located on an American base in Cuba. It was created after September 11 to detain, outside the classical American legal framework, individuals suspected of terrorism.

course_38_le_11_septembre_2001|Saddam Hu.explanation: Dictator of Iraq from 1979 to 2003. Although he had no link with Al-Qaeda, he was overthrown by the United States in 2003 under the pretext of possessing weapons of mass destruction.

course_39_la_democratie_athenienne|Solon.explanation: Athenian statesman elected archon in 594 BC to resolve a social crisis. He canceled debts, abolished debt slavery, and reorganized the city by wealth rather than birth - the first step toward democracy.

course_39_la_democratie_athenienne|Cleis.explanation: Athenian reformer (508-507 BC) considered the true founder of democracy. He reorganized the city into 10 mixed geographical tribes, breaking traditional family solidarities in favor of political citizenship.

course_39_la_democratie_athenienne|Ostra.explanation: Athenian procedure by which citizens could vote to exile for 10 years a man judged dangerous for democracy. Names were inscribed on pottery shards (ostrakon). Its objective was preventive, not punitive.

course_39_la_democratie_athenienne|Polit.explanation: From the Greek 'polis' (the city). Refers to the art of managing the city's affairs and the space for common deliberation between citizens.

course_39_la_democratie_athenienne|Boule.explanation: Council composed of 500 citizens drawn by lot (50 per tribe) responsible for studying draft laws before their presentation to the Ecclesia.

course_39_la_democratie_athenienne|Misth.explanation: Financial allowance paid to Athenian citizens to compensate for the loss of income linked to the exercise of public duties (courts, assembly).

course_39_la_democratie_athenienne|Isego.explanation: The equal right for every citizen to speak before the assembly of the people (Ecclesia).

course_39_la_democratie_athenienne|Helia.explanation: The supreme popular court of Athens, whose members were chosen by lot from among volunteer citizens.

course_39_la_democratie_athenienne|Demag.explanation: An orator seeking to win the people's favor by flattering their passions rather than by appealing to their reason.

course_40_la_guerre_de_secession_america.explanation: Lincoln's decree freeing slaves in the Confederate States. It transformed the war into a moral crusade against slavery, prevented Great Britain from recognizing the Confederacy, and opened the army to Black soldiers.

course_40_la_guerre_de_secession_america.displayTerm: States' rights vs. the federal government
course_40_la_guerre_de_secession_america.explanation: Fundamental tension in American politics: Southern states claimed their right to decide for themselves on slavery against federal authority. This question structured the U.S. Constitution and continues to define American political debate.

Post-war period where the Southern states were placed under federal military control and the civil rights of former slaves were established. Its abandonment in 1877 led to the Jim Crow laws which lasted until the 1960s.
An American statesman, he was the sole president of the Confederate States of America (1861-1865) during the Civil War.
General-in-chief of the Union armies at the end of the war, he accepted Lee's surrender before becoming the 18th president of the United States.
The most famous Confederate general. Despite his tactical genius, he had to surrender at Appomattox in the face of the North's numerical and industrial superiority.
An amendment to the United States Constitution ratified in December 1865, officially abolishing slavery and involuntary servitude.
White supremacist terrorist organization founded in 1865 in Tennessee to violently oppose the rights of African Americans.

course_41_pourquoi_le_ciel_est_il_bleu|R.explanation: Phenomenon by which small molecules in the atmosphere scatter short wavelengths (blue, violet) much more than long ones (red). Described by Lord Rayleigh in 1871, it also explains why sunsets are red and orange.

course_41_pourquoi_le_ciel_est_il_bleu|T.explanation: White sunlight is composed of all the colors of the rainbow (from 380 nm for violet to 700 nm for red). Each color corresponds to a different wavelength that interacts differently with matter.

course_41_pourquoi_le_ciel_est_il_bleu|M.explanation: Phenomenon of light scattering by particles larger than the wavelength (dust, water droplets), explaining the white appearance of clouds or misty skies.

course_42_pourquoi_reve_t_on|REM sleep (.explanation: Sleep phase characterized by rapid eye movements, muscle paralysis, and intense brain activity close to wakefulness. This is the phase where the majority of dreams occur and where memory consolidation is most active.

course_42_pourquoi_reve_t_on|The Freudia.explanation: For Freud (The Interpretation of Dreams, 1900), dreams express repressed desires in symbolic form. This theory is now widely criticized by neurosciences, which instead attribute them a role in memory and emotional consolidation.

course_42_pourquoi_reve_t_on|Muscle aton.explanation: Temporary inhibition of voluntary muscle activity during REM sleep, aimed at preventing the body from mimicking dream movements.

course_42_pourquoi_reve_t_on|Limbic syst.explanation: Group of brain structures playing a major role in emotion management and memory formation, highly active during dreaming.

course_42_pourquoi_reve_t_on|Prefrontal.explanation: Anterior part of the brain responsible for executive functions (logic, planning) which is usually deactivated during dreaming, except during lucid dreams.

course_42_pourquoi_reve_t_on|Norepinephr.explanation: Neurotransmitter linked to stress and arousal, whose absence during REM sleep explains both the forgetting of dreams and their emotional therapeutic dimension.

course_42_pourquoi_reve_t_on|Encoding.explanation: Process of transforming external or internal information into a stable memory trace in the nervous system.

course_43_pourquoi_la_glace_flotte_t_ell.explanation: Weak attractive forces between water molecules, caused by the polarity of the H₂O molecule. In ice they lock into an orderly, airy crystal structure that takes up more room than liquid water, which is why ice is less dense.

Contrary to almost all substances, water is denser at 4°C than at 0°C. When cooling from 4°C to 0°C, it expands. This anomaly is essential to aquatic life: ice floats and insulates the liquid water beneath it.
Liquid organic compound whose solid state is denser than its liquid state, illustrating the 'normal' behavior of substances unlike water.
Microscopic living beings (bacteria, plankton) whose winter survival depends directly on the insulating layer formed by ice on the surface.
The reflective power of a surface. Ice has a high albedo, reflecting solar energy back into space, which cools the planet.

Unlike almost all substances, water is denser at 4°C than at 0°C. As it cools from 4°C to 0°C, it expands. This density anomaly of water is essential for aquatic life: ice floats and insulates the liquid water beneath it.

course_44_pourquoi_l_eau_de_mer_est_elle.displayTerm: The hydrological cycle and salt accumulation
course_44_pourquoi_l_eau_de_mer_est_elle.explanation: Water evaporates from the oceans, leaving salts behind. It falls back as rain, dissolves minerals from rocks, and transports them back to the oceans via rivers. This accumulation process has been ongoing for 4 billion years.

Global system of deep ocean currents driven by differences in temperature and salinity. Dense salinity causes cold water to sink, creating a "conveyor belt" that transports heat around the globe and regulates the climate.
Molten rock located beneath the Earth's surface, whose heat feeds underwater hydrothermal vents.
A solid sedimentary deposit formed by the evaporation of ancient seas or lagoons, also known as halite.
A warm surface ocean current originating in the Gulf of Mexico that warms the climate of Western Europe.
A tectonic depression home to the Jordan River and the Dead Sea, located between Israel, Jordan, and Palestine.

Water evaporates from the oceans, leaving salts behind. It falls back as rain, dissolves minerals from rocks, and carries them to the oceans via rivers. This accumulation process has been ongoing for 4 billion years.

course_45_pourquoi_y_a_t_il_des_saisons|.explanation: The 23.5° tilt of Earth's axis relative to its orbital plane - and not the distance from the Sun - causes the seasons. The same tilt always points toward the North Star, alternately creating solstices and equinoxes.

The points in the orbit closest to (perihelion, in January) and farthest from (aphelion, in July) the Sun. The difference in distance is 5%, too small to explain the seasons. Paradoxically, the northern winter coincides with the perihelion.
The geometric shape of the Earth's orbit, resembling a slightly flattened circle.
The imaginary plane containing Earth's orbit around the Sun.
The time of year when the Sun reaches its northernmost or southernmost position relative to the equator, marking the start of summer or winter.
The ratio between the length of day and the length of night over 24 hours.

course_46_comment_les_avions_volent_ils|.explanation: The cross-sectional shape of the wing, with a curved upper surface and a flatter lower surface. This asymmetry forces the air to move faster above than below, creating a pressure difference that generates lift.

In a fluid in movement, where the speed increases, the pressure decreases. The air moving faster on the upper surface of the wing exerts less pressure than on the lower surface, creating an upward "suction" that lifts the plane.
Daniel Bernoulli (1700-1782), a Swiss mathematician whose principle explains how the speed of a fluid influences its pressure.
The action of the wing forcing the airflow downward, generating an upward thrust by reaction (Newton's 3rd law).
A sudden loss of lift occurring when the angle of attack is too high, causing the separation of airflow on the upper surface.
Side control stick used by the pilot to transmit instructions to the electric flight systems.

course_47_pourquoi_baille_t_on|Cerebral.explanation: Most serious current theory: yawning cools the brain by inhaling fresh air and stretching cranial vessels. This would explain why we yawn more when the ambient temperature is high.

course_47_pourquoi_baille_t_on|Mirror ne.explanation: Contagious yawning is linked to mirror neurons and contagiousness which mimic observed behaviors. Humans are more sensitive to the yawns of people they know, and autistic children are less sensitive to them - evidence of a link with empathy.

course_47_pourquoi_baille_t_on|Andrew Ga.explanation: Researcher in evolutionary psychology who formalized the brain thermoregulation theory as the primary function of yawning.

course_47_pourquoi_baille_t_on|Frontal s.explanation: Air-filled cavities located in the forehead bones. The air circulating there while yawning is thought to help cool the blood vessels near the brain.

course_47_pourquoi_baille_t_on|Synaptoge.explanation: Process of forming synapses between neurons in the nervous system. Fetal yawning is thought to help stimulate this development.

course_47_pourquoi_baille_t_on|Biomarker.explanation: A biological signal you can measure, such as how often a movement occurs, used to judge the health or the stage of development of a living thing.

course_47_pourquoi_baille_t_on|Autonomic.explanation: Part of the nervous system responsible for the body's automatic functions (heart rate, digestion, breathing).

course_48_comment_fonctionne_la_memoire|.explanation: A sea-horse-shaped brain structure in the temporal lobe, essential for the formation of new conscious memories. Its surgical removal (case H.M.) results in a total inability to form new memories, without erasing old ones.

Cognitive system that temporarily maintains a small amount of information (7±2 items) available for current processing. Managed by the Prefrontal cortex, it is limited in capacity and duration (a few seconds without repetition).
The brain's ability to modify the organization of its neural networks based on experience, notably by strengthening or weakening synaptic connections.
Outer part of the cerebral hemisphere involved in higher cognitive functions (language, consciousness, long-term storage).

Seahorse-shaped brain structure in the temporal lobe, essential for forming new conscious memories. Its surgical removal (case H.M.) leads to a total inability to form new memories, without erasing old ones.

course_49_pourquoi_a_t_on_des_frissons|T.explanation: Branch of the autonomic nervous system that prepares the body for action ("fight or flight"). Faced with a threat, it triggers adrenaline, accelerates the heart, dilates the pupils, and contracts the arrector pili muscles - the chills of fear.

course_49_pourquoi_a_t_on_des_frissons|C.explanation: A series of rapid and involuntary muscle contractions intended to produce heat or reflecting strong nervous excitement.

course_49_pourquoi_a_t_on_des_frissons|T.explanation: Part of the nervous system responsible for the body's automatic functions (digestion, heart rate, temperature) without voluntary control.

course_49_pourquoi_a_t_on_des_frissons|H.explanation: Structure located at the base of the brain that regulates vital functions such as hunger, thirst, or body temperature (the biological thermostat).

course_49_pourquoi_a_t_on_des_frissons|D.explanation: Chemical neurotransmitter in the brain playing a central role in the reward circuit, pleasure, and motivation.

course_50_comment_le_savon_tue_t_il_les_.explanation: A molecule with one hydrophilic end (water-loving) and one hydrophobic end (fat-loving). This dual nature allows it to insert itself into the lipid membranes of viruses and physically disintegrate them.

Certain viruses (coronavirus, influenza, HIV) are surrounded by a fatty membrane. This is their weak point: soap dissolves it, destroying the virus. Non-enveloped viruses (norovirus, poliovirus) are more resistant to soap.
Rigid protein shell that protects the genetic material of viruses, particularly resistant in so-called 'naked' viruses.
Substances capable of modifying the surface tension between two surfaces, allowing soap to mix water and fatty substances.
Oily substance secreted by the skin's sebaceous glands, in which viruses and bacteria can remain trapped.
Spherical clusters of soap molecules trapping fatty substances (or viral debris) at their center to isolate them from water.

A molecule with one hydrophilic end (water-loving) and one hydrophobic end (fat-loving). This double nature allows it to insert itself into the lipid membranes of viruses and physically disintegrate them.

Some viruses (coronavirus, flu, HIV) are surrounded by a fatty membrane. This is their weak point: soap dissolves it, destroying the virus. Non-enveloped viruses (norovirus, poliovirus) are more resistant to soap.

course_51_la_decouverte_de_la_penicillin.displayTerm: Howard Florey and Ernst Boris Chain
course_51_la_decouverte_de_la_penicillin.explanation: Oxford researchers who purified penicillin starting in 1939 and tested it on humans in 1941. Without their work, Fleming's discovery would have remained a laboratory curiosity. They shared the 1945 Nobel Prize with Fleming.

An evolutionary phenomenon by which bacteria develop mechanisms to resist antibiotics. Predicted by Fleming as early as 1945, it now kills 1.27 million people per year - one of the main health threats of the 21st century.
Australian pharmacologist who, with Ernst Chain, transformed Fleming's observation into a stable and injectable medicine on an industrial scale.
A serious sexually transmitted infection, once an incurable plague, which was the first major successful target of penicillin.
A genus of bacteria responsible for various infections in humans, some strains of which are now famous for their resistance to treatments.

A spontaneous phenomenon by which an unstable atomic nucleus transforms by emitting particles (alpha, beta) or radiation (gamma). Marie Curie understood that radioactivity was a property of the atom itself, not a chemical reaction.

course_52_la_decouverte_de_l_electricite.explanation: Self-taught British physicist who discovered electromagnetic induction (1831): a varying magnetic field generates an electric current. This principle is the basis of all modern electric generators and transformers.

course_52_la_decouverte_de_l_electricite.displayTerm: The War of Currents (Edison vs. Tesla)
course_52_la_decouverte_de_l_electricite.explanation: Edison championed direct current (DC), Tesla and Westinghouse alternating current (AC). AC won because it can be transported over long distances. Edison organized public electrocutions of animals to demonstrate the "danger" of AC.
