An ancient Greek term referring to yellow amber, whose property of attraction after friction gave electricity its name.
An aqueous solution of salt (sodium chloride) used by Volta in his battery to allow the passage of electrical charges between the metal disks.

course_53_la_decouverte_des_rayons_x_ron.explanation: Röntgen and his first users were unaware of the dangers of X-rays. Doctors developed cancers after years of exposure. Marie Curie herself died of aplastic anemia caused by her years of contact with radioactive materials.

course_53_la_decouverte_des_rayons_x_ron.displayTerm: The "Little Curies" during World War I
course_53_la_decouverte_des_rayons_x_ron.explanation: Marie Curie equipped 20 mobile radiography trucks that traveled the French front, saving countless lives by making it possible to locate bullets without exploratory surgery. These vehicles were nicknamed "little Curies".
A negative electrode from which electrons are emitted in a vacuum tube.
A positive electrode that receives electrons and emits X-rays after thermal shock.
Necrosis of living tissue caused by an infection or a cessation of blood supply.
Skin lesion caused by excessive exposure to ionizing radiation.
Blood and bone marrow cancers, often linked at the time to chronic irradiation.
Natural physical phenomenon by which unstable atomic nuclei spontaneously transform by emitting radiation.
Celestial objects so dense that their gravitational force prevents any matter or light from escaping, emitting violent X-rays during the absorption of matter.
Massive stellar explosions signaling the death of a very massive star, releasing colossal energy in the form of X-ray radiation.

course_54_la_decouverte_du_micro_ondes_p.explanation: A self-taught engineer at Raytheon, orphaned at 18 months, with no degree. His curiosity led him to test magnetrons on food after feeling his chocolate bar melt. He filed several hundred patents during his career.
Electromagnetic waves with a wavelength intermediate between infrared and radio waves, used for both telecommunications and heating food.
The 2.45 GHz frequency, adopted worldwide for domestic ovens to ensure sufficient energy penetration into biological tissues without major interference.
Polar molecules (H2O) that react to the alternating electromagnetic field of microwaves by rotating on themselves.

course_55_la_theorie_de_la_gravitation_n.explanation: Astronomer (1571-1630) who worked out the three laws of planetary motion from observation: elliptical orbits, equal areas swept in equal times, and the square of the orbital period tied to the size of the orbit. Newton later supplied the law of gravitation that explained all three.

General Relativity (1915) surpassed Newton: gravity is not a force but a curvature of space-time caused by mass. It predicts phenomena that Newton could not explain: the precession of Mercury, the deflection of light, gravitational waves.
Newton's work (1687) laying the foundations of classical physics and introducing the law of universal gravitation.
Astronomical model inherited from Antiquity placing the Earth, motionless, at the center of the universe.
Danish astronomer (1546-1601) whose precise observations of the planets allowed Kepler to establish his laws.
Latin phrase by Newton meaning 'I feign no hypotheses', expressing his refusal to speculate on the hidden nature of gravity without mathematical proof.
Theoretical physicist (1879-1955) whose theories of special and general Relativity complemented and surpassed Newton's mechanics.

course_56_la_decouverte_de_la_radioactiv.explanation: French physicist who discovered radioactivity in 1896 almost by accident: uranium salts had fogged a photographic plate through black paper. He shared the 1903 Nobel Prize with the Curies.

Spontaneous phenomenon by which an unstable atomic nucleus transforms by emitting particles (alpha, beta) or radiation (gamma). Marie Curie understood that radioactivity was a property of the atom itself, not a chemical reaction.
Clandestine educational organization in Poland at the end of the 19th century, intended to brave Russian censorship and allow the education of women.
Black and dark uranium ore from which the Curies isolated polonium and radium.
Medical technique using radioactive sources placed internally or in the immediate vicinity of the area to be treated (often cancers).
Rare and serious disease where the bone marrow stops producing enough new blood cells, often caused by prolonged exposure to radiations.

An evolutionary phenomenon by which bacteria develop mechanisms to resist antibiotics. Predicted by Fleming as early as 1945, it now kills 1.27 million people per year - one of the main health threats of the 21st century.

course_57_l_invention_d_internet|The TCP.explanation: A set of rules defining how data is broken down into packets, addressed, transmitted, and reassembled. Invented by Cerf and Kahn (1974), it is the "universal language" that allows heterogeneous networks to communicate with each other.

course_57_l_invention_d_internet|The lau.explanation: The first Soviet artificial satellite, its launch created a shockwave in the United States. This fear led to the creation of ARPA and, indirectly, ARPANET - the ancestor of the Internet - to maintain decentralized communications in the event of a nuclear attack.

course_57_l_invention_d_internet|CERN.explanation: European Organization for Nuclear Research, located in Geneva, where the Web was invented to facilitate data sharing between physicists.

course_57_l_invention_d_internet|Globali.explanation: Process of market integration and interdependence of economies and cultures on a global scale, greatly facilitated by the Internet.

course_57_l_invention_d_internet|Sputnik.explanation: First artificial satellite sent into space by the USSR in 1957, provoking the American reaction that would lead to the creation of ARPA.

course_58_la_structure_de_l_adn_watson_c.explanation: A crystallographer whose Photo 51 (an X-ray diffraction image of DNA) was passed to Watson and Crick without her consent. She had understood the helical structure, but the data was "borrowed" from her. Having died in 1958, she could not receive the 1962 Nobel Prize.

The process by which the double helix unwinds and each strand serves as a template for the synthesis of a complementary strand. This mechanism ensures the faithful transmission of genetic information during each cell division.
Swiss biologist who first isolated a substance he called "nuclein" (DNA) in the nuclei of white blood cells in 1869.
Analytical technique used to determine the atomic structure of a crystal by observing how it deflects a beam of X-rays.
Method used to determine the precise order of nitrogenous bases (A, T, C, G) all along a DNA molecule.
Genius American chemist, rival to Watson and Crick, who mistakenly proposed a triple helix structure for DNA shortly before 1953.

course_59_la_decouverte_de_l_anesthesie|.explanation: An American dentist who performed the first public demonstration of ether anesthesia in 1846. He attempted to patent it under a code name, but the process was too simple - it spread freely throughout the world in a few months.

Even before anesthesia, post-operative infections killed patients. Semmelweis (1847) then Lister (1867) imposed hygiene: hand washing, sterilized instruments. These two revolutions - anesthesia and antisepsis - transformed surgery.
Bodies of knowledge with universal reach, each with its own subject and method, built on relationships that can be checked.
State of acute circulatory failure caused, in this context, by pain of an intensity unbearable for the nervous system.
Technique of animal magnetism developed by Franz-Friedrich-Anton Mesmer, ancestor of hypnosis, sometimes used in the 19th century to try to reduce pain.
Colorless and flammable liquid whose inhaled vapors were the first effective general anesthetic agent used in surgery.
Liquid chemical compound discovered in 1831, used as a general anesthetic after ether, notably for its potency and speed of action.
Scottish physician who popularized the use of chloroform in obstetrics and surgery starting in 1847.
Sovereign of the United Kingdom whose use of chloroform during her childbirths in 1853 and 1857 helped lift religious taboos on anesthesia.
The triumph of the capture of Granada released resources and created a momentum of national ambition that explains Isabella of Castile's support for Columbus.
An agreement arbitrated by the Pope dividing the world into two spheres of influence between Spain (west) and Portugal (east).
Sovereign of the United Kingdom whose use of chloroform during her childbirths in 1853 and 1857 helped to remove religious taboos regarding anesthesia.

course_60_la_theorie_de_l_evolution_de_d.explanation: A naturalist who independently developed a theory identical to Darwin's in 1858. His letter precipitated the publication of On the Origin of Species. Their joint presentation to the Linnean Society established their shared priority - Wallace is often forgotten.

Darwinian mechanism: individuals carrying advantageous variations survive and reproduce better, passing these traits to their offspring. Over millennia, this process creates adaptations and new species.
Royal Navy ship that served as the base for Charles Darwin's scientific tour of the world between 1831 and 1836.
Nicknamed 'Darwin's finches', these thirteen species of birds from the Galápagos served as crucial evidence to demonstrate the adaptation of species to their environment.
Anglican Bishop of Oxford, famous for his virulent opposition to Darwin's theory during a historical debate in 1860.
British biologist nicknamed 'Darwin's bulldog' for his zeal in defending and spreading the theory of evolution.
Molecule carrying genetic information, the understanding of which allowed for the validation and explanation of the mechanisms of hereditary transmission theorized by Darwin.
Royal Navy ship that served as a base for Charles Darwin for his scientific tour of the world between 1831 and 1836.

course_61_le_big_bang|The cosmic microwa.explanation: Fossil radiation emitted 380,000 years after the Big Bang, when the universe cooled sufficiently. Detected by Penzias and Wilson in 1965 (Nobel 1978), it is one of the most direct proofs of the Big Bang - a sort of "echo" of the birth of the universe.

course_61_le_big_bang|The accelerated ex.displayTerm: The accelerated expansion of the universe
course_61_le_big_bang|The accelerated ex.explanation: Discovered in 1998, the expansion of the universe is accelerating instead of slowing down. This acceleration is attributed to "dark energy" (68% of the total content of the universe), which remains completely misunderstood by current physics.

course_61_le_big_bang|singularity.explanation: Point in space-time where density and curvature become infinite, making current laws of physics inapplicable.

course_61_le_big_bang|primordial nucleos.explanation: Process that took place during the first minutes of the universe, leading to the formation of light atomic nuclei (hydrogen, helium, lithium).

course_61_le_big_bang|supernovae.explanation: Titanic explosions marking the death of certain stars, used as 'standard candles' to measure cosmic distances and expansion.

course_61_le_big_bang|accelerated expans.explanation: Discovered in 1998, the expansion of the universe is accelerating instead of slowing down. This acceleration is attributed to "Dark energy" (68% of the total content of the universe), which remains completely misunderstood by current physics.

course_62_pourquoi_les_volcans_entrent_i.explanation: Theory established in the 1960s: the Earth's surface is divided into rigid plates that move. Volcanoes form at plate boundaries (subduction zones, ridges) or above hotspots like Hawaii.

Process by which an oceanic plate sinks beneath a lighter continental plate. As it descends, it melts and generates magma that rises to the surface. The Pacific "Ring of Fire" results from subduction all around the ocean.
Underwater mountain ranges located at the boundary of two tectonic plates that are moving apart, allowing magma to rise and create new oceanic crust.
A mixture of hot gases, ash, and rock fragments that rushes down the flanks of a volcano at speeds exceeding 100 km/h during explosive eruptions.
A volcanic structure capable of producing eruptions with a volume greater than 1,000 km3, often characterized by an immense caldera rather than a classic cone.
Hydrothermal vents located on the seabed that discharge fluids rich in minerals and metals at very high temperatures.

course_63_comment_se_forment_les_tremble.explanation: A 1,300 km fault running through California: the Pacific plate slides northwest relative to the North American plate at 6 cm/year. Los Angeles is moving closer to San Francisco - they will be neighbors in 15 million years.
Logarithmic measurement of the energy released by an earthquake. Each degree represents 31.6 times more energy: a magnitude 8 earthquake releases 1,000 times more energy than a 6.
A geodynamic process where an oceanic tectonic plate sinks beneath another plate (oceanic or continental) before plunging into the Earth's mantle.
A geodynamic process where an oceanic tectonic plate sinks beneath another plate (oceanic or continental) before plunging into the Earth's mantle.
The ductile part of the Earth's upper mantle located beneath the rigid lithosphere, allowing for the movement of tectonic plates.
Field of civil engineering studying the design and construction of buildings capable of resisting seismic shocks without collapsing.
Name of an extensive European project and sensor network aiming to use existing undersea fiber optics to detect seismic vibrations on the ocean floor.
Ductile part of the Earth's upper mantle located beneath the rigid lithosphere, allowing the movement of tectonic plates.

course_64_la_catastrophe_de_tchernobyl_1.explanation: Water-cooled and graphite-moderated nuclear reactor. Its design included a fatal flaw: at low power, it became unstable and could run away. This flaw, known to Soviet engineers, was concealed for ideological reasons.

Area evacuated in an emergency after the accident. Paradoxically, 40 years later, it has become one of the most important nature reserves in Europe: the total absence of human activity benefits wildlife despite residual contamination.
International Nuclear Event Scale, ranging from 1 (anomaly) to 7 (major accident). Chernobyl and Fukushima are the only two level 7 events.
Name given to the civil and military personnel dispatched to the site after the explosion to decontaminate the area and build the first sarcophagus.
Last leader of the USSR (1985-1991), he admitted that Chernobyl had been one of the triggering factors of the collapse of the Soviet Union.
World Association of Nuclear Operators, an organization created in 1989 to promote global nuclear safety through the exchange of information between operators.

course_65_pourquoi_la_lune_ne_tombe_t_el.explanation: Every mass attracts every other mass, with a force inversely proportional to the square of the distance. The same force explains the falling of the apple and the Moon's orbit - Newton unified terrestrial and celestial physics for the first time.

Since lunar gravity is stronger on the side of the Earth facing it, it creates ocean tides. Conversely, the Earth has slowed the Moon's rotation until synchronization occurred - which is why we always see the same face of the Moon.
Minimum velocity a body must reach to stay in orbit around a celestial body without crashing into it or escaping from it.
Property of a body to maintain its speed and direction in the absence of external force, pushing it to move in a straight line in space.
Precise speed at which the centrifugal force exactly compensates for the gravitational attraction force.

course_66_y_a_t_il_de_la_vie_ailleurs_da.explanation: Region around a star where the temperature allows water to exist in liquid form on the surface of a planet. Neither too close nor too far - "just like Goldilocks". Our solar system has three potential planets: Venus, Earth, Mars.

Probabilistic formula by Frank Drake (1961) to estimate the number of communicating civilizations in our galaxy. It multiplies factors (stars, habitable planets, duration of civilizations...) - all very uncertain values, making the equation more philosophical than scientific.
Scientific discipline that studies the conditions and processes allowing life to appear in the Universe, as well as its detection.
Gravitational effects exerted by a massive celestial body on another, causing deformations and internal heating through friction.
Substances, structures, or phenomena providing scientific evidence of past or present life (e.g., simultaneous oxygen and methane in an atmosphere).
Hypothesis according to which an extremely difficult evolutionary barrier exists, explaining the rarity of advanced civilizations.
Hypothesis according to which an extremely difficult evolutionary barrier exists, explaining the rarity of advanced civilizations.
Theory suggesting that advanced civilizations observe us from a distance without interfering, to let us evolve naturally.
Study of the light spectrum to determine the chemical and physical composition of the matter that is emitting or being passed through.

Region around a star where the temperature allows water to exist in a liquid state on a planet's surface. Neither too close nor too far - "like Goldilocks". Our solar system has three potential planets: Venus, Earth, Mars.

Probabilistic formula by Frank Drake (1961) to estimate the number of communicating civilizations in our galaxy. It multiplies factors (stars, habitable planets, duration of civilizations...) - all values being very uncertain, making the equation more philosophical than scientific.

course_67_qu_est_ce_qu_un_trou_noir|The.explanation: The "boundary" of a black hole beyond which nothing can return, not even light. It is not a physical surface but a mathematical limit: the speed required to escape exceeds that of light.

Point at the center of a black hole where density theoretically becomes infinite. The equations of known physics cease to function there - a quantum theory of gravity (not yet developed) would be necessary to describe what happens there.

course_67_qu_est_ce_qu_un_trou_noir|Accr.explanation: Structure of gas and dust rotating around a massive object (such as a black hole), heated by friction and shining intensely.

course_67_qu_est_ce_qu_un_trou_noir|Inte.explanation: Technique consisting of combining signals from several distant telescopes to obtain a resolution equivalent to that of a giant telescope.

course_67_qu_est_ce_qu_un_trou_noir|Hawk.explanation: Theoretical thermal radiation emitted by black holes due to quantum effects, leading to their very slow evaporation.

course_67_qu_est_ce_qu_un_trou_noir|Even.explanation: "Boundary" of a black hole beyond which nothing can return, not even light. It is not a physical surface but a mathematical limit: the speed required to escape exceeds that of light.

course_68_la_theorie_de_la_relativite_po.explanation: Equivalence between mass and energy: a small mass corresponds to an enormous energy, amplified by the square of the speed of light (300,000 km/s). This is the principle behind the atomic bomb and nuclear energy.

Time runs more slowly for an object moving fast or sitting in a strong gravitational field. GPS satellites correct for this shift of 45 microseconds a day; without the correction, their accuracy would drift by 11 km a day.
English physicist (1643-1727) who formulated the law of universal gravitation, seeing gravity as a force of attraction between masses.
Branch of physics studying the nucleus of atoms and the resulting reactions, based on mass-energy equivalence (E=mc²).
Celestial objects so dense that their gravitational field prevents any form of matter or radiation from escaping.
Branch of astronomy that studies celestial bodies by observing the radio waves they emit.
Cosmological model describing the origin and evolution of the Universe from a phase of extreme density and temperature.

course_69_comment_se_forment_les_eclairs.explanation: In storm clouds, updrafts push ice crystals upward and heavy droplets downward. Their friction creates a potential difference of 100 to 300 million volts between the bottom of the cloud and the ground.

For lightning to form, the electric field must be intense enough to strip electrons from air molecules, making it conductive. This channel forms in a few microseconds, heated to 30,000°C - five times the surface of the Sun.
Cloud of great vertical development, anvil-shaped, responsible for storm phenomena, hail, and lightning.
Ice particle smaller and denser than hail, formed by the freezing of raindrops, playing a key role in cloud electrification.
Phenomenon of electrostatic charging created by friction or collision between two materials of different natures.
Red-colored lightning occurring above thunderstorms in the mesosphere, very brief and difficult to observe with the naked eye.
Red-colored lightning occurring above thunderstorms in the mesosphere, very brief and difficult to observe with the naked eye.
Rapidly expanding luminous disks appearing in the upper atmosphere during powerful lightning strikes, due to electromagnetic pulses.

For a lightning bolt to form, the electric field must be intense enough to strip electrons from air molecules, making it conductive. This channel forms in a few microseconds, heated to 30,000°C - five times the sun's surface.

course_71_qu_est_ce_que_l_effet_de_serre.explanation: Gases that absorb infrared radiation emitted by the Earth and re-emit it, warming the atmosphere. The main ones are: water vapor (natural), CO₂, methane (CH₄, 80x more powerful than CO₂ over 20 years), and N₂O.

The ability of a surface to reflect solar radiation. Ice and snow have a high albedo (reflect a lot), oceans have a low albedo (absorb more). Melting ice reduces the global albedo, accelerating warming.
Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, created in 1988 to assess scientific information related to climate change.
Part of a soil permanently frozen for at least two consecutive years, storing huge amounts of organic carbon.
Geological epoch spanning from approximately 5.3 to 2.5 million years before the present, often used as a comparison point for current CO2 levels.
Natural warming process of a planet by its atmosphere, where certain gases adsorb and re-emit thermal radiation from the surface.

course_72_pourquoi_dort_on|The glymphati.explanation: A network of brain channels that opens during deep sleep to drain metabolic waste from the brain, notably beta-amyloid proteins linked to Alzheimer's disease. Chronic lack of sleep is correlated with an increased risk of dementia.

course_72_pourquoi_dort_on|Circadian rhy.explanation: Internal clock set to 24 hours, regulated by the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the brain. Melatonin, produced at night, signals the need to sleep. Artificial nocturnal light disrupts this rhythm and degrades sleep quality.

course_72_pourquoi_dort_on|Microsleeps.explanation: Involuntary sleep episodes lasting from fractions of a second to 30 seconds, occurring during severe sleep deprivation.

course_72_pourquoi_dort_on|Neocortex.explanation: Outer area of the brain involved in higher functions (perception, reasoning, language) where long-term memories are stored.

course_72_pourquoi_dort_on|Cytokines.explanation: Cell signaling substances produced notably during sleep to regulate the immune response against infections.

course_72_pourquoi_dort_on|REM sleep.explanation: Sleep phase characterized by intense brain activity, rapid eye movement, and muscle paralysis, associated with dreams.

course_72_pourquoi_dort_on|paradoxical s.explanation: Sleep phase characterized by intense brain activity, rapid eye movement, and muscle paralysis, associated with dreams.

course_72_pourquoi_dort_on|Synaptogenesi.explanation: Process of forming synapses (connections) between neurons, particularly intense during sleep in newborns.

course_73_comment_le_cerveau_stocke_t_il.explanation: The lasting strengthening of synapses between neurons that activate together: "neurons that fire together, wire together". This is the molecular mechanism of learning, notably involving the NMDA receptor.
A form of automatic memory that allows for the learning of gestures and motor skills without a conscious effort of recall.
Region of the brain located behind the temples, housing the hippocampus and involved in processing memories and auditory information.

course_74_pourquoi_certaines_especes_son.explanation: Repeated DNA sequences at the ends of chromosomes, which shorten with each cell division. When they become too short, the cell stops dividing and dies. Telomerase can lengthen them - cancer cells use it to make themselves "immortal".

A tiny jellyfish capable of returning to its juvenile polyp stage after the adult stage - and starting over indefinitely. This process of cellular transdifferentiation is unique and inspires research on cellular reprogramming.
Acronym for 'mammalian Target of Rapamycin', a protein that regulates cell growth in response to nutrients. Its overactivity is linked to premature aging.
Undifferentiated cells capable of dividing indefinitely and specializing into different types of cells to repair tissues.
Study of modifications that influence gene expression without changing the DNA sequence, often compared to a 'software layer' that alters with age.

A tiny jellyfish capable of returning to its juvenile polyp stage after the adult stage - and starting over indefinitely. This process of cellular transdifferentiation is unique and inspires research on cellular reprogramming.

course_75_la_photosynthese_expliquee_sim.explanation: A green pigment contained in chloroplasts. It absorbs red and blue light (reflecting green, hence the color of plants) to power the light-dependent phase of photosynthesis.

The "dark" phase of photosynthesis, occurring in the stroma of chloroplasts. It uses the ATP produced during the light phase to reduce atmospheric CO₂ into glucose - the central reaction of plant nutrition.
Small adjustable openings on the epidermis of leaves that allow gas exchange (CO2, O2) and plant transpiration.
Adenosine triphosphate. A universal molecule that serves as the primary energy carrier within living cells.
High-energy electron carrier molecule used in the chemical reactions of glucose synthesis.

course_76_pourquoi_les_feuilles_changent.explanation: Red and purple pigments synthesized in the autumn in leaves. Unlike the carotenoids already present, anthocyanins are newly produced. Their probable role: to protect the leaf during nutrient recovery before it falls.

A layer of cells that forms at the base of the petiole in autumn, blocking the circulation of nutrients. In response to the shortening of days, it develops progressively until it causes the leaf to fall.
Protein photoreceptors in plants used to detect light variations and adjust their biological cycle (flowering, leaf drop).
Brown and bitter phenolic substances that remain in dead leaves once all other pigments have degraded.
Parasitic insects of plants; according to the honest signal theory, autumn colors deter them from settling on the tree.
Essential nutrient that the tree seeks to reclaim from its leaves before winter to ensure its growth the following spring.

course_77_qu_est_ce_que_la_matiere_noire.explanation: A measurement of the speed of stars at different distances from the center. According to Newton, peripheral stars should rotate more slowly. However, they rotate at the same speed - evidence of an invisible mass "gluing" the stars together.

A mysterious force responsible for the acceleration of the universe's expansion, representing 68% of its total content. Distinct from dark matter (27%), it acts as a repulsive energy of the vacuum, still completely misunderstood.
Physical theory that describes elementary particles (quarks, electrons, etc.) and three of the four fundamental forces, but fails to explain dark matter.
Invisible spherical structure surrounding a galaxy, composed mostly of dark matter and explaining its rotational stability.
Effect of light distortion from a distant object as it passes near a massive object (such as a dark matter cluster) that curves space-time.
Effect of light distortion from a distant object as it passes near a massive object (such as a dark matter cluster) that curves space-time.
Refers to ordinary matter composed of protons and neutrons, as opposed to dark matter whose nature is non-baryonic.
Physics theory that describes elementary particles (quarks, electrons, etc.) and three of the four fundamental forces, but fails to explain dark matter.

course_78_comment_fonctionne_l_electrici.explanation: An all-or-nothing electrical signal triggered when the depolarization of a neuron exceeds a threshold. It propagates along the axon at 1 to 100 m/s depending on myelination. It is the "click" of information that the neuron sends.

Chemical molecules released in the synapse that transmit the signal between neurons. The main ones: glutamate (excitatory), GABA (inhibitory), dopamine, serotonin. Psychoactive drugs act on these systems.
Membrane proteins that use cellular energy (ATP) to maintain the ionic concentration gradients necessary for the resting potential.
The primary excitatory neurotransmitter of the central nervous system, playing a crucial role in neuronal plasticity and memory.
Stable state of the electrical voltage across a neuron's membrane when it is not transmitting a signal (approximately -70 millivolts).

Sea-horse-shaped brain structure in the temporal lobe, essential for the formation of new conscious memories. Its surgical removal (case H.M.) leads to a total inability to form new memories, without erasing old ones.

Cognitive system that temporarily maintains a small amount of information (7±2 items) available for current processing. Managed by the prefrontal cortex, it is limited in capacity and duration (a few seconds without repetition).

Contracts by which buyers and sellers commit to a future transaction at a price fixed today. Speculators with no intention of physical delivery represent the vast majority of transactions, amplifying price fluctuations.
Massive boom in American production in the 21st century thanks to hydraulic fracturing, modifying the world's geopolitical energy balance.

course_79_pourquoi_certains_sons_nous_do.explanation: Key mechanism of chills: the brain constantly anticipates the continuation of a melody. When this expectation is violated in a satisfying way (unexpected chord, sudden surge), an emotional release occurs.

Key mechanism of chills: the brain constantly anticipates the continuation of a melody. When this expectation is violated in a satisfying way (unexpected chord, sudden surge), an emotional release occurs.

Personality trait associated with curiosity and the appreciation of beauty. People who are highly "open" have an auditory cortex more connected to emotional zones and are significantly more likely to feel musical chills.
Researcher in neurosciences, author of pioneering studies (2016-2017) on structural brain differences in people who experience musical chills.
Refers to the deep regions of the brain (such as the striatum or amygdala) located below the cortex, responsible for instinctive and emotional functions.
The transition from an unstable chord (tension) to a stable chord (rest) in classical music theory.

course_80_pourquoi_les_saisons_existent_.explanation: Uranus's axis is almost lying flat on its orbital plane. Each pole receives about 42 years of continuous sunlight followed by 42 years of total darkness - extreme and very long-lasting seasons, with no equivalent in our solar system.

Mars's orbit is significantly more elliptical than Earth's: the Sun-Mars distance varies from 207 to 249 million km. The Martian southern hemisphere has short, hot summers and long, cold winters - much more pronounced than here.
The angle between a planet's rotation axis and the perpendicular to its orbital plane; it is the major cause of seasons.
The point in the orbit of a celestial body where the distance of this body from the Sun is minimal.
A system of planetary rings composed of ice and dust encircling Saturn, whose appearance varies according to the planet's seasons.
Planets located outside the solar system, orbiting a star other than the Sun.
The rotation direction of a planet that rotates from East to West, contrary to the majority of planets in the solar system.

Uranus's axis is almost lying flat on its orbital plane. Each pole receives about 42 years of continuous sunlight and then 42 years of total darkness - extreme seasons of very long duration, with no equivalent in our solar system.

Mars's orbit is significantly more elliptical than Earth's: the Sun-Mars distance varies from 207 to 249 million km. The Martian southern hemisphere has short, hot summers and long, cold winters - much more marked than here.

course_81_l_odyssee_homere|The Homeric Q.explanation: Were the Iliad and the Odyssey composed by a single poet named Homer or are they the result of a long collective oral tradition? Most researchers today believe in one or two authors who fixed an older tradition.

course_81_l_odyssee_homere|The Homeric f.displayTerm: The Homeric formula and the oral epic
course_81_l_odyssee_homere|The Homeric f.explanation: The Homeric epics were composed orally before being written. Repeated formulas ("Rosy-fingered Dawn", "Resourceful Odysseus") facilitated memorization and improvised composition - a technique studied by Milman Parry in the 20th century.

course_81_l_odyssee_homere|aedes.explanation: Poet-singers of ancient Greece who improvised or recited epics while traditionally accompanying themselves with a lyre (the phorminx).

course_81_l_odyssee_homere|Homeridae.explanation: Brotherhood or guild of singers and poets who claimed to be descendants of Homer and ensured the transmission of his works.

course_81_l_odyssee_homere|Milman Parry.explanation: American philologist who proved, through the study of Balkan bards, that Homer's works were based on a technique of improvised oral composition.

course_81_l_odyssee_homere|oral traditio.explanation: Mode of cultural transmission through speech, without written support, relying on specific memorization techniques.

course_81_l_odyssee_homere|Homeric Greek.explanation: Archaic and artificial literary language used by Homer, mixing different Greek dialects for reasons of meter and rhythm.

course_81_l_odyssee_homere|dactyl.explanation: Unit of measurement of the Greek verse (the dactylic hexameter) composed of one long syllable followed by two shorts, imitating the rhythm of a gallop.

course_81_l_odyssee_homere|in media res.explanation: Latin phrase meaning 'in the midst of things', designating a narrative process where the story begins in the heart of the plot.

course_81_l_odyssee_homere|analepsis.explanation: Technical term designating a move back in time within a narrative (flashback).

course_81_l_odyssee_homere|nekyia.explanation: Ritual episode during which the hero invokes the dead to question their shadows about the future.

course_81_l_odyssee_homere|nekya.explanation: Ritual episode during which the hero invokes the dead to question their shadows about the future.

course_81_l_odyssee_homere|James Joyce.explanation: Major 20th-century Irish writer, author of the experimental novel 'Ulysses' (1922).

course_81_l_odyssee_homere|Homeric formu.explanation: The Homeric epics were composed orally before being written down. Repeated formulas ("Rosy-fingered Dawn", "Odysseus of many wiles") facilitated memorization and improvised composition - a technique studied by Milman Parry in the 20th century.

course_82_l_iliade_homere|Mênis (wrath).explanation: Achilles' wrath is not a simple emotion: it is a quasi-cosmic power. The first word of the Iliad, "Mênis", announces this central theme. This divine wrath, which demands reparation, destabilizes the order of the world.

course_82_l_iliade_homere|wrath in Greek.explanation: Achilles' wrath is not a simple emotion: it is a quasi-cosmic power. The first word of the Iliad, "Mênis", announces this central theme. This divine wrath, which demands reparation, destabilizes the order of the world.

course_82_l_iliade_homere|Menis (anger).explanation: Achilles' wrath is not a simple emotion: it is a quasi-cosmic power. The first word of the Iliad, "Mênis", announces this central theme. This divine wrath, which demands reparation, destabilizes the order of the world.

course_82_l_iliade_homere|Homeric ariste.explanation: A set piece of epic poetry: a long stretch in which one hero performs superhuman feats. Every great warrior of the Iliad has his aristeia. These passages let the poet build up the hero's character and tie his line back to the gods.

course_82_l_iliade_homere|timē.explanation: In Ancient Greece, the honor or public recognition granted to a hero based on his exploits. It is the lack of timē inflicted by Agamemnon that causes Achilles' withdrawal.

course_82_l_iliade_homere|Trojan Horse.explanation: Famous stratagem by Odysseus consisting of introducing Greek soldiers into Troy via a huge wooden horse. This episode is not told in the Iliad but in the Odyssey and the Aeneid.

course_82_l_iliade_homere|Homeric Ariste.explanation: Literary genre of the epic: a long sequence where a hero performs superhuman feats. Each great warrior of the Iliad has his aristeia. These passages allowed the hero's character to be developed and his lineage to be linked to the gods.

course_82_l_iliade_homere|Homeric Aristi.explanation: Literary genre of the epic: a long sequence where a hero performs superhuman feats. Each great warrior of the Iliad has his aristeia. These passages allowed the hero's character to be developed and his lineage to be linked to the gods.

course_83_dipe_roi_sophocle|Fate and fre.displayTerm: Fate and free will in Greek tragedy
course_83_dipe_roi_sophocle|Fate and fre.explanation: Tragedy explores the tension between inevitable fate (predicted by oracles) and human choices. Oedipus fulfills his tragic destiny precisely while attempting to flee it - a paradox at the heart of the human condition according to the Greeks.

course_83_dipe_roi_sophocle|Destiny and.displayTerm: Destiny and free will in Greek tragedy
course_83_dipe_roi_sophocle|Destiny and.explanation: Tragedy explores the tension between inevitable fate (predicted by oracles) and human choices. Oedipus fulfills his tragic destiny precisely while attempting to flee it - a paradox at the heart of the human condition according to the Greeks.

course_83_dipe_roi_sophocle|The Oedipus.explanation: Freud borrowed the myth of Oedipus to name the child's unconscious desire for the parent of the opposite sex. This central psychoanalytic concept has very little to do with the reflection of Sophocles, which dealt with fate and free will.

course_83_dipe_roi_sophocle|Poetics.explanation: Treatise by Aristotle analyzing the rules of tragedy and epic, making Oedipus Rex the model of the genre.

course_83_dipe_roi_sophocle|Antigone.explanation: Tragedy by Sophocles telling the fate of the daughter of Oedipus, confronted with the conflict between divine laws and human laws.

course_83_dipe_roi_sophocle|Oedipus at C.explanation: Last play by Sophocles describing the death of the exiled Oedipus, who became a sacred figure after his sufferings.

course_83_dipe_roi_sophocle|tritagonist.explanation: Third actor introduced by Sophocles, allowing the dramatic play to be enriched beyond a simple one-on-one.

course_83_dipe_roi_sophocle|loimos.explanation: Greek term referring to the plague or a religious pollution striking a city as punishment for a sin.

course_83_dipe_roi_sophocle|Tiresias.explanation: Blind seer of Thebes who possesses dual knowledge (past and future) and reveals his fault to Oedipus.

course_83_dipe_roi_sophocle|anagnorisis.explanation: Moment in the tragedy where a character moves from ignorance to knowledge (the recognition).

course_83_dipe_roi_sophocle|peripeteia.explanation: The sudden reversal of a character's situation, turning from happiness to extreme misfortune.

course_83_dipe_roi_sophocle|pharmakos.explanation: Scapegoat in Ancient Greece, purging the city of its evil through their expulsion or sacrifice.

course_83_dipe_roi_sophocle|ainigma.explanation: Greek word meaning enigma, referring to a game of the mind but also the obscure speech of oracles.

course_84_antigone_sophocle|Natural law.explanation: Tension at the heart of Antigone: divine and moral law (burying the dead) against the human law of Creon. This conflict runs through all political philosophy, from Plato to Rousseau and modern theorists of natural rights.

course_84_antigone_sophocle|Hybris in Gr.explanation: Hybris (excess, overweening pride) is the Greek tragic sin above all others. Creon commits hybris by believing his law outranks the law of the gods, and as punishment for that presumption he loses everyone he loved.

course_84_antigone_sophocle|Seven Agains.explanation: Military expedition led by Polynices and six other leaders against their own city of Thebes to reclaim the throne from Eteocles.

course_84_antigone_sophocle|Hades.explanation: The realm of the dead in Greek mythology, where souls reside after receiving funeral rites.

course_84_antigone_sophocle|peripeteia.explanation: A sudden reversal in a play that carries the action toward its ending.

course_84_antigone_sophocle|adventure.explanation: A sudden reversal in a play that carries the action toward its ending.

course_84_antigone_sophocle|Hubris in Gr.explanation: Hubris (excess, overweening pride) is the quintessential Greek tragic sin. Creon commits hubris by believing his law outranks the law of the gods, and as punishment for that presumption he loses everyone he loved.

course_85_le_banquet_platon|Platonic Ero.explanation: Plato distinguishes between physical love and spiritual love aspiring to absolute Beauty. Diotima's speech describes a "ladder of love": starting from a beautiful body, then loving the beauty of souls, then ideal Beauty-itself.

course_85_le_banquet_platon|The Athenian.explanation: A Greek masculine banquet following dinner, combining the consumption of diluted wine and intellectual discussions. Respectable women were excluded from it. It was within this framework that much of Athenian philosophy developed.

course_85_le_banquet_platon|androgynes.explanation: Mythical beings possessing both masculine and feminine characteristics. In Aristophanes' account, they represent one of the three original forms of humanity before being split by the gods.

course_85_le_banquet_platon|daimon.explanation: In Greek mythology and in Plato's work, an intermediary being between gods and mortals, serving as a messenger or mediator. Eros is described as a daemon because he links human desire to divine perfection.

course_85_le_banquet_platon|Eros.explanation: Greek god of love and desire. In Plato, he stands for the pull that draws the soul toward beauty and knowledge.

course_85_le_banquet_platon|Alcibiades.explanation: Athenian politics figure and general famous for his charisma, beauty, and instability. His crashing entrance at the end of the Symposium offers a vivid portrait of Socrates.

course_86_la_republique_platon|Plato's t.explanation: Sensible realities are imperfect copies of perfect and eternal Forms. Philosophy is the effort to contemplate these Forms. The allegory of the cave illustrates this fundamental distinction between appearances and true reality.

course_86_la_republique_platon|Plato's T.explanation: Sensible realities are imperfect copies of perfect and eternal Forms. Philosophy is the effort to contemplate these Forms. The allegory of the cave illustrates this fundamental distinction between appearances and true reality.

course_86_la_republique_platon|The philo.explanation: For Plato, only the philosopher, the one who has contemplated the Form of the Good, is fit to rule. His ideal city is a strict intellectual meritocracy, very far from the Athenian democracy he deeply despised.

course_86_la_republique_platon|Epithumia.explanation: In Plato's psychology, the desiring part of the soul linked to biological needs and material appetites.

course_86_la_republique_platon|Thumos.explanation: The 'irascible' or 'spirited' part of the soul, the seat of courage, noble anger, and strength of character.

course_86_la_republique_platon|Logos.explanation: The rational part of the soul, capable of accessing the truth and guiding the other parts toward harmony.

course_86_la_republique_platon|Kallipoli.explanation: Name meaning 'beautiful city', designating the ideal city constructed by Socrates and his interlocutors in The Republic.

course_86_la_republique_platon|Karl Popp.explanation: 20th-century philosopher and author of 'The Open Society and Its Enemies', a radical critic of the Platonic model which he deems a precursor to totalitarianism.

course_86_la_republique_platon|Alfred No.explanation: British philosopher and mathematician famous for his quote emphasizing the hegemonic influence of Plato on the history of thought.

course_86_la_republique_platon|Graeae.explanation: Three divine sisters born old, possessing only one eye and one tooth between them, guardians of the path to the Gorgon.

course_86_la_republique_platon|Nereids.explanation: Sea nymphs, daughters of Nereus, offended by the vanity of Queen Cassiopeia.

course_86_la_republique_platon|Fates.explanation: Divinities in charge of human destiny, represented as spinners (the Roman equivalent of the Moirai).

course_87_l_apologie_de_socrate_platon|S.explanation: Socrates' method of teaching through interrogation: asking questions to lead the interlocutor to discover the truth for themselves. Socrates compared himself to a midwife who helps to "give birth" to ideas already latent in the mind.

course_87_l_apologie_de_socrate_platon|“.explanation: The Oracle of Delphi declared that Socrates was the wisest of the Athenians. Socrates concluded that this was because he alone knows that he knows nothing, while others believe they know without having verified it. This humility founds all philosophical pursuit.

The Oracle of Delphi declared that Socrates was the wisest of the Athenians. Socrates concluded that this was because he alone knows that he knows nothing, while others believe they know without having verified it. This humility founds all philosophical pursuit.

course_87_l_apologie_de_socrate_platon|a.explanation: Greek term meaning 'defense'. In the ancient context, it refers to a speech intended to justify one's actions during a trial, rather than to express regret.

course_87_l_apologie_de_socrate_platon|s.explanation: Masters of rhetoric and eloquence in Ancient Greece who taught the art of persuasion for a fee, often criticized by Socrates for their lack of concern for absolute truth.

course_87_l_apologie_de_socrate_platon|P.explanation: Public building in Athens where magistrates sat and where deserving citizens and victorious athletes were fed at the city's expense.
A public building in Athens where magistrates sat and where deserving citizens and victorious athletes were fed at the city's expense.

course_88_la_poetique_aristote|Catharsis.explanation: A key term for Aristotle: tragedy provokes pity and terror which achieve a "purification" of these emotions in the spectator. A 2,500-year debate: emotional purge, intellectual clarification, or aesthetic pleasure?

course_88_la_poetique_aristote|Aristotel.explanation: For Aristotle, art is an improved imitation (mimesis) of nature: a selective imitation that shows things not as they are but as they could be. Unlike Plato, he sees positive value in it.

course_88_la_poetique_aristote|Abu Bishr.explanation: 10th-century Christian philosopher and translator who enabled the transmission of the Poetics in the Arab world.

course_88_la_poetique_aristote|Averroes.explanation: 12th-century Andalusian philosopher and theologian whose commentaries on Aristotle strongly influenced medieval Europe.

course_88_la_poetique_aristote|Theatre o.explanation: One of the best-preserved theaters of ancient Greece, renowned for its exceptional acoustics.

course_88_la_poetique_aristote|Epidaurus.explanation: One of the best-preserved theaters of ancient Greece, renowned for its exceptional acoustics.

course_88_la_poetique_aristote|Theater o.explanation: One of the best-preserved theaters of ancient Greece, renowned for its exceptional acoustics.

course_89_les_travaux_et_les_jours_hesio.explanation: Hesiod describes five successive eras of humanity, each worse than the last: the ages of gold, silver, bronze, heroes, and iron (our own). It is one of the first pessimistic visions of the course of human history.
Hesiod's other great poem, telling the genealogy of the Greek gods from the original Chaos. These two works, along with Homer, constitute the founding texts of Greek religion and mythology.
A region of central Greece, north of Attica, whose capital was Thebes. Perceived by the Athenians as a land of boorish peasants, it is the homeland of Hesiod.
A Greek notion referring to hubris, the insane pride that drives man to believe he is the equal of the gods. It is the supreme crime that triggers divine punishment (Nemesis).
A Greek notion referring to hubris, the insane pride that drives man to believe he is the equal of the gods. It is the supreme crime that triggers divine punishment (Nemesis).
Renaissance humanist who, by translating Hesiod into Latin, replaced the Greek term 'pithos' (jar) with 'pyxis' (box), thus creating the erroneous but famous expression 'Pandora's box'.
A Latin didactic poem by Virgil dealing with agriculture, directly inspired by the work of Hesiod.

course_90_medee_euripide|The figure of t.displayTerm: The figure of the stranger in Greek tragedy
course_90_medee_euripide|The figure of t.explanation: Medea is a barbarian (from Colchis), a sorceress, and a woman: a triple outsider in the Greek city. Euripides uses her to criticize Athenian values about women, marriage, and the law.

course_90_medee_euripide|Revenge and hon.displayTerm: Revenge and honor in the Greek world
course_90_medee_euripide|Revenge and hon.explanation: Honor (timē) was a fundamental value in Greece. A betrayal demanded reparation. Medea cannot accept the dishonor of being repudiated: her revenge follows a logic of reciprocity which, pushed to the extreme, becomes monstrous.

course_90_medee_euripide|Aeschylus.explanation: The oldest of the three great authors of Greek tragedies, known for the religious and collective dimension of his plays.

course_90_medee_euripide|Sophocles.explanation: Greek tragedian, author of Oedipus Rex, who introduced the third actor and focused on heroic solitude.

course_90_medee_euripide|Barbarian.explanation: For the Greeks, this refers to anyone who does not speak Greek and is foreign to their culture. The term was not initially insulting but marks a radical state of otherness.

course_90_medee_euripide|Barbarous.explanation: For the Greeks, this refers to anyone who does not speak Greek and is foreign to their culture. The term was not initially insulting but marks a radical state of otherness.

course_90_medee_euripide|Argonauts.explanation: A group of heroes who, according to mythology, accompanied Jason on the ship Argo to seek the Golden Fleece.

course_90_medee_euripide|Thumos.explanation: Greek concept referring to the irascible soul, the seat of anger, courage, and the sense of honor.

course_90_medee_euripide|Deus ex machina.explanation: Theatrical technique consisting of having a god or a divine force intervene at the end of a play to resolve an inextricable situation.

course_91_les_miserables_victor_hugo|The.displayTerm: The penal colonies and the penal system in the 19th century
course_91_les_miserables_victor_hugo|The.explanation: The penal colonies of Toulon, Brest, and Rochefort were places of forced labor where convicts suffered dehumanizing living conditions, illustrating the severity of a justice system that criminalized poverty.

course_91_les_miserables_victor_hugo|Ins.explanation: The incorruptible police officer who pursues Jean Valjean. He personifies the strict and blind law, incapable of conceiving of forgiveness or the moral evolution of a criminal.

course_91_les_miserables_victor_hugo|Dig.explanation: Interruption of the main narrative by the author to address a historical, philosophical, or sociological subject (e.g., Waterloo in Les Misérables).

course_91_les_miserables_victor_hugo|Sew.explanation: Subterranean world of the capital used by Hugo as a metaphor for the social unconscious and the site of Jean Valjean's heroic escape.

course_91_les_miserables_victor_hugo|ABC.explanation: Name of the fictional secret society of republican students led by Enjolras, whose name is a pun on 'les abaissés' (the downtrodden).

course_91_les_miserables_victor_hugo|Eng.explanation: Writing in which the author puts their art at the service of a political, social, or moral cause in order to change society.

course_91_les_miserables_victor_hugo|Pen.displayTerm: Penal colony and the 19th-century penal system
course_91_les_miserables_victor_hugo|Pen.explanation: The penal colonies of Toulon, Brest, and Rochefort were hells of forced labor. Jean Valjean spent 19 years there for a stolen loaf of bread, illustrating the brutality of a system that did not distinguish between crime and poverty.

course_92_madame_bovary_flaubert|Bovarys.explanation: A state of chronic dissatisfaction born from the disproportion between dreams nourished by the imagination (reading, fantasies) and lived reality.

course_92_madame_bovary_flaubert|Free in.explanation: A narrative technique that reports a character's words or thoughts indirectly but without an introducing verb, so the narrator's voice and the character's voice blur together.

course_92_madame_bovary_flaubert|free in.explanation: A narrative technique that reports a character's words or thoughts indirectly but without an introducing verb, so the narrator's voice and the character's voice blur together.

course_92_madame_bovary_flaubert|realism.explanation: 19th-century literary movement aiming to represent social and human reality in the most faithful way possible, without idealizing it.

course_92_madame_bovary_flaubert|Homais.explanation: Pharmacist of Yonville, a figure of the triumphant, pedantic, and mediocre bourgeoisie, who stands in contrast to Emma's distress through his social success.

course_93_le_rouge_et_le_noir_stendhal|T.displayTerm: The symbolism of The Red and the Black
course_93_le_rouge_et_le_noir_stendhal|T.explanation: Argued over since 1830: red is said to stand for the Napoleonic army, one road to success, and black for the priest's robe, the other road open under the Restoration. Julien Sorel moves between the two, and neither really fits him.

course_93_le_rouge_et_le_noir_stendhal|T.displayTerm: The symbolism of Red and Black
course_93_le_rouge_et_le_noir_stendhal|T.explanation: Argued over since 1830: red is said to stand for the Napoleonic army, one road to success, and black for the priest's robe, the other road open under the Restoration. Julien Sorel moves between the two, and neither really fits him.

A period where the Bourbons were restored to the throne after Waterloo. Society was dominated by the nobility and the Church, hostile to revolutionary values. Stendhal saw it as a society of hypocrisy and provincial mediocrity.

course_93_le_rouge_et_le_noir_stendhal|V.explanation: Latin translation of the Bible, used by the Catholic Church. Mastering this text by heart was a sign of immense biblical erudition, used by Julien Sorel to impress the clergy and the nobles.

course_93_le_rouge_et_le_noir_stendhal|C.explanation: Alternative title and subtitle of the novel highlighting Stendhal's desire to anchor his narrative in the burning social and politics news of his time.

course_93_le_rouge_et_le_noir_stendhal|B.explanation: Stendhal's philosophy of life and writing, combining a lucid analysis of the world, the quest for individual happiness, and the rejection of romantic emphasis.

course_94_candide_voltaire|Leibniz's opt.explanation: Philosophy according to which God created the best of all possible worlds and that apparent evil serves a higher good. Voltaire wrote Candide in response, notably to the Lisbon earthquake (1755) which killed 60,000 people in a few minutes.

course_94_candide_voltaire|The Enlighten.explanation: 18th-century intellectual movement built on reason, the criticism of prejudice, and progress. Voltaire, Rousseau, Diderot, Hume, and Kant challenged religious and political authority, and so prepared the ground for later revolutions.

course_94_candide_voltaire|The philosoph.explanation: 18th-century intellectual movement built on reason, the criticism of prejudice, and progress. Voltaire, Rousseau, Diderot, Hume, and Kant challenged religious and political authority, and so prepared the ground for later revolutions.

course_94_candide_voltaire|Seven Years'.explanation: Major conflict (1756-1763) primarily opposing France and Great Britain. Voltaire uses it to denounce the "heroic butchery" of battles.

course_94_candide_voltaire|Inquisition.explanation: Ecclesiastical court responsible for hunting down heresy. In Candide, it illustrates the religious fanaticism that Voltaire fights.

course_94_candide_voltaire|Auto-da-fé.explanation: Public penance ceremony where heretics are sometimes burned. Voltaire turns it into a demonstration of superstitious absurdity.

course_94_candide_voltaire|Leibniz.explanation: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646-1716), a German philosopher whose Theodicy defends the idea that God created the 'best of all possible worlds'.

course_94_candide_voltaire|Leibnizian op.explanation: The philosophy according to which God created the best of all possible worlds and that apparent evil serves a higher good. Voltaire wrote Candide in response, notably to the Lisbon earthquake (1755) which killed 60,000 people in a few minutes.

course_95_les_confessions_rousseau|Rouss.explanation: Rousseau postulated that man is naturally good and that it is society that corrupts him. This idea, opposed to Hobbes, deeply influenced the French Revolution and romanticism.

course_95_les_confessions_rousseau|Mme d.explanation: Woman from the Savoyard nobility who welcomed the young Rousseau at age 16, converted him to Catholicism, and became his protectress and then his mistress. Rousseau calls her "Maman" in The Confessions, mixing filial affection and a romantic relationship.

course_95_les_confessions_rousseau|autob.explanation: Concept theorized by Philippe Lejeune referring to the author's commitment to telling the truth about themselves, creating an identity between the author, the narrator, and the character.

course_95_les_confessions_rousseau|Roman.explanation: European cultural movement emphasizing the expression of feelings, imagination, and the exaltation of nature, of which Rousseau is considered one of the spiritual fathers.

course_96_l_etranger_camus|The absurd in.explanation: A feeling born from the clash between the human desire for meaning and the silence of the universe. Camus does not see the absurd as a cosmic truth but as a lived experience - the response is not suicide but lucid and conscious revolt.

course_96_l_etranger_camus|Colonial Alge.explanation: The Stranger takes place in French Algeria during the 1940s. The Arab whom Meursault kills remains nameless in the novel - a major postcolonial critique: the novel is said to reproduce the invisibility of Arabs in French colonial Literature.

course_96_l_etranger_camus|Gallimard.explanation: Prestigious French publishing house that published The Stranger in 1942 and for which Camus would later become one of the influential readers.

course_96_l_etranger_camus|Nuveau Roman.explanation: Literary movement of the 1950s that rejected the conventions of the traditional novel (plot, character psychology), finding a precursor in Camus's neutral style.

course_96_l_etranger_camus|New Novel.explanation: Literary movement of the 1950s that rejected the conventions of the traditional novel (plot, character psychology), finding a precursor in Camus's neutral style.

course_96_l_etranger_camus|Nouveau Roman.explanation: Literary movement of the 1950s that rejected the conventions of the traditional novel (plot, character psychology), finding a precursor in Camus's neutral style.

course_96_l_etranger_camus|Kamel Daoud.explanation: Contemporary Algerian writer, author of 'Meursault, contre-enquête', who gives an identity and a voice to the brother of the Arab killed by Meursault.

course_96_l_etranger_camus|postcolonial.explanation: Critical studies that examine the cultural, political, and social effects of colonization, and in particular how art has pictured the colonized.

course_96_l_etranger_camus|The Absurd in.explanation: A feeling born from the clash between the human desire for meaning and the silence of the universe. Camus does not see the absurd as a cosmic truth but as a lived experience - the response is not suicide but lucid and conscious rebellion.

course_96_l_etranger_camus|Colonial Alge.explanation: The Stranger takes place in 1940s French Algeria. The Arab that Meursault kills remains nameless in the novel - a major postcolonial critique: the novel is said to reproduce the invisibility of Arabs in French colonial literature.

course_97_le_mythe_de_sisyphe_camus|The.explanation: An attitude of living to the peak of one's consciousness while refusing any hope of transcendent meaning, thus transforming finitude into freedom.

Camus critiques the "leap" that some philosophers take when faced with the absurd: leaping into faith (Kierkegaard) or revolutionary hope (Marx). These "philosophical suicides" avoid the absurd instead of confronting it honestly.

course_97_le_mythe_de_sisyphe_camus|Thea.explanation: Theatrical trend of the 1950s (Beckett, Ionesco) that breaks with naturalism to stage the meaninglessness of the human condition and the failure of language.
Theatrical trend of the 1950s (Beckett, Ionesco) that breaks with naturalism to stage the meaninglessness of the human condition and the failure of language.

course_98_a_la_recherche_du_temps_perdu_.explanation: A memory suddenly triggered by a sensation (taste, smell) resurrects a lived past in its emotional entirety, unlike voluntary memory, which is cold and intellectual. The madeleine is the canonical example.

In the final volume, the narrator understands that only art can snatch lived moments from the destruction of time. Literature can restore the past - this is the justification for the entire Recherche and its final revelation.
Places of sociability for high society where people gather to discuss politics, art, and literature, decisive in the narrator's social apprenticeship.
French writer and major figure of the NRF who initially refused Proust's manuscript before becoming one of his greatest admirers.
A central and complex character in the Recherche, a cultured aristocrat whose fate Proust uses to explore homosexuality and social decline.

course_99_le_pere_goriot_balzac|Balzac's.explanation: A project of 90 interconnected novels and short stories describing the whole of French society. Characters return from one novel to another - an innovation unheard of at the time. Rastignac appears in about twenty works of the cycle.

course_99_le_pere_goriot_balzac|Vautrin.explanation: An escaped convict and criminal genius, he is the cynical mentor to Rastignac. A recurring figure in the Comédie humaine, he represents out-of-law society - powerful, lucid and without illusions about the respectable world.

course_99_le_pere_goriot_balzac|World.explanation: Balzacian term designating high society, the Parisian elite (aristocracy and upper bourgeoisie) with its ruthless codes, its Salons, and its permanent concern for appearances.

course_99_le_pere_goriot_balzac|The Huma.explanation: A project of 90 interconnected novels and short stories describing the totality of French society. Figures return from one novel to another - an innovation that was unprecedented at the time. Rastignac appears in about twenty works within the cycle.

course_100_les_fleurs_du_mal_baudelaire|.explanation: Baudelaire is the father of symbolism: he tried not to describe reality but to hint at secret links between sensations, feelings, and ideas. Verlaine, Rimbaud, Mallarmé, and later most of 20th-century poetry claim him as an influence.

Cosmic boredom, a feeling of the futility of the world, an inability to find meaning or joy - faced with an inaccessible ideal. Spleen and ideal are the two opposing poles between which all the poetry of Les Fleurs du Mal oscillates.

Literary and artistic movement of the early 19th century emphasizing the expression of feelings, lyricism, and the relationship with nature, from which Baudelaire detached himself through his refusal of idealization.
Novel by Gustave Flaubert published in 1857, famous for its realism and having undergone, like Les Fleurs du Mal, a trial for immorality that same year.
Baudelairean concept consisting of finding the beautiful and the eternal within the ephemeral and contemporary urban life, rather than in ancient models.
Prefect of the Seine under Napoleon III, responsible for the major transformation works of Paris that inspired Baudelaire's 'Tableaux parisiens'.
Poetic form without rhymes or measured verse, of which Baudelaire was the pioneer with 'Le Spleen de Paris', seeking a musical prose adapted to the shocks of urban life.
Posthumous collection of short prose poems where Baudelaire continues his exploration of modernity and urban wandering.

course_101_1984_george_orwell|Newspeak (.explanation: The official language of Oceania whose objective is to make dissident thought impossible by eliminating the words that would allow it to be formulated. The more the vocabulary is reduced, the more complex ideas become unthinkable.

course_101_1984_george_orwell|Soviet tot.explanation: Orwell had observed Stalinism in Spain during the Civil War and experienced the Blitz in London. 1984 is inspired by Staline but embodies a universal totalitarianism: the claim to control not only bodies but reality itself ("2+2=5").

course_101_1984_george_orwell|POUM.explanation: Workers' Party of Marxist Unification. Anti-Stalinist revolutionary organization in Spain in which Orwell fought.

course_101_1984_george_orwell|Censorship.explanation: Action of limiting or prohibiting the dissemination of ideas, information, or works by a public or religious authority.

course_101_1984_george_orwell|Doublethin.explanation: Ability to accept two contradictory beliefs as true at the same time, allowing one to ignore physical reality in favor of the Party's doctrine.

course_102_la_ferme_des_animaux_george_o.displayTerm: The allegory of the Russian Revolution
course_102_la_ferme_des_animaux_george_o.explanation: Old Major = Marx/Lenin, Napoleon = Stalin, Snowball = Trotsky, Squealer = propaganda. The commands, progressively modified, illustrate the betrayal of revolutionary ideals by the bureaucracy in power.

Soviet regime under Stalin (1924-1953): cult of personality, political terror (Gulag, Great Purges), planned economy, forced collectivization. The Farm was written in 1943-1944, while the USSR was an ally of Great Britain.
Global conflict (1939-1945) during which the USSR was the ally of Great Britain and the United States against Nazi Germany.
Social class composed of workers who do not own the means of production and sell their labor power to survive.
The last Emperor of Russia, overthrown during the 1917 Revolution, represented by farmer Jones in the novel.
Orwellian concept designating a simplified and manipulated language aimed at preventing any critical or oppositional thought.
Events of 1917 that led to the overthrow of the tsarist regime and the seizure of power by the Bolsheviks led by Lenin.

Old Major = Marx/Lenin, Napoleon = Stalin, Snowball = Trotsky, Squealer = propaganda. The progressively modified commandments illustrate the betrayal of revolutionary ideals by the bureaucracy in power.

course_103_hamlet_shakespeare|Elizabetha.explanation: Revenge is a central theme of Elizabethan theater. A man of honor had to avenge an offense to his family - but this duty conflicted with the law and Christian morality. This paradox fuels Hamlet's fundamental hesitation.

course_103_hamlet_shakespeare|Melancholy.explanation: In Shakespeare's time, melancholy was a medical "humor" (black bile) associated with people of intellect, creativity, and inaction. Hamlet's hesitation corresponds to this medical diagnosis of the period, which explains his inability to act.

course_103_hamlet_shakespeare|Hamlet, Pr.explanation: Tragedy by William Shakespeare published around 1603, considered one of the pinnacles of world literature for its psychological depth.

course_103_hamlet_shakespeare|Wittenberg.explanation: German city famous for its university where Hamlet is supposed to have studied, a highly symbolic place as the cradle of the Protestant Reformation.

course_103_hamlet_shakespeare|lex talion.explanation: Principle of punitive justice consisting of inflicting upon the guilty the same damage they caused (an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth).

course_103_hamlet_shakespeare|Oedipus co.explanation: Psychoanalytic concept theorized by Freud, often applied to Hamlet to explain his troubled relationship with Gertrude and his hesitation to kill Claudius.

course_104_romeo_et_juliette_shakespeare.explanation: A literary tradition glorifying the secret and suffering love of a knight for a lady (often married). Romeo begins the play in this stereotypical role (in love with Rosaline) before his love for Juliet becomes real and tragic.

course_104_romeo_et_juliette_shakespeare.displayTerm: The Italian source of the narrative
course_104_romeo_et_juliette_shakespeare.explanation: Romeo and Juliet is based on a novella by Matteo Bandello (1554), itself inspired by earlier tales. Shakespeare adapted it by tightening the timeframe (from months to a few days) to intensify the tragedy's fatality.
Tragedy by William Shakespeare written around 1595, recounting the passion of two lovers whose feuding families prevent their union.
16th-century Italian writer whose novella served as the primary source for Shakespeare for his plot.
Hereditary hatred or vengeance between two families or clans, the driving force of the tragedy in the play.
Here, an attitude that consists of mocking ideal values and feelings through a critical or disillusioned spirit, as Mercutio does.
In the broad sense in theater, the art of developing a thought through the action and movement of the figures.
Famous 1957 musical that adapts the plot of Shakespeare to the conflict between two gangs in New York.
Here, an attitude that consists of mocking ideal values and feelings through a critical spirit or disillusionment, as Mercutio does.

course_105_le_meilleur_des_mondes_aldous.explanation: Industrial organization methods that rationalized production through extreme division of labor and the assembly line. Huxley applies them to human reproduction and conditioning - Ford is the deity of the novel.

Fictional drug in the novel that brings happiness and forgetfulness with no side effects. It stands for every chemical or technological addiction that lets people put up with an empty life, a foreshadowing of social media.
George Orwell's novel published in 1949 describing a totalitarian dystopia based on constant surveillance, repression and the manipulation of language (Newspeak).
In the novel, a technique consisting of using thermal or chemical shocks to cause multiple buddings from a single egg, allowing the creation of up to 96 identical twins.
An essay published by Aldous Huxley in 1958 where he analyzes, 27 years later, the evolution of society in relation to his own fictional predictions.

course_106_frankenstein_mary_shelley|The.explanation: Subtitle of the novel: "The Modern Prometheus". Victor Frankenstein creates something extraordinary without accepting the consequences. The real monster may not be the creature but its creator who abandons it at birth.

The eruption of Mount Tambora in 1815 projected ash that darkened the global atmosphere, causing a freezing summer in Europe in 1816. In this apocalyptic context, Mary Shelley (18 years old) wrote Frankenstein during a stay on the shores of Lake Geneva.

course_106_frankenstein_mary_shelley|Gal.explanation: Physical theory of Luigi Galvani in the 18th century suggesting that animal muscles are activated by an electrical fluid, opening up the imagination to the reanimation of the dead.

course_106_frankenstein_mary_shelley|Rom.explanation: Literary and artistic movement of the 19th century prioritizing the expression of feelings, imagination, wild nature and the torments of the soul.

course_106_frankenstein_mary_shelley|Hub.explanation: Greek term designating the excessive pride of a human who seeks to equal the gods, leading inevitably to their downfall.

course_106_frankenstein_mary_shelley|Tab.explanation: Philosophical concept according to which the human mind is born blank of all knowledge or moral inclination, and is built only through experience and education.

course_106_frankenstein_mary_shelley|Pos.explanation: Current of thought exploring the idea of a humanity transformed or surpassed by technological and biological progress.

course_106_frankenstein_mary_shelley|Soc.explanation: Principle according to which an individual's social conditions and environment determine their behavior and fate.

course_106_frankenstein_mary_shelley|Par.explanation: Epic poem by John Milton dealing with the fall of man and Satan's revolt against God, a key book that the creature reads to understand its own condition.

course_106_frankenstein_mary_shelley|Yea.explanation: The 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora ejected ash that darkened the global atmosphere, causing a freezing summer in Europe in 1816. It was in this apocalyptic context that Mary Shelley (18 years old) wrote Frankenstein during a stay on the shores of Lake Geneva.

course_107_crime_et_chatiment_dostoievsk.explanation: Intellectual movement rejecting all moral and religious authority in the name of reason and science. Real-life nihilists assassinated Tsar Alexander II in 1881. Raskolnikov embodies a tragic and individualized version of this ideology.

Central theme in Dostoyevsky: it is accepted suffering and voluntary humiliation that purify the soul. Raskolnikov will heal not through reason but through humiliating confession and the love of Sonia, a figure of Christ-like sacrifice.
Novel by Fyodor Dostoyevsky published in 1866, a pillar of Russian literature exploring themes of guilt, morality, and redemption.
Russian intellectual discussion group of socialist inspiration to which Dostoyevsky belonged, which earned him a death sentence.
Place of detention in Siberia where Dostoyevsky spent four years of forced labor, an experience that forged his vision of human suffering.
The method used by the character Porfiry Petrovich, who reads a suspect's nerves and state of mind instead of gathering physical evidence.
Episode from the Gospel according to John where Jesus brings Lazarus back to life, a central symbol of Raskolnikov's spiritual renewal in the novel.

course_108_le_proces_kafka|The Kafkaesqu.explanation: Adjective that has entered every language to describe an absurd bureaucratic situation where an individual is crushed by an impersonal and incomprehensible system, with no possible recourse. It often precedes the knowledge of the novel itself.

course_108_le_proces_kafka|Existential g.explanation: Josef K. is perhaps guilty simply of existing, in a world whose rules are incomprehensible. This existential reading of Kafka influenced Sartre and Camus in their own explorations of the human condition.

course_108_le_proces_kafka|Austro-Hungar.explanation: Multicultural political entity in Central Europe ruled by the Habsburgs from 1867 until its dissolution in 1918 after the First World War.

course_108_le_proces_kafka|Before the La.explanation: Key episode located at the end of The Trial, told by a priest to Josef K., illustrating the impenetrability of the law and human helplessness.

course_109_don_quichotte_cervantes|Metaf.explanation: Don Quixote is one of the first novels to comment on itself: in the second part (1615), the figures have read the first part (1605) and discuss it. This play with the reality of the novel anticipates literary postmodernism by several centuries.

course_109_don_quichotte_cervantes|The B.displayTerm: The Battle of Lepanto (1571) and Cervantes' captivity
course_109_don_quichotte_cervantes|The B.explanation: Cervantes fought at the Battle of Lepanto and was wounded (losing the use of his left hand). Captured by pirates in 1575, he was an enslaved person in Algiers for five years. These experiences forged the writer and nourish the humor and depth of the novel.

course_109_don_quichotte_cervantes|James.explanation: Major 20th-century Irish writer, author of Ulysses, whose complex narrative structure and exploration of human psychology are direct heirs to the structural innovations established by Cervantes.

course_109_don_quichotte_cervantes|Battl.displayTerm: Battle of Lepanto (1571) and Cervantes' captivity
course_109_don_quichotte_cervantes|Battl.explanation: Cervantes fought at Lepanto and was wounded (losing the use of his left hand). Captured by pirates in 1575, he was an enslaved person in Algiers for five years. These experiences forged the writer and nourished the humor and depth of the novel.

course_110_les_raisins_de_la_colere_stei.explanation: Agricultural disaster in the Great Plains caused by drought and destructive farming practices. Dust storms blackened the sky as far as New York, forcing hundreds of thousands of families (the "Okies") to migrate to California.

course_110_les_raisins_de_la_colere_stei.displayTerm: The American labor movement of the 1930s
course_110_les_raisins_de_la_colere_stei.explanation: The Great Depression radicalized American workers: the rise of the CIO, massive strikes, socialism. Steinbeck's novel is part of this context of social struggle that influenced Roosevelt's New Deal.
Name given to the shantytowns built by homeless people in the United States during the Great Depression, in ironic reference to President Herbert Hoover, held responsible for the crisis.
A superior force that guides human events toward a determined end, often identified here with divine will.
Three divine sisters born old, sharing only one eye and one tooth between them, guardians of the path to the Gorgons.
Sea nymphs, daughters of Nereus, offended by the vanity of Queen Cassiopeia.
Divinities in charge of human destiny, represented as spinners (the Roman equivalent of the Moirai).

course_111_to_kill_a_mockingbird_harper_.displayTerm: Jim Crow laws and the segregated South
course_111_to_kill_a_mockingbird_harper_.explanation: Jim Crow laws (1877-1965) organized segregation in the South. A Black man accused by a white woman was condemned in advance by all-white juries, and that is the central reality of justice in the novel.
