Fictional lawyer who became the archetype of American moral integrity. His defense of Tom Robinson, whom he knows is innocent but cannot save, illustrates the tragedy of a society where law and justice do not coincide.
Narrative trope where a white character comes to the aid of non-white individuals in a desperate situation, often used to criticize the white-centered perspective in racial struggle narratives.
Second novel by Harper Lee published in 2015. Written before 'To Kill a Mockingbird', it presents an older and more ambiguous version of Atticus Finch.
American actor who won the Academy Award for Best Actor in 1963 for his iconic portrayal of Atticus Finch on screen.

course_112_le_grand_gatsby_fitzgerald|Th.displayTerm: The American Dream and its corruption
course_112_le_grand_gatsby_fitzgerald|Th.explanation: The novel is the most famous critique of the American Dream, the idea that anyone can rise on merit alone. Gatsby succeeds but discovers that social class and the past cannot be escaped: old money despises the newly rich.

course_112_le_grand_gatsby_fitzgerald|Pr.explanation: Constitutional ban on making and selling alcohol. It gave rise to organized crime and let men like Gatsby get rich fast through bootlegging, the glittering facade of a morally corrupt era.

course_112_le_grand_gatsby_fitzgerald|Hi.explanation: Recurring theme in the novel linked to T.J. Eckleburg's billboard, suggesting a modern world where spirituality has been replaced by commerce and where morality only persists as a simulacrum.

course_113_le_seigneur_des_anneaux_tolki.explanation: Tolkien's idea of "sub-creation": the writer builds a secondary world with its own laws and its own consistency. The reader steps into it through "secondary belief", a willing suspension of disbelief. Tolkien saw this as an almost divine act.

Tolkien, a professor of Old English at Oxford, was deeply inspired by Beowulf, the Norse Edda, and the Finnish Kalevala. His avowed goal: to create a mythology for England, which did not possess one like Greece or Scandinavia.
Subgenre of fantasy taking place in a completely imaginary world, involving epic stakes of the struggle between good and evil and strong mythological consistency.
Also called Anglo-Saxon, it is the ancient form of the English language spoken between the 5th and 11th centuries, of which Tolkien was a world expert.
In Tolkien's mythology, divine spirits of lower rank than the Valar (the gods). Sauron and Gandalf are Maiar.
The principal kingdom of Men in the south of Middle-earth, the bastion of resistance against Sauron.
Informal literary circle at Oxford centered around Tolkien and C.S. Lewis, where members read their works currenty in progress.

course_114_fahrenheit_451_bradbury|McCar.explanation: A period of anti-communist witch hunts, when artists and writers were blacklisted. What worried Bradbury was censorship by fear, the social and political pressure on thought, far more than the burning of books.

course_114_fahrenheit_451_bradbury|The e.displayTerm: The entertainment society and fragmented attention
course_114_fahrenheit_451_bradbury|The e.explanation: Bradbury anticipated self-censorship through entertainment: people so saturated with fast media that they no longer wish to read. The "parlors" (wall-screens) in the novel anticipate television and later smartphones.

course_114_fahrenheit_451_bradbury|1984.explanation: Novel by George Orwell (1949) describing a totalitarian dictatorship based on surveillance and the direct repression of thought by the state.

course_114_fahrenheit_451_bradbury|mass.explanation: Economic and social model that appeared in the 20th century, characterized by the standardization of products and the permanent stimulation of the desire to buy among citizens.

course_114_fahrenheit_451_bradbury|enter.explanation: Bradbury anticipated self-censorship through entertainment: people so saturated with fast-paced media that they no longer have the desire to read. The "parlors" (wall-screens) in the novel anticipate television and then smartphones.

course_114_fahrenheit_451_bradbury|provi.explanation: A superior force that guides human events toward a specific end, often identified here with divine will.

course_115_cent_ans_de_solitude_garcia_m.explanation: A literary style that presents magical events with the same naturalness as real events, without surprise or explanation. Emerging from a Latin American tradition where the marvelous is part of daily life.

course_115_cent_ans_de_solitude_garcia_m.displayTerm: The United Fruit Company and the "banana republics"
course_115_cent_ans_de_solitude_garcia_m.explanation: The banana company in the novel refers to the American United Fruit Company which economically dominated several Central American countries. A massacre of striking workers that it caused inspired a key scene in the novel.
Novel by Gabriel García Márquez published in 1967, considered one of the summits of 20th-century world literature.
Classical language of ancient India used by Melquíades in the novel to encode the prophecies about the Buendía family.
Peruvian writer, major figure of the Latin American Literature Boom and friend (then rival) of García Márquez.

course_116_la_metamorphose_kafka|The Met.explanation: Major novella of world literature (1915) relating the sudden transformation of Gregor Samsa into an insect.

course_116_la_metamorphose_kafka|Max Bro.explanation: Close friend and literary executor of Kafka who, contrary to his wishes, published his manuscripts posthumously.

course_116_la_metamorphose_kafka|Kafkaes.explanation: Adjective designating a situation that is absurd, oppressive, and illogical, typical of the bureaucratic and distressing universe described by the author.

course_116_la_metamorphose_kafka|boarder.explanation: Individuals who rent a room and take their meals in a private home; their presence at the Samsas' accelerates Gregor's exclusion.

course_116_la_metamorphose_kafka|Metamor.explanation: A major work of world Literature (1915) recounting the sudden transformation of Gregor Samsa into an insect.

course_117_le_maitre_et_marguerite_boulg.explanation: NKVD of the USSR under Stalin, ancestor of the KGB, responsible for the repression and surveillance of citizens.
System of clandestine distribution of writings banned by the Soviet power, reproduced by hand or by typewriter.
Official artistic doctrine of the USSR requiring art to serve the party and represent reality in a heroic and pro-communist light.
Three divine sisters born old, possessing only one eye and one tooth for the three of them, guardians of the path to the Gorgons.
Sea nymphs, daughters of Nereus, offended by the vanity of Queen Cassiopeia.
A superior force that guides human events toward a specific end, often identified here with divine will.
Deities in charge of human destiny, represented as spinners (Roman equivalent of the Moirai).

course_118_moby_dick_melville|American l.explanation: The body of literary works produced in the United States, marked in the 19th century by the emergence of a national voice distinct from Europe.

course_118_moby_dick_melville|Marquesas.explanation: An archipelago in French Polynesia where Melville stayed in 1842 after deserting his whaleship, an experience that inspired his first novels.

course_118_moby_dick_melville|Typee.explanation: Melville's first novel (1846), a semi-autobiographical account of his adventures among a cannibalistic tribe, which was his greatest success during his lifetime.

course_118_moby_dick_melville|Literary c.explanation: A collection of works considered fundamental, exemplary, and worthy of being taught within a given culture.

course_118_moby_dick_melville|New Bedfor.explanation: A coastal city in Massachusetts that was the whaling industry capital of the world in the mid-19th century.

course_118_moby_dick_melville|Queequeg.explanation: Tattooed Polynesian harpooner of the Pequod, Ishmael's loyal friend, representing savage nobility and pre-Christian wisdom.

course_118_moby_dick_melville|Starbuck.explanation: First mate of the Pequod, a pragmatic and courageous Quaker who opposes Ahab's vengeful madness in the name of common sense.

course_118_moby_dick_melville|Stubb.explanation: Second mate of the Pequod, characterized by his jovial phlegm and his pipe, facing the dangers of the sea with indifference.

course_118_moby_dick_melville|Flask.explanation: Third mate of the Pequod, nicknamed 'King-Post', seeing the whale as mere prey to be killed without any sentiment.

course_118_moby_dick_melville|Cetology.explanation: Branch of zoology that studies cetaceans (whales, sperm whales, dolphins).

course_118_moby_dick_melville|Sperm whal.explanation: Large toothed marine mammal, hunted in the 19th century for its oil and the spermaceti located in its head.

course_118_moby_dick_melville|Spermaceti.explanation: Or spermaceti, a waxy substance located in the head of the sperm whale, used to make high-quality candles.

course_118_moby_dick_melville|Leviathan.explanation: Marine monster from Biblical mythology, often used to refer to a creature or structure of colossal and terrifying power.

course_118_moby_dick_melville|Malignity.explanation: Propensity to do evil, deliberate wickedness. In the novel, Ahab projects this intention onto the animal.

course_118_moby_dick_melville|Providence.explanation: A superior force that guides human events toward a specific end, often identified here with divine will.

course_119_le_petit_prince_saint_exupery.explanation: City of exile for Saint-Exupéry between 1940 and 1943, where he wrote The Little Prince.
Island near New York where Saint-Exupéry resided while writing the tale.
American publishing house that published the very first edition of The Little Prince in 1943.
Twin-engine reconnaissance aircraft model piloted by Saint-Exupéry during his final mission.
Giant trees that, in the tale, symbolize dangers or bad thoughts that must be rooted out as soon as they appear.
Name given to a real asteroid as a tribute to asteroid B-612 from The Little Prince.
French airmail company where Saint-Exupéry worked.

course_120_l_alchimiste_paulo_coelho|The.explanation: Novel by Paulo Coelho published in 1988, telling the initiatory quest of a shepherd named Santiago.

course_120_l_alchimiste_paulo_coelho|the.explanation: Novel by Paulo Coelho published in 1988, telling the initiatory quest of a shepherd named Santiago.

course_120_l_alchimiste_paulo_coelho|Rau.explanation: Famous Brazilian rocker from the 1970s with whom Paulo Coelho collaborated as a lyricist.

course_120_l_alchimiste_paulo_coelho|San.explanation: Famous Catholic pilgrimage that Coelho walked, inspiring his spiritual renewal and his writing.

course_120_l_alchimiste_paulo_coelho|Roc.explanation: Major Brazilian publishing house that took over the publication of The Alchemist and made it a success.

course_120_l_alchimiste_paulo_coelho|mai.explanation: Dominant cultural movements aimed at the widest possible audience and benefiting from massive distribution.

course_120_l_alchimiste_paulo_coelho|Tan.explanation: Port city in Morocco where Santiago arrives at the beginning of his African journey.

course_120_l_alchimiste_paulo_coelho|Sah.explanation: The largest hot desert in the world, which Santiago must cross to reach Egypt.

course_120_l_alchimiste_paulo_coelho|Mak.explanation: Arabic expression meaning 'it was written', highlighting the conviction that certain events are predestined.

course_120_l_alchimiste_paulo_coelho|per.explanation: Movement of thought and Literature aimed at improving the quality of life and realizing one's potential.

course_120_l_alchimiste_paulo_coelho|Alc.explanation: Novel by Paulo Coelho published in 1988, telling the initiatory quest of a shepherd named Santiago.

course_121_la_renaissance_italienne|Rena.explanation: An intellectual movement centering reflection on the human being, drawing inspiration from rediscovered Greek and Roman texts. Humanists (Petrarch, Erasmus) valued liberal education, human dignity, and the development of individual faculties.

course_121_la_renaissance_italienne|Line.explanation: A technique developed by Brunelleschi around 1415: parallel lines converge toward a vanishing point, creating an illusion of depth on a flat surface. This revolution in gaze radically distinguishes Renaissance painting from medieval art.

course_121_la_renaissance_italienne|Patr.explanation: Financial and politics support provided by a powerful figure (the patron) to artists or writers, often in exchange for the production of works to their glory.

course_121_la_renaissance_italienne|Pico.explanation: Italian humanist philosopher, author of the 'Oration on the Dignity of Man', a founding text that places human freedom at the heart of creation.

course_121_la_renaissance_italienne|Temp.explanation: Medieval painting technique using egg yolk to bind pigments, replaced during the Renaissance by oil painting, which was more flexible and luminous.

course_121_la_renaissance_italienne|Chia.explanation: Painting technique consisting of producing violent contrasts between areas of light and areas of shadow to create volume and drama.

course_121_la_renaissance_italienne|Mann.explanation: Artistic movement from the end of the Renaissance (c. 1520-1580) characterized by the rejection of classical harmony in favor of elongated forms and complex compositions.

course_121_la_renaissance_italienne|Rena.explanation: Intellectual movement centering reflection on the human being, inspired by rediscovered Greek and Roman texts. Humanists (Petrarch, Erasmus) valued liberal education, human dignity, and the development of individual faculties.

course_122_la_naissance_de_l_impressionn.explanation: Annual exhibition of the Academy of Fine Arts, the only showcase for art in France in the 19th century. Being rejected meant commercial invisibility.

course_122_la_naissance_de_l_impressionn.displayTerm: Paint tubes and the plein air
course_122_la_naissance_de_l_impressionn.explanation: The invention of the metal paint tube in 1841 let painters work outdoors. Before that, paint oxidized too quickly. This humble technical advance was what made the impressionist revolution physically possible.
Artistic or intellectual movement that breaks with the conventions of the past to explore new aesthetic paths.
French chemist whose 'law of simultaneous contrast of colors' (1839) theoretically founded the use of complementary colors by the impressionists.
Famous Parisian establishment where the avant-garde (Manet, Monet, Renoir, Zola) met to debate modern painting.
Bold art dealer who financially supported the impressionists and enabled their international success, particularly in the United States.
Woodblock prints (Ukiyo-e) that arrived in Europe in the 19th century, whose asymmetrical framing and flat areas of color fascinated Degas and Monet.
Movement succeeding impressionism, led by Georges Seurat, scientifically applying the decomposition of color in the form of dots.
State body that ran art education and the Salon in Paris in the 19th century, imposing strict classical standards.
Emperor of the French who, faced with the artistic crisis of 1863, authorized the creation of the Salon des Refusés.
Exhibition organized in 1863 to present the works rejected by the official Salon jury, marking the beginning of the divide between modern and academic art.
Painter and precursor of modernity, whose painting [Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe] caused a major scandal in 1863.
Leader of the impressionism movement, famous for his series exploring light such as [Les Nymphéas] or [La Cathédrale de Rouen].
Ability of the visual system to merge two images to perceive depth and, in the case of impressionism, to merge juxtaposed brushstrokes of color.
Colors opposite each other on the chromatic circle (e.g., red/green). Their juxtaposition reinforces the vibrancy of each.
One of the major figures of impressionism, known for her scenes of bourgeois life and her clear touch.
National museum in Paris housing the largest collection of impressionist and post-impressionist works in the world.
The invention of metal paint tubes (1841) allowed painters to work outdoors. This innovation was a material condition for the Impressionist revolution.

course_123_le_caravage_et_le_clair_obscu.explanation: 17th-century artistic style characterized by movement, dramatic contrast, theatricality, and a strong emotional charge aiming to impress the viewer.
Major Italian painter (1593-1656), follower of Caravaggism, famous for her scenes of strength and female vengeance with striking realism.
Birth name of Caravaggio, which he abandoned in favor of the name of his home village to avoid confusion with Michelangelo (Buonarroti).
Coastal town in Tuscany where Caravaggio died of illness and exhaustion in 1610, while attempting to return to Rome to obtain his pardon.
Movement of the Catholic Church aiming to strengthen faith and respond to the Protestant Reformation, notably using art as a tool of persuasion and emotion.
Artistic style of the late Renaissance characterized by elongated forms, complex compositions and a deliberate rejection of naturalism in favor of artifice.

course_124_rembrandt_et_l_ecole_flamande.explanation: In the 17th century, the United Provinces became the world's leading commercial power. This prosperity created a wealthy Protestant middle class that wanted portraits, genre scenes, and landscapes - a market that allowed Rembrandt and Vermeer to exist.

Rembrandt went bankrupt at the height of his reputation, after spending lavishly on art collections. His possessions were sold at auction. This ruin forced him to paint under the names of his wife Hendrickje and his son Titus.
Pictorial technique playing on violent contrasts between light and shadow areas to create volume and dramatic depth.
In 1656, following massive debts related to his lifestyle and collections, Rembrandt was declared insolvent, losing all his material possessions.
Headquarters of the Amsterdam musketeers, where the large group portraits of the civic guards were originally displayed.
Dutch painter contemporary of Rembrandt, famous for his quiet interior scenes and his masterful use of natural light.
Frans Hals, great Dutch portraitist of the Golden Age, famous for his quick touch and for capturing the laughing psychology of his models.
Italian painter from the late 16th century, inventor of the tenebrist style which uses violent light contrasts to dramatize the scene.
20th-century British painter, whose work on the deformation of flesh and the expression of pain is directly inspired by Rembrandt's technical freedom.

course_125_le_romantisme_en_peinture_del.explanation: Dominant style in France from the Revolution until the 1820s: clarity, noble subjects from Antiquity, primacy of drawing over color. The Revolution and Napoleon made it their official style.
English playwright (1564-1616) whose tragic and passionate works were a major source of inspiration for romantic painters.
Lord Byron (1788-1824), a British poet embodying the tormented and committed romantic hero, who died during the Greek War of Independence.
A current of thought aimed at the abolition of slavery, a cause supported by Géricault in his portraits of Black men.
The Parisian revolution of July 27, 28, and 29, 1830, which overthrew King Charles X in favor of Louis-Philippe I.
A 19th-century artistic movement fascinated by the cultures of North Africa and the Near East, often fantasized or discovered during expeditions.
Théodore Géricault (1791-1824), French painter whose brief career laid the foundations of romanticism with dramatic works rooted in reality.
Eugène Delacroix (1798-1863), leader of the French Romantic school, famous for his bold use of color and his politics and exotic subjects.
French painter (1780-1867), champion of Neoclassicism and great rival of Delacroix, favoring the perfection of line over colorful emotion.

course_126_le_cubisme_picasso_et_braque|.displayTerm: African and Oceanic art as influence
course_126_le_cubisme_picasso_et_braque|.explanation: Picasso's discovery of African masks around 1906-1907 was a revelation: an art that did not seek to imitate reality but to provide a symbolic and structural representation of it. Decisive for the Demoiselles d'Avignon.

Innovation of synthetic Cubism (1912): Braque and Picasso pasted pieces of newspapers and wallpaper into their paintings. By integrating fragments of reality into the work of art, they blurred the boundary between representation and reality.
Refers to the 15th century in Italy, a period marked by the invention of linear perspective and the renewal of the arts.
A pictorial technique initiated by Cézanne, consisting of sliding planes into one another to break the continuity of volumes.
A collection of ritual works (masks, sculptures) whose geometric and symbolic structure inspired Picasso to move away from European realism.
Former Parisian museum of ethnography where avant-garde artists discovered non-Western arts at the beginning of the 20th century.
French poet and art critic (1880-1918), tireless defender of Cubism and author of 'The Cubist Painters'.
Collective of Cubist artists (Duchamp, Léger, Delaunay) who favored a more theoretical and colorful approach than that of Picasso.
Discipline that uses imagery and typography to communicate; it inherited the deconstruction of layout from Cubism.
Innovation consisting of integrating fragments of reality (newspapers, fabrics) into the work, blurring the boundary between representation and reality.

course_127_le_surrealisme_dali_et_magrit.explanation: Surrealism was directly inspired by Freud: the unconscious as a reservoir of repressed images, dreams as the royal road to the unconscious, free association. André Breton had met Freud in 1921 and wanted to liberate the unconscious in art.

Surrealist method: writing or painting without conscious control, letting the unconscious speak directly. Breton used it as a poetic tool, and Dalí built his own painterly version of it with the paranoiac-critical method.

Collective game invented by the surrealists consisting of composing a sentence or a drawing by several people, without any of them being able to take into account the previous collaboration or collaborations.
Pictorial or literary style that integrates marvelous or irrational elements into a realistic framework, creating a sense of strangeness without shifting into pure fantasy.
Artistic and literary movement (1916-1923) born out of horror at the Great War, which attacked conventions, meaning, and institutions at the root.
Small fishing village in Catalonia where Salvador Dalí established his primary residence and studio, whose rocky landscapes appear in many of his canvases.

course_128_l_expressionnisme_munch_et_le.displayTerm: German Expressionism (Die Brücke, Der Blaue Reiter)
course_128_l_expressionnisme_munch_et_le.explanation: German artistic currents (1905-1920) pushing expressionism to the extreme: radical distortion of forms, gaudy colors, distressing themes. Kirchner, Kandinsky, Nolde reacted to modernization and heralded the trauma of 1914.

course_128_l_expressionnisme_munch_et_le.displayTerm: The eruption of Krakatoa (1883) and the red sky
course_128_l_expressionnisme_munch_et_le.explanation: The catastrophic eruption of Krakatoa threw ash into the air that colored sunsets blood-red around the world for months. Munch noted in his diary that he had seen a sky of "blood and fire", probably this very phenomenon.
Process of breaking with traditional beliefs and the sense of loss of meaning in the face of the rationalization and modernization of society.
What belongs to the person looking rather than to the thing looked at. In art, it means putting personal, emotional perception ahead of factual observation.
Absence of meaning or foundation of existence, a central theme of existentialist philosophy that finds a visual echo in the work of Munch.
Hill overlooking Oslo where Munch was walking when he had the visual epiphany that inspired "The Scream".
Norwegian museum holding the most famous version (1893) of the painting "The Scream".
Artistic movement exploring the mechanisms of the unconscious and dreams, partly influenced by the freedom of expression found in expressionism.
19th-century philosophical doctrine which considers that only the knowledge of scientific facts and law is real, rejecting metaphysics.
Aesthetic concept from Antiquity designating the imitation or faithful representation of reality in art.

course_128_l_expressionnisme_munch_et_le.displayTerm: Eruption of Krakatoa (1883) and the red sky
course_128_l_expressionnisme_munch_et_le.explanation: The catastrophic eruption of Krakatoa threw up ash that colored sunsets blood-red around the world for months. Munch noted in his diary that he had seen a red sky "of blood and fire", probably this very phenomenon.

course_129_l_art_abstrait_kandinsky_et_m.displayTerm: The Bauhaus and the art-industry synthesis
course_129_l_art_abstrait_kandinsky_et_m.explanation: School of art and design founded in Weimar in 1919 which attempted to reconcile the major arts and applied arts. Kandinsky and Klee taught there. Its minimalist and functional aesthetic is omnipresent in contemporary design.

Dutch movement founded in 1917: reducing art to its purest elements - horizontal and vertical lines, primary colors, white and black. Mondrian sought a universal visual language beyond any specific culture.
Greek term designating the imitation of nature or the real world in art. Abstraction is the first total break with this several-millennia-old principle.
Metaphorical process by which an artist like Mondrian progressively purifies his vision of reality to keep only its essential lines of force.
Trend in abstract art, initiated by Kandinsky, which favors the direct expression of emotions and interiority through organic forms and free color play.
German architect (1883-1969), founder of the Bauhaus. He advocated rationalist architecture and the marriage between craftsmanship and industrial methods.
Post-war artistic movement, primarily American, favoring the artist's instinctive gesture (action painting) and the raw expression of emotions.
Artistic current of the 1960s advocating extreme simplicity, often using simple geometric shapes and industrial materials.
Movement where the definition or the idea of the work takes precedence over its aesthetics or material realization.

School of art and design founded in Weimar in 1919 which attempted to reconcile fine arts and applied arts. Kandinsky and Klee taught there. Its minimalist and functional aesthetic is omnipresent in contemporary design.

course_130_le_pop_art_warhol_et_lichtens.explanation: After the war, the American economy produced unprecedented abundance. Advertising and mass media created a culture of standardized images that Pop Art used as artistic material, questioning the boundary between art and product.

course_130_le_pop_art_warhol_et_lichtens.displayTerm: The aura and mechanical reproduction (Walter Benjamin)
course_130_le_pop_art_warhol_et_lichtens.explanation: Benjamin (1935) analyzed how technical reproduction destroys the "aura" of the unique work. Warhol radicalized this idea: by mechanically reproducing popular images, he questioned the very notion of original and author.
Collective of British artists, architects and critics formed in 1952 in London, considered the precursor of Pop Art through its interest in American popular culture.
Printing technique using a silk screen as a stencil. Andy Warhol used it to produce series of works of art, challenging the unique nature of painting.
Industrial printing process created by Benjamin Day in 1879, consisting of small colored dots. Lichtenstein reproduced them by hand to imitate the aesthetic of comic books.

Dominant artistic movement after the Second World War (Pollock, Rothko), prioritizing subjective expression, spontaneous gesture, and the rejection of figuration, which Pop Art would oppose through its return to mundane reality.

Benjamin (1935) analyzed how technical reproduction destroys the "aura" of the unique work. Warhol radicalized this idea: by mechanically reproducing popular images, he questioned the very notion of original and author.

course_131_la_naissance_de_la_musique_el.explanation: First electronic instrument (1920), played without physical contact: two antennas detect the position of the hands and control pitch and volume. Its ethereal sound was used in 1950s horror films and by the Beach Boys.

House (Chicago, 1984) used drum machines and deep bass lines. Techno (Detroit, 1986-1988) was colder and more mechanical. Both emerged from marginalized Black and Latino communities and became world phenomena.
Weekly rankings of best-selling or most-played records.
Process of extracting a sound snippet (sample) to reintegrate it into a new composition.
Digital Audio Workstation. A set of digital tools for composing, recording and mixing music on a computer.
Musical genre born in the mid-1980s in Chicago clubs (such as the Warehouse), characterized by a repetitive 4/4 rhythm and soul and disco influences.

course_132_bob_dylan_et_la_folk_protest|.explanation: Rediscovery of traditional American music by urban artists in the 1950s-60s. Pete Seeger and Woody Guthrie made folk the soundtrack of the labor and civil rights movements. Dylan was its prodigal heir.

In the Guthrie tradition, protest folk used accessible melodies to spread political messages. Dylan's "Blowin' in the Wind" and "The Times They Are A-Changin'" became anthems of the Civil Rights Movement.
Literary and artistic movement born in the 1950s (Kerouac, Ginsberg) advocating sexual liberation, spiritual quest and spontaneous writing. It strongly influenced Dylan's writing.
One of the oldest and most powerful American record labels, which signed Bob Dylan in 1961.
Iconic electric guitar model. The one used by Dylan at Newport in 1965 became one of the most famous instruments in the history of rock.

course_133_le_hip_hop_naissance_d_une_cu.explanation: New York urban planner who built urban highways devastating working-class neighborhoods in the Bronx during the 1950s-60s. The Cross-Bronx Expressway destroyed 60,000 housing units, creating the conditions of dereliction in which hip-hop was born.

Technique consisting of using extracts from existing records as the basis for a new work. Legally problematic, sampling was recognized as a form of legitimate artistic creation after long legal battles.
A major highway crossing the Bronx, whose construction between 1948 and 1972 physically and socially restructured the neighborhood.
New York urban planner whose massive infrastructure projects favored automobiles, leading to the economic decline of working-class neighborhoods like the Bronx.
Financial practice aimed at profiting from price variations of goods; in the Bronx of the 1970s, it led to intentional fires to collect insurance money.
DJ technique consisting of manipulating a vinyl record by hand to produce rhythmic, percussive sounds.
Iconic East Coast (New York) rapper in the 1990s, recognized for his technical virtuosity and autobiographical narratives.
Central figure of West Coast rap, poet and actor, who became a global icon after his tragic death in 1996.

course_134_l_opera_de_verdi|The Italian.explanation: Movement for Italy's national reunification (circa 1815-1871). Verdi's operas - notably "Va, pensiero" from Nabucco - became nationalist anthems. Verdi himself was a symbol: his name was used as an acronym for Vittorio Emanuele, Re D'Italia.

course_134_l_opera_de_verdi|Opera seria.explanation: Two Italian genres: opera seria (noble subjects, tragedy) and opera buffa (comic subjects, ordinary characters). Verdi excelled in opera seria but renewed the genres by integrating realistic psychological drama and social tension.

course_134_l_opera_de_verdi|Bel canto.explanation: Italian singing style favoring the beauty of the timbre, the fluidity of melodic lines and technical virtuosity, sometimes at the expense of dramatic veracity.

course_134_l_opera_de_verdi|Recitative.explanation: A form of declaimed singing, close to speech, used in opera to move the action forward between two more melodic arias.

course_134_l_opera_de_verdi|Verismo.explanation: A trend in late 19th-century Italian opera (Puccini, Mascagni) that seeks to represent social reality in a raw and violent way.

course_134_l_opera_de_verdi|Cavour.explanation: Camillo Benso, Count of Cavour (1810-1861), Piedmontese statesman and the politics architect of Italian unification.

course_134_l_opera_de_verdi|Opera seria.explanation: Two Italian genres: opera seria (noble subjects, tragic) and opera buffa (comic subjects, ordinary characters). Verdi excelled in opera seria but renewed the genres by integrating realistic psychological drama and social tension.

course_135_mozart_enfant_prodige_et_vie_.displayTerm: The status of the musician in the 18th century
course_135_mozart_enfant_prodige_et_vie_.explanation: Social status where the musician is considered a servant attached to a nobleman or a prelate, having to compose and play according to the desires of his patron.

The Magic Flute (1791) is a masonic allegory: Tamino's initiatory trials, the struggle between light/darkness reflect the masonic rituals and ideals of the Enlightenment to which Mozart had adhered since 1784.
19th-century artistic movement favoring the expression of feelings and individuality, of which Mozart is considered a precursor due to his sensitivity.
17th-century Italian composer, author of the famous 'Miserere' which Mozart transcribed from memory at the age of 14.
Fraternal organization with initiatory rituals whose ideals of liberty and equality strongly influenced the philosophy and the final works of Mozart.
Period of the history of music (1750-1820) characterized by clarity, balanced forms, and restraint, of which Mozart is the most accomplished representative.
Mozart's last opera (1791), blending folk tale and Masonic symbolism, written in German for a popular theater.

course_136_beethoven_genie_et_surdite|\".explanation: Absolute music (Beethoven) expresses pure emotions without external reference. Program music (Berlioz, Liszt) tells a story. This distinction structures the great aesthetic debate of the romantic 19th century.

course_136_beethoven_genie_et_surdite|Th.displayTerm: The Ode to Joy and the European anthem
course_136_beethoven_genie_et_surdite|Th.explanation: The last movement of the 9th Symphony, based on Schiller's poem, became the official anthem of the European Union in 1985. The universalism of its message (brotherhood of humanity) makes it the symbol of the European ideal of unity.

course_136_beethoven_genie_et_surdite|Mo.explanation: Prodigious Austrian composer (1756-1791) whose immediate successor Beethoven's father wanted his son to become.

course_136_beethoven_genie_et_surdite|Br.explanation: German composer (1833-1897) who took more than twenty years to complete his first symphony, crushed by the monumental shadow of Beethoven.

course_136_beethoven_genie_et_surdite|Ma.explanation: Composer and conductor (1860-1911) who pushed the symphony genre to its expressive and structural limits after Beethoven.

course_136_beethoven_genie_et_surdite|ab.explanation: Aesthetic concept designating music that does not depend on any external narrative or visual support, existing for its own sonic structures.

course_136_beethoven_genie_et_surdite|Na.explanation: General then Emperor of the French whose initial republican ideals fascinated Beethoven, before his imperial coronation provoked the composer's anger.

course_136_beethoven_genie_et_surdite|he.explanation: Creative period of Beethoven marked by grandiose works evoking struggle, victory, and resilience in the face of fate.

course_136_beethoven_genie_et_surdite|Bo.explanation: City in North Germany, capital of the Electorate of Cologne, where Beethoven was born and spent his youth.

course_136_beethoven_genie_et_surdite|Vi.explanation: Capital of the Austrian Empire and world center of classical music where Beethoven spent most of his career.

course_136_beethoven_genie_et_surdite|Ro.explanation: 19th-century artistic movement emphasizing the expression of feelings, imagination, and subjectivity over classical rigor.

course_136_beethoven_genie_et_surdite|\".explanation: The absolute music (Beethoven) expresses pure emotions without external reference. Program music (Berlioz, Liszt) tells a story. This distinction structures the great aesthetic debate of the romantic 19th century.

course_136_beethoven_genie_et_surdite|Od.explanation: The last movement of the 9th Symphony, based on Schiller's poem, became the official anthem of the European Union in 1985. The universalism of its message (brotherhood of humanity) makes it the symbol of the European ideal of unity.

course_137_la_naissance_du_rock_n_roll|S.displayTerm: Segregation in the American music industry
course_137_la_naissance_du_rock_n_roll|S.explanation: American radio stations in the 1940s and 50s refused to broadcast "race music" (blues, R&B) on "white" stations. The birth of rock'n'roll occurred largely when white artists covered Black styles, raising questions of cultural appropriation.

course_137_la_naissance_du_rock_n_roll|R.explanation: A 1940s genre combining electrified blues, jazz, and gospel, created by Black artists. Rhythm and blues was the direct foundation of rock'n'roll: Elvis and Chuck Berry were directly inspired by it.

course_137_la_naissance_du_rock_n_roll|G.explanation: Christian vocal music of Afro-American tradition, characterized by rich harmonies and strong emotional intensity.

course_137_la_naissance_du_rock_n_roll|S.explanation: Founder of the Sun Records studio in Memphis, he is the producer who discovered Elvis Presley and was looking for a white man capable of singing the blues.
Social and politics process of physical and institutional separation of populations according to their racial origin in force in the United States until the 1960s.

course_137_la_naissance_du_rock_n_roll|J.explanation: Set of state and local laws enforcing racial segregation in the Southern United States between 1877 and 1964.

course_137_la_naissance_du_rock_n_roll|C.explanation: Practice of re-recording an original song by another artist, often used in the 1950s to have Black hits performed by White artists.
Politics and social struggle in the United States (1954-1968) to end racial segregation and guarantee voting rights for African Americans.

course_137_la_naissance_du_rock_n_roll|S.explanation: Independent record label founded in Memphis by Sam Phillips, specialized in blues and country, driving force behind the birth of rockabilly.

course_137_la_naissance_du_rock_n_roll|A.explanation: Influential American disc jockey credited with popularizing the term "rock'n'roll" on the radio to describe this new hybrid style.

course_138_bach_et_la_musique_baroque|Co.explanation: Counterpoint is the art of combining several independent melodies according to harmonic rules. The fugue is its most elaborate form: a theme is stated by different voices in turn, then developed in increasingly complex combinations.

course_138_bach_et_la_musique_baroque|Eq.explanation: Bach's "Well-Tempered Clavier" (48 preludes and fugues in all keys) demonstrated that a uniform tuning allowed playing in all keys without sounding out of tune. This system is the one used by all modern instruments.

course_138_bach_et_la_musique_baroque|ca.explanation: Title given to the director of music and choirs of a church or religious school in Germany, responsible for liturgical music.

course_138_bach_et_la_musique_baroque|Co.explanation: Musical ensemble founded in Leipzig by Telemann and directed by Bach, composed of students and professionals performing secular concerts in coffee houses.

course_138_bach_et_la_musique_baroque|st.explanation: Musical aesthetic of the mid-18th century favoring simplicity, melodic clarity, and elegance, opposing the Baroque complexity of Bach.

course_138_bach_et_la_musique_baroque|nu.explanation: Practice of assigning numbers to letters or notes to insert hidden meanings or names into a score.

course_138_bach_et_la_musique_baroque|Go.explanation: Disk onboard the Voyager probes containing sounds and images from Earth, including Bach's Prelude and Fugue No. 1.

course_138_bach_et_la_musique_baroque|Th.explanation: School attached to St. Thomas Church in Leipzig, where Bach taught music and Latin to the boys of the choir.

course_138_bach_et_la_musique_baroque|ca.explanation: Vocal musical genre composed of several movements (arias, recitatives, choruses) with instrumental accompaniment, central to the Lutheran liturgy.

course_139_la_naissance_du_jazz_americai.explanation: Place where Louisiana law allowed enslaved people to gather on Sundays to play and dance. This unique location in North America allowed for the preservation of African musical traditions which, combined with European harmony, gave birth to jazz.

Unlike classical music, jazz makes improvisation its heart: the musician invents their melodic line in real time, over an agreed harmonic grid, in response to the others. It is both total freedom and a demanding discipline.
City in Louisiana, a major cultural crossroads where the blend of French, Spanish, African, and Caribbean influences allowed for the birth of jazz.
Characteristic notes of blues and jazz whose frequency is lowered by a semitone, creating an expressive and melancholic tension.
Series of state and local laws in the United States imposing racial segregation between 1877 and 1964.
Style of jazz based on the use of modes (scales) rather than rapid chord changes, favoring a freer and more melodic improvisation.
avant-garde movement born in the 1960s seeking to break the conventional structures of jazz (tempo, fixed chords).
Style combining jazz improvisation with rock electric instruments and funk rhythms.
Balanced rhythmic effect produced by shifted accentuation of beats, creating a propulsion sensation characteristic of jazz.
Style of jazz that emerged in the 1940s, characterized by fast tempos, complex harmonies, and an orientation toward intellectual listening rather than dancing.
Renewal movement of African-American culture in the 1920s in New York, spanning literature, arts, and jazz music.
Massive movement of six million African Americans from the rural Southern United States to the industrial North and West between 1916 and 1970, encouraging the spread of jazz.

course_140_le_blues_racines_de_toute_la_.explanation: The founding harmonic architecture of the blues: a sequence of 12-bar in three parts (tonic, subdominant, dominant) that repeats. This infinitely variable structure is the grid upon which the blues is improvised and is found in rock, jazz, and pop.

"Bent" notes between two notes of the standard scale, played slightly below their usual pitch. These microtonal inflections come from the African vocal tradition and give blues its specific expressive and poignant character.
Sociocultural and geographical region of the southeastern United States (Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia...), the historical heart of slavery and the birthplace of African-American music.
A cappella calls or songs improvised by Black workers on plantations, vocal precursors to the blues used to express emotion or communicate.
Collective work songs structured by a regular rhythm, helping to coordinate repetitive movement (cotton picking, track laying) and to endure the hardship.
Literally "bottle neck". Object slid onto a finger to play the guitar, producing a sliding and mournful sound typical of Delta blues.
Christian religious songs created by African-American slaves, blending spiritual fervor and the hope for earthly liberation.
Guitar technique consisting of plucking the strings directly with the fingers rather than with a plectrum, allowing the bass and melody to be played simultaneously.
The 'intersection', a symbolic place in African-American folklore where the physical and spiritual world meet, central to the myth of Robert Johnson's pact.
Process consisting of isolating a sound excerpt from a pre-existing recording to reuse it in a new composition, the technical basis of hip-hop.
Three divine sisters born old, possessing only one eye and one tooth between the three, guardians of the path to the Gorgons.

course_141_la_naissance_de_la_photograph.explanation: Photographic process on paper (circa 1840) allowing for several prints to be made from a negative - unlike the unique daguerreotype. It is the direct ancestor of film photography used until the digital age.

course_141_la_naissance_de_la_photograph.displayTerm: The impact of photography on figurative painting
course_141_la_naissance_de_la_photograph.explanation: Photography freed painting from its documentary function. Painters no longer had to immortalization faces or battles - photography did it better and for less. This liberation is one of the conditions for impressionism and then abstraction.
Optical device (camera obscura) consisting of a closed box with a small hole letting light through to project an inverted image of the outside world onto a wall.
Natural photosensitive substance used by Niépce for the first photograph; it has the property of hardening under the action of light.
Portrait photograph format patented by Disdéri in 1854, allowing multiple prints to be made on the same plate and drastically reducing prices.
Pictorial movement born in reaction to photography, favoring the rendering of light sensations and the moment rather than the precision of the line.
Artistic movement from the early 20th century that deconstructs objects into geometric shapes, definitively breaking with realistic perspective.
Set of ways in which a society perceives, interprets, and consumes images, which became predominant with the advent of photography.

course_141_la_naissance_de_la_photograph.displayTerm: Impact of photography on figurative painting
course_141_la_naissance_de_la_photograph.explanation: Photography liberated painting from its documentary function. Painters no longer had to immortalize faces or battles - photography did it better and cheaper. This liberation was one of the conditions for Impressionism and then abstraction.

course_142_charlie_chaplin_et_le_cinema_.displayTerm: The Lumière brothers and early cinema
course_142_charlie_chaplin_et_le_cinema_.explanation: Cinema was born in France (Enlightenment, 1895) but became industrialized in the United States. Hollywood established itself in the 1910s-1920s thanks to the Californian sun, the diversity of landscapes, and the massive immigration of European talent.

A comic genre of silent cinema based on physical gags, falls, chases, and grotesque violence. The term comes from a theater prop. Charlot brought this genre to its perfection by adding emotional depth and social criticism.
Apparatus invented by the Lumière brothers serving as both a shooting camera and a cinema projector.
French filmmaker and illusionist, pioneer of special effects and creator of the famous film 'A Trip to the Moon' (1902).
Variety show (songs, gags, acrobatics) very popular in the United Kingdom where Chaplin got his start on stage.
American Federal Bureau of Investigation which, under the leadership of J. Edgar Hoover, tracked Chaplin for his politics deemed too far-left.
Period of geopolitical tensions between the United States and the USSR (1947-1991), marked by anti-communist paranoia in America.
Film studio founded in 1919 by Chaplin and other artists to maintain total control over their works and their income.
Swiss commune on the shores of Lake Geneva where Charlie Chaplin lived in exile from 1953 until his death in 1977.
A period in American history in the early 1950s marked by an intense hunt for suspected communist sympathizers in government and in the arts.

course_143_orson_welles_et_citizen_kane|.explanation: Cinematographic technique where all planes of the image (foreground, middle ground, background) are sharp simultaneously, allowing for complex action within a single frame.
American press tycoon of the early 20th century whose life served as a model for the figure of Charles Foster Kane.
Sovereign right granted to a director to validate the editing and the definitive version of his film without intervention from the production studio.
One of the major studios of the Hollywood Golden Age which took the risk of producing Citizen Kane by offering total freedom to Orson Welles.
French film movement of the 1950s-60s that rehabilitated Citizen Kane and theorized the director's role as the sole author of his work.
Gigantic and melancholy fictional estate built by Kane, inspired by Hearst Castle, symbolizing both material success and emotional isolation.

course_144_la_nouvelle_vague_francaise|A.explanation: Theory by Truffaut in the Cahiers du Cinéma (1954): the true author of a film is the director, who expresses his personal vision. It promoted Hollywood filmmakers like Hitchcock or Hawks whom French academic critics despised.

course_144_la_nouvelle_vague_francaise|S.displayTerm: Shooting on location and the lightweight camera
course_144_la_nouvelle_vague_francaise|S.explanation: The Nouvelle Vague technically reinvented cinema: lightweight portable cameras, fast film stocks allowing filming without artificial lighting. These budgetary constraints became a revolutionary aesthetic - cinema "taken to the streets".

course_144_la_nouvelle_vague_francaise|A.explanation: Influential French film critic and theorist, co-founder of Cahiers du Cinéma, he was the spiritual mentor of the Nouvelle Vague.

course_144_la_nouvelle_vague_francaise|f.explanation: Imaginary boundary separating the actors from the audience. Looking or speaking directly to the camera 'breaks' it.

course_144_la_nouvelle_vague_francaise|É.explanation: Portable and lightweight camera model that appeared after the war, essential for the Nouvelle Vague's outdoor filming.

course_144_la_nouvelle_vague_francaise|C.explanation: Brazilian film movement of the 1960s influenced by the Nouvelle Vague, focused on social criticism and realism.

course_144_la_nouvelle_vague_francaise|D.explanation: Movement launched in 1995 by Lars von Trier advocating for a return to the purity of cinema (no special effects, handheld cameras).

course_144_la_nouvelle_vague_francaise|J.explanation: French actor discovered in 'Breathless', who became the face of the freedom and insolence of the Nouvelle Vague.
François Truffaut's favorite actor, he portrays Antoine Doinel in several films, becoming the director's alter ego.

course_144_la_nouvelle_vague_francaise|F.displayTerm: Filming on location and lightweight camera
course_144_la_nouvelle_vague_francaise|F.explanation: The French New Wave technically reinvented cinema: lightweight portable cameras, fast film allowing filming without artificial lighting. These budgetary constraints became a revolutionary aesthetic - cinema "taking to the streets".

course_145_kubrick_2001_l_odyssee_de_l_e.explanation: British science fiction author who co-wrote the screenplay for 2001 from the short story "The Sentinel" (1948). He invented the concept of the geostationary communication satellite in 1945 - long before its technical realization.

HAL 9000 is one of the first representations of a conscious AI in conflict with its creators. Its anthropomorphism (calm voice, implacable logic, self-preservation) prefigures current debates about AI safety.
Famous German manufacturer of high-precision optics. Its lenses were used by Kubrick to film by candlelight in 'Barry Lyndon'.
Photographic effect used by Douglas Trumbull to create the psychedelic light trails at the end of 2001.
American space agency. Its research and engineers served as consultants to ensure the technical realism of the film 2001.
German composer (1864-1949) whose symphonic poem 'Also Sprach Zarathustra' opens the film during key moments of evolution.
19th-century Austrian composer, author of 'The Blue Danube', used by Kubrick to pace the space ballets.
Science fiction short story published by Arthur C. Clarke in 1948, whose idea of a cubic artifact left by extraterrestrials served as the basis for the screenplay of 2001.

course_146_hitchcock_et_le_suspense|The.explanation: Hitchcock's term for the object that all characters pursue (the suitcase, the secret plans) but whose content has no importance for the viewer. What matters is the desire it arouses and the narrative dynamics it generates.

course_146_hitchcock_et_le_suspense|Subj.explanation: Technique where the camera adopts the point of view of a character, making the viewer experience exactly what they see. In Vertigo, Scottie's vertigo is transmitted by a zoom-out/dolly-in technique invented for the film.

course_146_hitchcock_et_le_suspense|sequ.explanation: A film sequence composed of a single, continuous shot, without any visible editing cuts.

course_146_hitchcock_et_le_suspense|Doll.explanation: An effect of spatial distortion achieved by combining a zoom in and a camera dolly back (or vice versa).

course_146_hitchcock_et_le_suspense|Bern.explanation: Iconic composer whose Music defined the atmosphere of Hitchcock's films, notably through the tense use of strings in Psycho.

course_146_hitchcock_et_le_suspense|Fran.explanation: French filmmaker whose interviews with Hitchcock helped theorize the master's work and have him recognized as an auteur.

course_146_hitchcock_et_le_suspense|edit.explanation: The assembly of a film's shots. Hitchcock used it to manipulate time and suggest actions without showing them explicitly.

course_146_hitchcock_et_le_suspense|psyc.explanation: A discipline exploring the unconscious, integrated by Hitchcock into his thrillers to deepen the psychological motivation of his characters.

course_147_l_architecture_gothique_les_c.displayTerm: The flying buttress and the rib vault
course_147_l_architecture_gothique_les_c.explanation: Structural innovations of Gothic architecture. The rib vault distributes weight onto ribs rather than the entire walls. The flying buttress transfers the thrust outwards, allowing walls to be opened into windows without the building collapsing.

Suger theorized that divine light, channeled through colored stained glass, elevated the soul toward God. This "metaphysics of light" inspired Gothic architecture in its pursuit of ever larger windows and ever higher arches.
An architectural element outside the building that supports the nave wall by transferring the thrust of the vaults to an abutment pier.
Abbot of Saint-Denis and advisor to the kings of France, considered the father of Gothic art through his reconstruction of the Basilica of Saint-Denis.
Necropolis of the kings of France where Abbot Suger had the first Gothic choir built around 1140.

Structural innovations of Gothic architecture. The rib vault distributes the weight onto ribs rather than the entire walls. The flying buttress transfers the thrust outwards, allowing walls to be opened into windows without the building collapsing.

course_148_le_bauhaus|Functionalism in d.explanation: The Bauhaus principle: form follows function. A well-designed object is beautiful because it does its job perfectly, with no needless decoration. This idea still shapes modern industrial design.

course_148_le_bauhaus|Shutdown by the Na.explanation: Hitler closed The Bauhaus in 1933, considering its aesthetics as "degenerate". Its teachers emigrated to the United States (Gropius to Harvard, Mies van der Rohe to Chicago), where they profoundly influenced American architecture and design.

course_148_le_bauhaus|Wassily Kandinsky.explanation: Russian painter and one of the pioneers of abstract art. A master at the Bauhaus, he taught the theory of form and color, linking artistic spirituality with geometric rigor.

course_148_le_bauhaus|De Stijl.explanation: Dutch artistic movement (which included Mondrian) advocating the use of straight lines and primary colors. Its aesthetic profoundly influenced the modernist turning point of The Bauhaus.

course_148_le_bauhaus|White City of Tel.explanation: Architectural ensemble in Israel built between 1930 and 1948 according to the principles of The Bauhaus, adapted to the Mediterranean climate. It is the largest ensemble of this style in the world.

course_148_le_bauhaus|sans-serif.explanation: Category of typefaces without serifs (the small extensions at the end of letters). The Bauhaus popularized this streamlined typography for its modern legibility.

course_149_la_joconde|Leonardian sfumato.explanation: Technique by Leonardo da Vinci: very thin layers of translucent glaze (sometimes 40 layers) create imperceptible transitions between light and shadow. It is this sfumato that makes the smile of The Mona Lisa so ambiguous and elusive.

course_149_la_joconde|The theft of the M.displayTerm: The theft of the Mona Lisa (1911)
course_149_la_joconde|The theft of the M.explanation: Vincenzo Peruggia, a Louvre employee, stole the Mona Lisa and kept it in his home in Florence for two years. The theft made headlines around the world and turned a painting the public barely knew into the most famous painting in the world.

course_149_la_joconde|Lisa Gherardini.explanation: Most likely identity of the model of The Mona Lisa, she was the wife of the silk merchant Francesco del Giocondo.

course_149_la_joconde|Aerial perspective.explanation: Pictorial technique consisting in creating an illusion of depth by making distant objects blurrier, lighter, and bluer, simulating the thickness of the air.

course_149_la_joconde|Peripheral vision.explanation: Part of the vision located outside the central fixation point, capable of perceiving shapes and movements but less precise regarding colors and sharp details.

course_149_la_joconde|Guillaume Apollina.explanation: Famous French poet, arrested and imprisoned for a week in 1911 as part of the investigation into the theft of The Mona Lisa.

course_149_la_joconde|Pablo Picasso.explanation: Major painter of the 20th century, questioned by the police in 1911 because he had bought statuettes stolen from the Louvre by a close associate of Apollinaire.

course_149_la_joconde|Bulletproof glass.explanation: High-resistance security device protecting the work from physical aggression and climatic variations since the 1950s.

course_149_la_joconde|Vincenzo Peruggia.explanation: Italian employee of the Louvre who stole the Mona Lisa in 1911, claiming he wanted to return the work to its country of origin.

course_150_la_nuit_etoilee_van_gogh|Art.explanation: Central concept for Van Gogh where the work does not seek to reproduce physical reality but the emotions and visions of the painter.

course_150_la_nuit_etoilee_van_gogh|The.explanation: Van Gogh invited Gauguin to share his yellow house in Arles. After two months of difficult coexistence, a violent argument precipitated Van Gogh's crisis, who cut off his ear and was voluntarily institutionalized in Saint-Rémy.

course_150_la_nuit_etoilee_van_gogh|Neth.explanation: Van Gogh's native country, whose architecture (notably church steeples) unconsciously influences his Provençal landscapes.

course_150_la_nuit_etoilee_van_gogh|The.explanation: Famous Japanese print by Hokusai whose curvilinear dynamism deeply influenced the structure of Van Gogh's swirls.

course_150_la_nuit_etoilee_van_gogh|Fauv.explanation: Artistic movement from the early 20th century (Matisse, Derain) using pure and violent colors, a direct heir to Van Gogh's research.

course_151_guernica_picasso|The Spanish.explanation: Conflict between the Spanish Republic and the Francoist uprising supported by Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy. Spain was the testing ground for the new bombing tactics of the coming Second World War.

course_151_guernica_picasso|The Condor L.explanation: Air military unit of the Luftwaffe sent to Spain to support Franco and test new saturation bombing tactics. The bombing of Guernica was its first massive use against a civilian city.

course_151_guernica_picasso|Second Spani.explanation: Democratic regime in place in Spain from 1931 to 1939, overthrown by the military coup and the civil war led by Franco.

course_151_guernica_picasso|Cold War.explanation: Period of global geopolitical tensions (1947-1991) during which Guernica became a symbol of struggle against oppression beyond the Spanish conflict.

course_151_guernica_picasso|UN.explanation: United Nations organization, where a reproduction of the painting reminds the leaders of the world of the horror of armed conflicts.

course_151_guernica_picasso|saturation b.explanation: A military tactic aimed at destroying an entire area with a continuous carpet of bombs, without distinction between civilian and military targets.

course_151_guernica_picasso|MoMA.explanation: Museum of Modern Art in New York, which housed Guernica for over forty years to protect it from the Francoist dictatorship.

course_152_la_liberte_guidant_le_peuple_.explanation: Three revolutionary days that overthrew King Charles X, who wanted to suppress freedom of the press and reduce voting rights. Louis Philippe I took the constitutional throne in his place.

An allegorical female figure embodying the French Republic since the Revolution. Her Phrygian cap (a symbol of ancient freedom) is her distinctive attribute. Delacroix's Liberty is its founding image, reproduced in every town hall in France.
19th-century art movement favoring the expression of feelings, imagination, and dynamism over classical rigor. Delacroix is its main representative in painting.
A period in French history (1814-1830) marked by the return of the Bourbon kings, Louis XVIII and then Charles X, after the fall of Napoleon.
The child hero of Victor Hugo's 'Les Misérables', inspired by the boy with pistols in Delacroix's painting.
The last King of the French (1830-1848), who came to power after the July Revolution; he purchased the painting by Delacroix before hiding it because he judged it too subversive.
Official exhibitions organized by the Academy of Fine Arts in Paris, where artists presented their works to the public and critics.

course_153_la_creation_d_adam_michel_ang.explanation: Painting done on fresh plaster (fresco = fresh in Italian). The pigments integrate into the plaster as it dries, making the color permanent and resistant over centuries. Michelangelo had to work in daily sections (giornata) on his back from a scaffold.

Theory by Frank Meshberger (1990): the shape of the red cloak surrounding God is said to exactly reproduce the anatomical cross-section of a human brain. If intentional, Michelangelo would have symbolized that God is a creation of the human mind.
Italian term for the 16th century, the high point of the Italian Renaissance, marked by artists such as Michelangelo, Raphael, and Leonardo da Vinci.
Artistic identity of Michelangelo, trained in Florence according to a tradition favoring volume, line, and physical strength over color alone.
Artistic identity of Michelangelo, trained in Florence according to a tradition favoring volume, line, and physical strength over color alone.
Architect and rival of Michelangelo. He is said to have suggested that the Pope hand the vault to Michelangelo in order to put him in a technically impossible position.
Italian aesthetic concept referring to the softness or fluidity of a body, used here to emphasize Adam's lack of vital energy before the divine intervention.
Italian aesthetic concept referring to the softness or fluidity of a body, used here to emphasize Adam's lack of vital energy before the divine intervention.
Scientific practice consisting of opening cadavers to study muscles and organs, essential to the realism of bodies in Michelangelo's work.
Scientific practice consisting of opening cadavers to study muscles and organs, essential to the realism of bodies in Michelangelo's work.
Stage of Renaissance painting characterized by a perfect mastery of anatomy and perspective, combined with an unprecedented dramatic force.
Stage of Renaissance painting characterized by a perfect mastery of anatomy and perspective, combined with an unprecedented dramatic force.

course_154_impression_soleil_levant_mone.displayTerm: Louis Leroy and the birth of the term "impressionism"
course_154_impression_soleil_levant_mone.explanation: An art critic for "Le Charivari", Louis Leroy wrote a sarcastic article in 1874: "Impression, I was certain of it!". He meant it as mockery, but the artists proudly adopted the name "impressionists" and turned the insult around.

course_154_impression_soleil_levant_mone.displayTerm: The industrialized port of Le Havre in the 19th century
course_154_impression_soleil_levant_mone.explanation: Le Havre was the leading French commercial port, transformed by industrialization. Monet shows exactly this industrial modernity (steam, cranes, small boats) in the morning mist, a fleeting glimpse of modern life in the making.
Famous photographer who lent his studio for the first independent exhibition of the impressionists in 1874.
Pictorial practice consisting of painting outside the studio, directly in front of the subject, facilitated by the invention of flexible paint tubes.
The primary art dealer for the Impressionists who financially supported the movement and organized exhibitions abroad, saving the artists from poverty.

Art critic for "Le Charivari", Louis Leroy wrote a sarcastic article in 1874: "Impression, I was certain of it!". He wanted to mock them - the term "impressionists" was adopted by the artists themselves with pride, turning the insult around.

Le Havre was the leading French commercial port, transformed by industrialization. Monet shows precisely this industrial modernity (steam, cranes, small boats) in the morning mist - a fleeting vision of modernity on the move.

course_155_nighthawks_hopper|American ur.explanation: Nighthawks was painted in 1942, a few weeks after Pearl Harbor. The loneliness of the figures in the American night carries a deep unease: an individualist society, no sense of community, an emptiness behind all the material comfort.

course_155_nighthawks_hopper|The America.explanation: An American institution: open around the clock, quick counter service, anonymous customers passing through. It is the perfect setting for shared loneliness, and it runs through American writing, film noir, and painting.

course_155_nighthawks_hopper|Robert Henr.explanation: American painter, leader of the Ashcan School, who was the teacher of Hopper and encouraged him to paint real and raw urban life.

course_155_nighthawks_hopper|Pearl Harbo.explanation: Surprise attack on December 7, 1941, by Japanese forces, leading to the entry of the United States into the Second World War and creating a climate of national anxiety at the time Hopper painted his canvas.

course_155_nighthawks_hopper|Ridley Scot.explanation: British director who explicitly cited 'Nighthawks' as a major visual influence for recreating the nocturnal and rainy atmosphere of the film Blade Runner.

course_155_nighthawks_hopper|Wim Wenders.explanation: German filmmaker fascinated by Hopper; he staged a tableau vivant of 'Nighthawks' in his film 'The End of Violence'.

course_156_les_demoiselles_d_avignon_pic.explanation: An early 20th-century trend seeking a lost vitality in African and Oceanic arts. Picasso found there a radical freedom of representation that broke the conventions of perspective held since the Renaissance.

A dilapidated building in Montmartre where Picasso lived and worked from 1904 to 1909, surrounded by artists and poets (Max Jacob, Apollinaire, Braque). It was there, in a studio without water or heating, that he painted the Demoiselles d'Avignon.
Aesthetic concept originating from Greek philosophy (Aristotle) referring to the imitation of nature by the artist.
First phase of Cubism (1908-1912) aiming to break down objects into simple geometric shapes and represent them from several simultaneous points of view.
A term once used for the art of traditional societies in Africa, Oceania, and the Americas, from which Picasso drew his expressive force.
A term once used for the art of traditional societies in Africa, Oceania, and the Americas, from which Picasso drew his expressive force.
Revolutionary artistic movement founded by Picasso and Braque, characterized by the deconstruction of forms and the rejection of classical perspective.

course_157_la_persistance_de_la_memoire_.explanation: Bergson distinguished between physical time (measurable) and lived time (subjective, elastic). Dalí's soft watches visually illustrate this "Bergsonian time": in dreams, time expands, contracts, and loses all rigidity.

A rocky coastal landscape of the Costa Brava visible in many of Dalí's paintings. The characteristic eroded granite geological formations of this cape fueled his imagination for ambiguous and melting forms.
20th-century artistic and literary movement seeking to release the unconscious and dreams from the control of reason.
Technique invented by Dalí consisting of using his own obsessions and delusions to create images with multiple meanings.
Physical theory by Albert Einstein postulating that time and space are linked and can warp according to speed and gravity.
Set of cultural practices and objects widely distributed and shared by the majority of a society.
Period of art history marked by a return to ancient models and the invention of geometric perspective.
The Museum of Modern Art in New York, one of the most influential modern art museums in the world, which has held the painting since 1934.
Spanish painter (1904-1989), one of the main representatives of surrealism, famous for his dreamlike imagery and provocative personality.
Born Elena Ivanovna Diakonova, she was Salvador Dalí's wife, muse, and agent, playing a crucial role in his career and artistic production.

Bergson distinguished between physical time (measurable) and lived time (subjective, elastic). The melting watches of Dalí visually illustrate this "Bergsonian time": in dreams, time expands, contracts, and loses all rigidity.

course_158_la_tragedie_grecque_et_le_the.explanation: A group of 12 to 15 citizens who sing, dance, and comment on the action between episodes. The chorus represents the voice of the community and provides a moral perspective on the heroes' actions. Its role gradually diminished under Sophocles and Euripides.

An ancient theater from the 4th century BC, capable of seating 14,000 spectators. Its extraordinary acoustics (a coin drop can be heard from any seat) remain mysterious and surpass the capabilities of modern acoustic engineering.
Concept theorized by Aristotle referring to the purgation of passions (fear, pity) in the spectator during a tragic performance.
Mythological creatures, half-man half-goat, companions of Dionysus, as whom actors would dress for the first theatrical rites.
From the Greek 'hypokritès', a term designating the actor who 'responds' to the choir.
Private tax by which a wealthy Athenian citizen financed the equipment and training of a dramatic choir.
Central circular space of the Greek theater where the choir stood to dance and sing.
The excessive pride or hubris of a hero who defies the divine order, causing their downfall.
Theatrical technique consisting of having a deity intervene (via a crane) to miraculously resolve a blocked plot.

course_159_le_theatre_de_shakespeare|The.explanation: A theater built on the south bank of the Thames, outside the limits of the City of London (which banned performances). Octagonal and open to the sky, it hosted 3,000 spectators standing (the "groundlings") or seated in the covered galleries.

course_159_le_theatre_de_shakespeare|Sha.explanation: Unrhymed ten-syllable line (iambic pentameter) that Shakespeare gives to noble characters, while commoners speak in prose. Marking rank through language is a convention of Elizabethan theater.

course_159_le_theatre_de_shakespeare|Gro.explanation: The least wealthy spectators of Elizabethan theater who, for a penny, attended the performance standing in the open-air pit.

course_159_le_theatre_de_shakespeare|Fir.explanation: The first printed collection of Shakespeare's plays, published in 1623 by his colleagues John Heminges and Henry Condell. Without it, half of his work would be lost.

course_159_le_theatre_de_shakespeare|Lor.explanation: theater company in which Shakespeare was a shareholder, actor, and lead playwright, protected by the English court.

course_160_la_liberte_de_la_presse_et_le.explanation: Fundamental tension: how far should a photographer get involved? Kevin Carter photographed a vulture waiting for a Sudanese child to die (1993) and was accused of not helping. He received the Pulitzer then committed suicide three months later.

course_161_la_naissance_des_dieux_grecs_.explanation: Poem (circa 700 BC) recounting the origin and genealogy of the Greek gods since Chaos. Our main source on Greek cosmogony, it presents passionate and violent gods, subjected like men to the forces of destiny.

course_162_promethee_le_voleur_de_feu|Th.displayTerm: The Promethean myth in modern culture
course_162_promethee_le_voleur_de_feu|Th.explanation: Prometheus has become the symbol of human emancipation through knowledge, defying the limits set by the gods. Goethe, Shelley (Frankenstein), Marx claimed him as a symbol - he embodies the modernity rebelling against the established order.

course_162_promethee_le_voleur_de_feu|Ep.explanation: His name means "the one who thinks after". He accepted without thinking Pandora's gift sent by Zeus. His recklessness introduced evils into the world. The Prometheus-Epimetheus pair illustrates the opposition between foresight and impulsivity.

course_162_promethee_le_voleur_de_feu|Fe.explanation: Mediterranean plant with a tall stem whose pith, once dry, burns slowly without consuming the bark, explaining how Prometheus was able to transport the fire.

course_162_promethee_le_voleur_de_feu|fe.explanation: Mediterranean plant with a tall stem whose pith, once dry, burns slowly without consuming the bark, explaining how Prometheus was able to transport the fire.

course_162_promethee_le_voleur_de_feu|Ga.explanation: French philosopher who analyzed the 'Prometheus complex' as the will to know and to surpass one's masters through scientific curiosity.

course_162_promethee_le_voleur_de_feu|Ae.explanation: One of the three great Greek tragic playwrights, author of a trilogy dedicated to the Titan of which 'Prometheus Bound' is the only surviving part.

course_162_promethee_le_voleur_de_feu|Me.explanation: Mythical place where the division of an ox between gods and men took place, the starting point of the discord between Zeus and Prometheus.

course_162_promethee_le_voleur_de_feu|Ep.explanation: Brother of Prometheus whose name means "the one who thinks after". He thoughtlessly accepted Pandora's gift sent by Zeus. His recklessness introduced evils into the world. The Prometheus-Epimetheus pair illustrates the opposition between foresight and impulsivity.

course_163_pandore_et_la_boite|Misogyny.explanation: The myth of Pandora is often read as a mythological justification for the Greeks' mistrust of women: it is a woman who introduces evil into the world, through curiosity or disobedience. A myth parallel to Eve in the Bible.

course_163_pandore_et_la_boite|Elpis (Ho.explanation: In Hesiod's version, Hope remains in the jar when Pandora closes it. A fundamental ambiguity: is it the last benevolent gift from the gods, or an additional evil (false hope, illusion) that tortures men by making them believe things will improve?

course_163_pandore_et_la_boite|Prometheu.explanation: Titan who created men from clay and who stole fire from the gods to offer it to them, provoking the wrath of Zeus.

course_163_pandore_et_la_boite|Erasmus o.explanation: Humanist of the Renaissance whose translation error from Greek to Latin is the origin of the term 'Pandora's box'.

course_163_pandore_et_la_boite|Misogyny.explanation: Contempt or hostility toward women, illustrated in this myth by the creation of Pandora as a punishment.

course_164_demeter_et_persephone_les_sai.explanation: Secret initiation ceremonies celebrated at Eleusis for over a millennium (600 BC - 400 AD). Based on the myth of Persephone, they promised initiates a blissful life after death. Plato and Marcus Aurelius were initiated into them.

course_164_demeter_et_persephone_les_sai.displayTerm: The agricultural cycle in Greek religion
course_164_demeter_et_persephone_les_sai.explanation: The myth of Persephone is a mythological explanation of the vegetative cycle: when she descends into the Underworld (autumn-winter), the earth is sterile; when she ascends (spring), the vegetation is reborn. Greek religion was linked to agricultural rhythms.
The great hall of assembly in Eleusis where the supreme initiation took place during the Mysteries.
Set of living beings coexisting in a defined space; here used to illustrate the interdependence of the divine and biological world.

course_165_orphee_et_eurydice|Catabasis:.displayTerm: Catabasis: the descent into the Underworld
course_165_orphee_et_eurydice|Catabasis:.explanation: A recurring mythological motif: the hero descends into the Underworld alive (Heracles, Odysseus, Aeneas, Orpheus). This "catabasis" symbolizes the initiatory journey into death and the confrontation with the unconscious.

course_165_orphee_et_eurydice|Orphism: G.explanation: A religious movement inspired by the myth of Orpheus, advocating for the purification of the soul and metempsychosis (transmigration of souls). It influenced Pythagoras and Plato in their conception of the immortality of the soul.
