course_165_orphee_et_eurydice|Ovid.explanation: Latin poet and author of the 'Metamorphoses', a monumental work compiling Greek and Roman myths, including that of Orpheus.

course_165_orphee_et_eurydice|Jason.explanation: Greek hero and leader of the Argonauts' expedition, who set out in search of the Golden Fleece with the help of Orpheus.

course_165_orphee_et_eurydice|Aristaeus.explanation: Son of Apollo and hunter whose attraction to Eurydice indirectly caused the young woman's death while she was fleeing from him.

course_165_orphee_et_eurydice|Styx.explanation: One of the rivers of the Underworld separating the world of the living from that of the dead, crossed by Charon the ferryman.

course_165_orphee_et_eurydice|Cerberus.explanation: Monstrous three-headed dog guarding the entrance to the Underworld to prevent the dead from leaving and the living from entering.

course_165_orphee_et_eurydice|Charon.explanation: The ferryman of the Underworld responsible for transporting the souls of the deceased on his boat in exchange for an obolus.

course_165_orphee_et_eurydice|Erinyes.explanation: Persecuting deities who punish crimes, particularly parricides, known for their inflexibility.

course_165_orphee_et_eurydice|Maenads.explanation: Women belonging to the retinue of Dionysus, devoted to rituals of trance and wild fury.

course_165_orphee_et_eurydice|Hebrus.explanation: River of Thrace (modern-day Bulgaria/Greece) into which the head of Orpheus was thrown after he was torn apart by the Maenads.

course_165_orphee_et_eurydice|Maurice Bl.explanation: 20th-century French writer and philosopher whose essay 'The Gaze of Orpheus' analyzes the link between myth and literary creation.

course_165_orphee_et_eurydice|Jean Cocte.explanation: Multidisciplinary French artist who reinterpreted the myth of Orpheus in cinema through a famous trilogy.

course_165_orphee_et_eurydice|Catabasis.explanation: The descent into the Underworld. A recurring mythological motif: the hero descends into the Underworld alive (Heracles, Odysseus, Aeneas, Orpheus). This journey symbolizes initiation through death and confrontation with the unconscious.

course_171_hercule_et_ses_12_travaux|Zeu.explanation: King of the gods and father of Heracles. He wishes for his son to become a great protector of men.

course_171_hercule_et_ses_12_travaux|Leo.explanation: Skin of the Nemean lion worn by Heracles as armor. It is his main attribute in iconography.

course_171_hercule_et_ses_12_travaux|Cen.explanation: Mythological creature half-man, half-horse. The blood of the centaur Nessus will cause the physical death of Heracles.

course_172_thesee_et_le_minotaure|The La.displayTerm: The Labyrinth of Knossos in Crete

course_172_thesee_et_le_minotaure|Ariadn.explanation: A phrase found in many languages for the clue that lets you find your way through something complicated. Ariadne gives Theseus a thread so he can get out of the labyrinth, a symbol of memory, method, and help from someone else.

course_172_thesee_et_le_minotaure|Daedal.explanation: Legendary architect and inventor, creator of the Labyrinth of Crete. His name became a common noun synonymous with labyrinth.

course_172_thesee_et_le_minotaure|Thalas.explanation: Politics power primarily based on the domination of the seas. Minos' Crete is often cited as the first historical (or mythical) example.

course_172_thesee_et_le_minotaure|Synoec.explanation: Founding act unifying several villages into a single city-state (Polis), attributed to Theseus for the birth of Athens.

course_172_thesee_et_le_minotaure|Panath.explanation: Annual religious and social festivals celebrated in Athens in honor of the goddess Athena, reorganized according to the myth by Theseus.

course_172_thesee_et_le_minotaure|Amazon.explanation: People of female warriors from Greek mythology that Theseus reportedly fought and whose queen, Antiope, he is said to have married.

course_172_thesee_et_le_minotaure|Labyri.explanation: Complex building constructed by Daedalus to imprison the Minotaur, designed so that anyone entering could never leave without help.

course_174_ulysse_et_les_sirenes|Sirens.explanation: Hybrid creatures (bird-women for the Greeks, fish-women as of the Middle Ages) whose divine and omniscient song caused the downfall of sailors.

course_174_ulysse_et_les_sirenes|Metis.explanation: A form of cunning and practical intelligence, characteristic of Odysseus, allowing for triumph over complex situations through ingenuity.

course_174_ulysse_et_les_sirenes|Trojan.explanation: Mythical conflict between the Greeks and the Trojans, the starting point of Odysseus' Odyssey.

course_174_ulysse_et_les_sirenes|Nudge.explanation: A concept of behavioral economics designating an indirect proposal allowing for the influence of individuals' behavior without coercion.

course_174_ulysse_et_les_sirenes|Precomm.explanation: Decision-making strategy consisting of voluntarily restricting one's future options to counter an anticipated temptation.

course_175_jason_et_la_toison_d_or|Colch.explanation: Region east of the Black Sea, described in Greek myths as the end of the eastern world. Shepherds there used sheep fleeces to filter gold from the gold-bearing rivers of the Caucasus - the "golden fleece" may have been real.

course_175_jason_et_la_toison_d_or|Medea.explanation: Daughter of the king of Colchis, she betrayed her father and sacrificed her brother for Jason. course_175_jason_et_la_toison_d_or|Argon.explanation: Crew of Greek heroes (including Heracles and Orpheus) who sailed aboard the Argo to conquer the Golden Fleece.

course_175_jason_et_la_toison_d_or|Chiro.explanation: Wise centaur and educator of many Greek heroes, including Jason and Achilles.

course_175_jason_et_la_toison_d_or|Hera.explanation: Queen of the gods, she protects Jason because Pelias neglected her worship.

course_175_jason_et_la_toison_d_or|Argo.explanation: Legendary ship capable of speaking, designed for the expedition to Colchis.

course_175_jason_et_la_toison_d_or|Dodon.explanation: Oldest oracle in Greece, dedicated to Zeus, famous for its sacred oaks, a piece of which was used for the Argo.

course_175_jason_et_la_toison_d_or|Ares.explanation: God of war, owner of the field that Aeetes forces Jason to plow.

course_175_jason_et_la_toison_d_or|Aphro.explanation: Goddess of love who sends Eros to strike Medea so that she helps Jason.

course_175_jason_et_la_toison_d_or|Hecat.explanation: Goddess of the moon and witchcraft, protector of Medea.

Latin poet of the 1st century AD, author of the Achilleid, who popularized the version of the bath in the Styx and of the physical invulnerability of Achilles.
Trojan captive whose confiscation by Agamemnon causes the anger and withdrawal of Achilles from the battles in the Iliad.

Modern anatomical term designating the tendon that connects the calf muscle to the heel bone, in direct reference to the myth.

Supreme value of heroic culture: the immortal glory acquired through exploits in war and transmitted by poets. Achilles deliberately chooses a short but glorious life rather than a long life without glory - a fundamental choice of Greek heroic ethics.

course_177_dipe_et_le_sphinx|The Sphinx.explanation: Hybrid creature present in many cultures: Egyptian Sphinx (lion, human head, royal symbol) and Greek Sphinx (female, winged, poser of deadly riddles). The same image takes on opposite meanings depending on the culture.

course_177_dipe_et_le_sphinx|Incest as a.explanation: Oedipus's incest (unintentional) represents the ultimate transgression of social order: the confusion of generations. For the Greeks, it provoked a defilement (miasma) affecting the entire community, visible in the pestilence striking Thebes.

course_177_dipe_et_le_sphinx|Creon.explanation: Jocasta's brother and regent of Thebes. He promises the throne and his sister's hand to anyone who solves the Sphinx's riddle.

course_177_dipe_et_le_sphinx|dialectics.explanation: Method of reasoning that proceeds through dialogue, argumentation, or the confrontation of opposing theses.

course_177_dipe_et_le_sphinx|plot twist.explanation: In dramaturgy, a moment where the action abruptly shifts in an opposite direction (peripeteia).

course_177_dipe_et_le_sphinx|Oedipus com.explanation: Psychoanalytic concept theorized by Freud referring to a child's unconscious desire for the parent of the opposite sex and rivalry with the parent of the same sex.

course_178_antigone_devoir_familial_vs_l.explanation: Hegel was the first, in 1807, to argue that in Antigone both characters are right by their own principle: family against state, divine law against human law. This is not good against evil but two goods that cannot both be honored, which is the very definition of the tragic.

Play performed in Paris under the Nazi occupation. Anouilh deliberately left its political meaning open: Creon could stand for the Germans or for Vichy, Antigone for the Resistance. Both sides found what they wanted in it, which was either genius or opportunism.
Powerful Greek city-state, setting for many tragic myths including those of Oedipus and Antigone.
River of the Greek Underworld that the souls of the deceased must cross to find rest.
Set of moral principles considered innate and superior to the written laws of governments.

Play performed in Paris during the Nazi occupation. Anouilh deliberately left its political meaning open: Creon could stand for the Germans or for Vichy, Antigone for the Resistance. Both sides found what they wanted in it, which was either genius or opportunism.

course_179_la_guerre_de_troie_et_le_chev.explanation: Schliemann located Troy in 1870 at Hisarlik, Turkey. Excavations brought to light nine successive cities. Troy VIIa (around 1184 BC) shows traces of fire compatible with Homer's account - the Trojan War may have taken place.

After the Trojan War, Greek heroes experience tragic returns: Agamemnon is murdered, Ajax dies. Only Menelaus finds Helen again. These "Nostoi" formed an epic cycle (now lost) that was as important as the Iliad for the ancient Greeks.
Other name for the city of Troy in Antiquity, which gave its title to the Iliad by Homer.
Natural region surrounding the ancient city of Troy, located in the northwest of Asia Minor (present-day Turkey).
Coastal river of the Troad flowing near the city of Troy, witness to many battles between the Greeks and the Trojans.
Last mythical king of Troy, father of Hector and Paris, symbol of the wise sovereign whose lineage is destroyed by war.
Form of practical intelligence among the Greeks, mixing cunning, skill and prudence, of which Odysseus is the representative par excellence.
Island located near the coasts of Troy where the Greek fleet hid to make the Trojans believe in their definitive departure.
Roman deities of Etruscan origin responsible for protecting the home and family; Aeneas carries them away in his flight from Troy.
Circular plan building, used here to designate the underground chamber where Danaë was imprisoned.

course_180_thor_et_loki_mythologie_nordi.explanation: A 13th-century Icelandic treatise on poetry and myth. Although it was written by a Christian, it is the most organized source we have on Norse belief, and it was meant to preserve the craft of the old poets.

Thor's hammer was the most widespread symbol of protection in medieval Scandinavia. Linked to a solar symbol (Norse swastika), it was misappropriated by the Nazis in the 20th century - giving this unfortunate symbol a lasting connotation.
Medieval manuscript containing a collection of mythological and heroic poems in Old Norse, considered a complementary and often older source than the Prose Edda.
The world-tree (often depicted as an ash tree) whose branches and roots connect the nine worlds of Norse cosmology.
Odin's eight-legged horse, renowned for its exceptional speed, born to Loki while the latter had taken the form of a mare.

A 13th-century Icelandic treatise on poetry and myth. Although it was written by a Christian, it is the most organized source we have on Norse belief, and it was meant to preserve the craft of the old poets.

course_181_ragnarok_la_fin_du_monde_nord.explanation: Norse cosmic ash tree connecting the nine worlds. Its roots delve into the realms of the gods, the giants, and the dead. The Norns (weavers of fate) live at its base. The cosmic tree is an almost universal mythological archetype.

The vision of Ragnarök shares traits with other eschatologies: the Christian Last Judgment, the Hindu Kali Yuga. These apocalyptic visions reflect a universal concern for the end of times and, often, the Renaissance that follows.
German translation of 'Ragnarök', popularized by Richard Wagner to designate the end of the gods' reign in his lyrical work.
Thor's hammer, the most powerful weapon in Asgard, capable of shattering mountains and systematically returning to the thrower's hand.
World of fire, located to the south of the primordial abyss, guarded by the giant Surtr and source of the forces of destruction by heat.
Mythical ship built from the nails of the dead, destined to transport the armies of chaos to the final battlefield.
Guardian god of the Bifröst bridge, possessing prodigious hearing and sight, who blows the horn Gjallarhorn to announce the beginning of Ragnarök.

Norse cosmic ash tree connecting the nine worlds. Its roots delve into the realms of the gods, the giants, and the dead. The Norns (weavers of fate) live at its base. The cosmic tree is a near-universal mythological archetype.

course_182_osiris_et_set_mythologie_egyp.explanation: Fundamental principle of Egyptian thought: cosmic order, truth and justice. The pharaoh was responsible for maintaining Ma'at against chaos. Osiris presides over the judgment of the dead, weighing their heart against the feather of Ma'at.

A collection of magical spells accompanying deceased Egyptians into the afterlife. It guided the soul through the trials of the underworld, notably the judgment before Osiris. Some illustrated papyri are among the most beautiful works of Egyptian art.
Jackal-headed god, protector of embalmers and guardian of necropolises, he helps Isis create the first mummy.
Species of Nile fish which, according to the myth, supposedly swallowed the phallus of Osiris after his dismemberment by Set.
Marshes of the Nile delta where Isis hid and secretly raised Horus to protect him from Set's search.
God of wisdom and writing who healed the eye of Horus broken by Set, restoring its integrity.
Solar god, ruler of the gods, who presides over the tribunal deciding the legitimacy of Horus against Set.
Gigantic serpent embodying absolute chaos, seeking every night to swallow the sun (Ra).
Hybrid creature (lion, hippopotamus, crocodile) that devours the hearts of the deceased judged unworthy during the weighing ceremony.

Fundamental principle of Egyptian thought: cosmic order, truth, and justice. The pharaoh was responsible for maintaining Ma'at against chaos. Osiris presides over the judgment of the dead, weighing their hearts against the feather of Ma'at.

course_183_gilgamesh_le_premier_heros_de.explanation: A collective term for the civilizations of the Fertile Crescent between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers (modern Iraq). They invented cuneiform writing, codified law (Code of Hammurabi), sexagesimal mathematics and astronomy.

course_183_gilgamesh_le_premier_heros_de.displayTerm: The Flood narrative in the Epic
course_183_gilgamesh_le_premier_heros_de.explanation: Tablet XI of the Epic contains a universal Flood myth earlier than the biblical Deluge: Utnapishtim builds a boat and brings all the animals on board. This parallel stunned biblical scholars when it was discovered in 1872.
Sumerian scribe considered to be the author or compiler of the standard (most complete) version of the Epic of Gilgamesh in the 12th century BC.
Last great king of Assyria who built a massive library in Nineveh where the tablets of the epic were rediscovered in the 19th century.
Mother goddess in Mesopotamian mythology who created Enkidu from a piece of clay.
Custom (legendary in this context) allowing the sovereign to have sexual relations with a bride on her wedding night; here a symbol of Gilgamesh's tyranny.
Mythical mountains guarded by scorpion-men, located at the edge of the world, which Gilgamesh must cross during his quest.
American mythologist famous for his analysis of the 'hero's journey', of which Gilgamesh is one of the first historical examples.

course_184_romulus_et_remus_la_fondation.explanation: The traditional Date of the founding of Rome, calculated by Varro in the 1st century BC. The Romans counted years "from the founding of the city" (AUC). This legendary Date corresponded to the monarchy of the seven kings of Rome.

A bronze statue of a she-wolf suckling Romulus and Remus, symbol of Rome. Long believed to be Etrusque (5th century BC), recent studies date it to the Middle Ages. The human twins were added by Pollaiolo in the 15th century.
Priestess of the goddess Vesta sworn to chastity, responsible for tending the sacred fire of Rome. Breaking her vow was punishable by death.
Wild fig tree located in front of the entrance to a cave (the Lupercal) where, according to legend, the basket containing Romulus and Remus washed ashore.
Roman divinatory practice consisting of interpreting signs sent by the gods, notably the flight and song of birds.
Sacred boundary of the city of Rome, ritually traced with a plow, separating civil territory from military territory.
Name borne by Roman citizens in their civil functions, emphasizing the union between Romans and Sabines.

Traditional Date of the founding of Rome (753 BC), calculated by Varro in the 1st century BC. The Romans counted years "since the founding of the city" (AUC). This Legendary Date corresponded to the monarchy of the seven kings of Rome.

course_185_vishnou_et_shiva_mythologie_h.explanation: Samsara: cycle of reincarnations of the soul. Karma: law of moral causality - every action has consequences for future lives. Vishnu descends to Earth in avatars specifically to restore disrupted cosmic Karma.

Central philosophical text of Hinduism extracted from the Mahabharata: Krishna (avatar of Vishnu) explains to Arjuna the meaning of duty (dharma) and selfless action before the battle. Admired by Thoreau, Emerson, Gandhi, and Oppenheimer.
Supreme, absolute, and infinite principle of the universe in Hinduism, of which all deities are manifestations.
Hindu trinity grouping the three fundamental forces: creation (Brahma), preservation (Vishnu), and destruction (Shiva).
Cosmic order, natural law, and moral duty that every being must follow to maintain the harmony of the world.
The ten main incarnations (avatars) of Vishnu that appear on Earth during different cosmic eras.
The fourth and final age of the current cosmic cycle, characterized by moral and spiritual decline.
Sacred mountain of the Himalayas considered as the home of Shiva and a major pilgrimage place.
Small hourglass-shaped drum held by Shiva, whose sound symbolizes the rhythm of the original creation.

course_186_les_valkyries_et_le_valhalla|.explanation: Norse warriors wanted to die with weapons in hand so the Valkyries would choose them. Dying of illness (a "straw death") did not open the gates of Valhalla. This vision of a warrior paradise shaped Viking culture.

Richard Wagner set Norse mythology to music in Der Ring des Nibelungen (1848-1874). "The Ride of the Valkyries" is among the best-known works of classical music in the world, often associated with American cinema.
The celestial realm of the Aesir gods, linked to the world of men (Midgard) by the rainbow bridge Bifröst.
The "doom of the powers": a prophecy of the end of the world in which gods, giants, and monsters kill one another and the present universe is destroyed.
Collection of Old Norse poems constituting the main source of Scandinavian mythology, written primarily in the 13th century.
Famous Valkyrie of heroic poetry, lover of the hero Helgi, illustrating the recurring theme of love between warrior goddesses and mortals.
A gold-combed rooster who lives in Valhalla and whose song announces every day the awakening of the warriors, and one day that of the Ragnarök.
The plain located in the center of Asgard where the gods gather and where the Einherjar practice combat.
The cook of the gods and the Einherjar, responsible for preparing the eternal stew of the boar Sæhrímnir.
A magical goat living on the roof of Valhalla, feeding on the leaves of the tree Yggdrasil to produce the mead for the warriors.

course_187_le_phenix_a_travers_les_cultu.explanation: The Phoenix bird was adopted by alchemists as a symbol of transmutation: as it is reborn from its ashes, base metals can be transformed into gold. Its presence is recurrent in hermetic and esoteric literature.

Chinese mythological bird symbol of virtue and grace, associated with the Empress (as the dragon is with the Emperor). Its reappearance announced a virtuous and just reign. It embodies the five Confucian virtues.
Ancient Egyptian city, a major center of sun worship, where the Bennu was venerated and where the Greek Phoenix was set to deposit its ashes.
Former imperial capital of Japan, home to many temples such as Kinkaku-ji where the Hōō bird is a central architectural motif.
In alchemy, the process of changing one substance into another, often compared to the rebirth of the Phoenix.
The 'blackening' phase in alchemy symbolizing the death and decomposition necessary before spiritual rebirth.

course_188_les_titans_vs_les_dieux_titan.displayTerm: Order and chaos in Greek mythology
course_188_les_titans_vs_les_dieux_titan.explanation: The Titanomachy represents the victory of Olympian order (Zeus, reason, law) over the primordial chaos of the Titans. This same story shape, a cosmic struggle between order and chaos, appears in all the great world mythologies.

Titan condemned to carry the heavens (and not the Earth, contrary to popular belief) on his shoulders for eternity. His name gave "Atlas" to map collections as early as the 16th century (Mercator illustrated him on the cover).
Titaness of justice and divine law. She remained neutral during the Titanomachy and later became one of the wives of Zeus, symbolizing moral order.
Monstrous creature fathered by Gaia to avenge the Titans. He is considered the last and most fearsome adversary of Zeus before the definitive establishment of the Olympian order.
German chemist (1743-1817) who named titanium in 1795, drawing inspiration from the strength of the Titans of Greek mythology.
Gerard Mercator (1512-1594), Flemish cartographer whose use of an image of the Titan Atlas on his maps popularized the term 'atlas' to describe a collection of geography.

After the Titanomachy, the Olympians had to face the giants (born from the blood of Uranus), who were nearly invincible. This second war of the gods foreshadows the permanent tensions between Olympian order and the primordial forces of chaos.

course_189_dionysos_le_dieu_du_vin_et_de.displayTerm: The birth of theater from Dionysus
course_189_dionysos_le_dieu_du_vin_et_de.explanation: Greek tragedies and comedies were born from Dionysian rituals. Thespis (6th century) was the first to introduce an actor distinct from the chorus - the founding act of Western theater. The theater of Athens was itself a place of worship for Dionysus.
Philosophical opposition between order/reason (Apollo) and chaos/intoxication (Dionysos) as drivers of artistic creation.
Performance space born in the 6th century BC in Athens as a religious act dedicated to Dionysus, aiming for the purification of emotions (catharsis).
Performance space born in the 6th century BC in Athens as a religious act dedicated to Dionysus, aiming for the purification of emotions (catharsis).
God of light, the arts, prophecy, and measure. He is the rational and ordered counterpart to Dionysus in Greek and Nietzschean thought.
Secret and initiatory religious rites guaranteeing the faithful a direct experience of the divine or a favorable fate in the afterlife.
Aristotelian term designating the purgation or purification of passions (pity and fear) in the spectator of a tragedy.
Lyrical and passionate choral song in honor of Dionysus, considered the direct ancestor of the theater genre.
Daughter of Cadmus and mortal mother of Dionysus, consumed by the radiance of Zeus while she was pregnant.
Philosophical opposition between order/reason (Apollo) and chaos/drunkenness (Dionysus) as drivers of artistic creation.

course_191_enee_et_la_fondation_de_rome_.explanation: Fundamental virtue according to Virgil: devotion to the gods, the homeland, and the family. Aeneas is the "pious Aeneas" - he escapes from Troy carrying his old father on his back. This value embodies the Roman ideal in opposition to Greek hybris.

The Aeneid was written as a commission for Augustus to legitimize the imperial regime by placing Rome within a divine destiny. The lineage of Aeneas, son of Venus, becomes the lineage of Caesar and Augustus himself - a narrative of founding politics as much as literary.
The classical verse form of Greek and Latin epic poetry, composed of six rhythmic units (feet).
A term meaning 'proppings,' referring to the verses that Virgil left unfinished in his manuscript while waiting to find a perfect formulation.
Roman deities responsible for watching over the household and provisions; Aeneas takes them from Troy to ensure the protection of his future nation.
The king of the gods in Roman mythology (Zeus for the Greeks), guarantor of order and Aeneas' destiny.
Series of three major conflicts between Rome and Carthage for dominance of the western Mediterranean (3rd-2nd centuries BC).
One of the oldest patrician families in Rome, claimed by Julius Caesar and to which Augustus belonged by adoption.
Major poem by Dante Alighieri (14th century) where Virgil appears as the narrator's guide through Hell and Purgatory.
Queen of the gods and wife of Jupiter, she is the divine antagonist of the Aeneid, seeking by all means to prevent the founding of Rome.
Legendary conflict between the Greek states and the Trojans, serving as the chronological starting point for the Aeneid.
City founded by Ascanius (Iulus), son of Aeneas, which became the seat of the Latin royalty before the founding of Rome.
Legendary conflict pitting the Greek states against the Trojans, serving as the chronological starting point for the Aeneid.
Legendary conflict pitting the Greek states against the Trojans, serving as the chronological starting point for the Aeneid.

course_192_les_dieux_azteques_et_les_sac.displayTerm: The cosmology of the Five Suns and the cosmic debt
course_192_les_dieux_azteques_et_les_sac.explanation: The gods had sacrificed their blood to create the fifth sun. Humans were in perpetual debt and had to repay with blood. This logic of cosmic exchange made sacrifices morally necessary in the Aztec vision of the world.
God of the Sun and war, protector of the Mexica. As the sun must "fight" darkness every morning, he needs the blood of captured warriors to complete his daily journey and rise again.
The name of the fifth sun in which we live according to the Aztecs, meaning '4-Movement'.
The Aztec myth explaining that the world underwent four previous creations and destructions before the current era.
God of Rain and fertility, feared for his ability to send lightning or famine.
The 'Feathered Serpent', god of wisdom, wind, and arts, opposed to Tezcatlipoca.
The 'Smoking Mirror', omnipotent god of destiny, night, and warriors, often associated with black magic.
Goddess of the Earth and birth, mother of Huitzilopochtli, represented by a skirt of snakes.
Name of the 'flower wars', ritual conflicts whose objective was the capture of prisoners for sacrifice.
Nahuatl term meaning 'precious water', used to designate human blood offered to the gods.

course_192_les_dieux_azteques_et_les_sac.displayTerm: Cosmology of the Five Suns and cosmic debt
course_192_les_dieux_azteques_et_les_sac.explanation: The gods had sacrificed their blood to create the fifth sun. Humans were in perpetual debt and had to repay it with blood. This logic of cosmic exchange made sacrifices morally necessary in the Aztec vision of the world.

course_193_quetzalcoatl|Teotihuacán.explanation: “The city of the gods”, a major metropolis in central Mexico (1st-7th century) where the first great temples dedicated to the Feathered Serpent were built.

course_193_quetzalcoatl|Kukulkán.explanation: Mayan name for Quetzalcoatl. At Chichén Itzá, during the equinoxes, the shadow cast by the pyramid mimics the descent of a serpent along the steps.

course_193_quetzalcoatl|Nahuatl.explanation: Language of the Aztecs (and other peoples of central Mexico), still spoken today by more than a million people.

course_193_quetzalcoatl|quetzal.explanation: Tropical bird with long iridescent green and red feathers, more precious than gold to Mesoamericans. The name Quetzalcoatl ("quetzal serpent") combines the snake (earth) and the bird (sky) into a cosmic being uniting both dimensions.

course_193_quetzalcoatl|Five Suns Cosmog.explanation: Aztec myth explaining that the universe went through four eras (suns) before our own, with Quetzalcoatl having presided over one of these cycles.

course_193_quetzalcoatl|Mictlán.explanation: The underworld or the realm of the dead in Aztec mythology, guarded by Mictlantecuhtli.

course_193_quetzalcoatl|Tlaloc.explanation: God of rain and lightning, often associated with Quetzalcoatl (Ehecatl) to fertilize the lands.

course_193_quetzalcoatl|Conquistadors.explanation: Spanish soldiers and explorers of the 16th century who conquered large territories in America.

course_193_quetzalcoatl|Tenochtitlán.explanation: Capital of The Aztec Empire, built on an island in Lake Texcoco, at the current site of Mexico City.

course_194_le_mahabharata|The Bhagavad G.displayTerm: The Bhagavad Gita as a philosophical text
course_194_le_mahabharata|The Bhagavad G.explanation: The 18 chapters of dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna constitute a major philosophical text, independent of the rest of the epic. Krishna teaches selfless action (karma yoga), devotion (bhakti) and knowledge (jnana) as paths to liberation.

course_194_le_mahabharata|Orality and th.displayTerm: Orality and the transmission of Indian epics
course_194_le_mahabharata|Orality and th.explanation: Like Homer, The Mahabharata was first an oral epic memorized and recited by griots. Its transcription spanned several centuries. These texts are still recited and sung throughout India, as alive as ever.

course_194_le_mahabharata|Hastinapura.explanation: Legendary capital of the Kuru kingdom, at the heart of the power struggles between the Pandavas and the Kauravas.

course_194_le_mahabharata|Somme.explanation: A work that exhaustively gathers all knowledge on a specific subject or field.

course_194_le_mahabharata|Summa.explanation: A work that exhaustively gathers all knowledge on a specific subject or field.

course_194_le_mahabharata|Brahmanism.explanation: Religious and social system of ancient India, based on the Veda texts and the predominant role of the Brahman caste.

course_194_le_mahabharata|Dharma.explanation: Universal law, order of things and moral or religious duty that every individual must follow according to their condition.

course_194_le_mahabharata|Bhagavad Gita.explanation: The 18 chapters of dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna constitute a major philosophical text, independent of the rest of the epic. Krishna teaches selfless action (Karma yoga), devotion (bhakti), and knowledge (jnana) as paths to liberation.

course_194_le_mahabharata|Orality and tr.displayTerm: Orality and transmission of Indian epics (Concept)
course_194_le_mahabharata|Orality and tr.explanation: Like Homer, The Mahabharata was originally an oral epic memorized and recited by griots. Its transcription stretched over several centuries. These texts are still recited and sung throughout India, as alive as ever.

course_195_lancelot_guenievre_et_la_tabl.explanation: Social code glorifying the secret and inaccessible love of a knight for a lady (often married). Lancelot and Guinevere are the perfect example. This adulterous passion, destructive yet sublime, is at the heart of medieval Literature.

course_195_lancelot_guenievre_et_la_tabl.displayTerm: The Quest for the Grail and medieval Christianity
course_195_lancelot_guenievre_et_la_tabl.explanation: The Grail was christianized: the chalice of the Last Supper or the cup that collected the blood of Christ. The quest becomes a spiritual quest for purity. Only Galaad - pure and without sin - can reach it. Lancelot, defiled by his love for Guinevere, fails.
Founding episode where Arthur proves his royal blood by removing the sword Excalibur (or an anonymous sword depending on sources) from a rock or an anvil, proving his divine legitimacy.
Empty seat at the Round Table reserved for the knight who must find the Grail. Anyone who sits there without being the chosen one is swallowed by the earth.
Latin expression meaning 'Once and Future King', referring to the myth of the sovereign who does not die but waits for his time to return and rule.

course_195_lancelot_guenievre_et_la_tabl.displayTerm: Quest for the Holy Grail and medieval Christianity
course_195_lancelot_guenievre_et_la_tabl.explanation: The Grail was christianized: chalice of the Last Supper or cup that collected the blood of Christ. The quest becomes a spiritual quest for purity. Only Galahad - pure and sinless - can achieve it. Lancelot, tainted by his love for Guinevere, fails.
Founding episode where Arthur proves his royal blood by pulling the sword Excalibur (or an anonymous sword according to sources) from a rock or an anvil, proving his divine legitimacy.

course_196_merlin_l_enchanteur|The figur.displayTerm: The figure of the archmage in literature
course_196_merlin_l_enchanteur|The figur.explanation: Merlin is the prototype of the archmage: Gandalf (Tolkien), Dumbledore (Rowling) are direct descendants. The wise old man with mysterious powers who guides the hero is a near-universal narrative archetype.

course_196_merlin_l_enchanteur|Prophecy.explanation: The prophecies of Merlin, collected by Geoffrey of Monmouth in 1136, became a literary genre of their own and were hugely popular in the Middle Ages. People reread them at every major political event, much as they reread the Book of Revelation.

course_196_merlin_l_enchanteur|Incubus d.explanation: In medieval demonology, a male demon supposed to take human form to seduce women during their sleep.

course_196_merlin_l_enchanteur|Baptism.explanation: Christian sacrament marking the entry into the community of believers and the washing away of original sin; for Merlin, it cancels out his demonic nature.

course_196_merlin_l_enchanteur|Celyddon.explanation: Ancient Welsh name referring to the Caledonian Forest, the wandering place of the mad bard Myrddin Wyllt.

course_196_merlin_l_enchanteur|Excalibur.explanation: Mythical sword of King Arthur, symbol of his legitimacy and divine protection, often associated with the Lady of the Lake.

course_196_merlin_l_enchanteur|Utherpend.explanation: Father of Arthur and King of Britain, whose name means 'Dragon's Head'.

course_196_merlin_l_enchanteur|Siege Per.explanation: The seat at the Round Table kept for the one knight destined to complete the Grail quest. Anyone else who sits in it is swallowed up.

course_196_merlin_l_enchanteur|Druidic.explanation: Relating to the druids, members of the priestly class of Celtic peoples, holders of religious and legal knowledge.

course_196_merlin_l_enchanteur|Archmage.displayTerm: Archmage in literature, figure of the
course_196_merlin_l_enchanteur|Archmage.explanation: Merlin is the prototype of the archmage: Gandalf (Tolkien), Dumbledore (Rowling) are direct descendants. The wise old man with mysterious powers who guides the hero is a quasi-universal narrative archetype.

course_197_les_mille_et_une_nuits_sheher.explanation: Fascination and idealization of the East by Europeans, often stereotyped. One Thousand and One Nights, notably in Antoine Galland's translation (1704), fueled this orientalism: harems, Caliphs, genies became the standard image of the Arab world in Europe.

Narrative technique: stories are nested within one another. Inherited from the Indian tradition, it was brought to its peak by Scheherazade and would influence Boccaccio, Chaucer, Cervantes, then Borges and postmodern narrative.
Persian title meaning 'Thousand tales', considered the original core that served as the basis for the One Thousand and One Nights before their Arabization.
Dynasty of Caliphs who reigned from 750 to 1258. Under their rule, Baghdad became the world center of culture and the place of the Arabization of the tales.
Dynasty that ruled over Egypt and Syria (1250-1517), a period during which the collection of the One Thousand and One Nights was stabilized and enriched with numerous urban tales.
Syrian Maronite storyteller who orally told Antoine Galland tales such as Aladdin and Ali Baba, allowing their integration into the collection.
Narrative device consisting of interrupting a story at a moment of high tension to encourage the audience to find out what happens next.

course_198_sindbad_le_marin|Medieval Ara.explanation: From the 7th to the 14th century, Arab merchants dominated maritime trade in the Indian Ocean. The adventures of Sinbad reflect these real networks, exotic goods (spices, silk, porcelain) and the dangers of long-distance navigation.

course_198_sindbad_le_marin|Marco Polo a.displayTerm: Marco Polo as a Western parallel
course_198_sindbad_le_marin|Marco Polo a.explanation: Marco Polo (1254-1324) made the inverse journey of Sinbad: from Venice to the China of Kublai Khan. His accounts seemed as fabulous as those of Sinbad. The Book of the Marvels of the World directly influenced Columbus in his plans to travel to Asia.

course_198_sindbad_le_marin|Islamic cosm.explanation: Medieval world view integrating Greek geographical knowledge, sailors' accounts, and the symbolic structures of the Quran (such as the seven heavens).

course_198_sindbad_le_marin|Serendib.explanation: Ancient Arabic name for the island of Ceylon (modern-day Sri Lanka), renowned in the tales of Sinbad for its precious stones and natural wonders.

course_198_sindbad_le_marin|Adventure no.explanation: Literary genre based on action and a change of scenery, of which Sinbad is considered one of the major ancestors for its structure centered on travel and the unexpected.

course_198_sindbad_le_marin|Basra.explanation: Historic Iraqi port on the Shatt al-Arab, the starting point of the great Arab sea voyages toward the Indian Ocean in the Abbasid era.

course_198_sindbad_le_marin|Marco Polo (.explanation: Marco Polo (1254-1324) made the opposite journey of Sinbad: from Venice to the China of Kublai Khan. His stories seemed as fabulous as those of Sinbad. The Book of Marvels directly influenced Columbus in his plans to travel to Asia.

course_199_les_titans_vs_les_dieux_la_ti.explanation: After the Titanomachy, the Olympians had to face the giants (born from the blood of Uranus), who were nearly invincible. This second war of the gods foreshadows the permanent tensions between Olympian order and the primordial forces of chaos.

Prometheus did not participate in the Titanomachy, having foreseen through prophecy that Zeus would win. This neutrality preserved his freedom - which subsequently allowed him to steal fire for humans. His particular position explains his unique role.
Mother goddess personifying the Earth, she first helps Zeus to overthrow Cronus before turning against him during the Gigantomachy.
Helmet of invisibility forged by the Cyclops for Hades during the Titanomachy.
Second-generation Titan, father of Atlas, Prometheus and Epimetheus, often representing the ancestor of men.
Monstrous creatures born from Gaia, whose defeat during the Gigantomachy requires the joint intervention of the gods and a mortal.
Mortal hero, son of Zeus, whose participation was essential to the victory of the gods during the Gigantomachy.

course_199_les_titans_vs_les_dieux_la_ti.displayTerm: Order and chaos in Greek mythology
course_199_les_titans_vs_les_dieux_la_ti.explanation: The Titanomachy represents the victory of Olympian order (Zeus, reason, law) over the primordial chaos of the Titans. This narrative structure - cosmic combat between order and chaos - is found in all major world mythologies.

course_200_re_et_la_creation_du_monde_eg.explanation: Theological system centered on Heliopolis ("city of the sun"), asserting that Atum/Ra was the primary creator god. It competed with other centers (Memphis: Ptah, Thebes: Amun) whose theologies coexisted and merged.

Egyptian gods could merge: Ra-Atum, Amun-Ra, Osiris-Ra. This syncretism allowed for the integration of local deities without eliminating them. Egyptian religion was thus inclusive and in perpetual evolution over 3,000 years.
The underworld in Egyptian mythology, crossed every night by Ra and the place of judgment for the souls of the deceased.
Lioness-headed goddess representing the destructive fury of the eye of Ra, capable of devastating humanity.
Immense religious complex in Thebes (Luxor) dedicated mainly to Amun-Ra, testifying to the power of the solar cult.

course_201_la_naissance_du_conflit_israe.explanation: Political movement founded by Theodor Herzl (The Jewish State, 1896) advocating for the creation of a Jewish national home in response to European antisemitism. He initially proposed Argentina or Uganda before settling on historical Palestine.

Letter from the British minister Balfour promising British support for "the establishment of a national home for the Jewish people" in Palestine, while preserving the rights of "non-Jewish communities". This foundational tension has never been resolved.
International organization created after the First World War to maintain peace, replaced by the UN in 1945.
Organization created to facilitate Jewish immigration to Palestine and the administration of Jewish communities under the British Mandate.
Hebrew term referring to Jewish immigration to the Land of Israel.
United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East, established in 1949.

course_202_la_rivalite_chine_etats_unis|.explanation: Starting in 2018, the United States (Trump) imposed massive customs duties on Chinese products, which China responded to in kind. This trade war reflects a technological and geopolitical rivalry deeper than mere exchanges.

American strategy aiming to separate technological supply chains between the two countries. Sanctions on Huawei and the ban on sales of advanced semiconductors to China reflect the fear of military use of American technologies.
Structure of the international system where power is primarily shared between two dominant poles (here China and the United States).
Theory by Graham Allison stating that when an emerging power threatens to displace an established power, the risk of war becomes almost inevitable.
Politics aimed at protecting territorial integrity and the economic or technological interests of a state against external threats, often used to justify sanctions.
Rivalry that is not limited to a specific field but encompasses political models, ideological values, and international norms.
Period of tensions (1947-1991) between the USA and the USSR without direct confrontation. The term is used again today to describe Sino-American technological tension.

course_203_les_tensions_autour_de_taiwan.explanation: Taiwanese manufacturer producing about 92% of the world's most advanced chips. This global dependence explains why a Chinese invasion would cause a global economic catastrophe - Taiwan's "silicon shield".

American policy that acknowledges "one China" without accepting Beijing's sovereignty over Taiwan, and that sells weapons without ever promising to fight. The vagueness is deliberate: it is meant to deter an invasion without provoking Beijing.
Chinese nationalist party that governed China before 1949 and established an authoritarian regime in Taiwan until the democratic reforms of the 1980s.
Voting system where all citizens vote directly to choose their representatives, adopted by Taiwan for the first time in 1996.
Air Defense Identification Zone: airspace beyond national territory where a state requires the identification of aircraft for security reasons.

course_204_le_concept_de_monde_multipola.explanation: Krauthammer described (1990) the post-Cold War era as a "unipolar moment" with the United States as the sole superpower. He predicted it would last 30 to 40 years - an accurate prediction, as the "unipolar moment" ended around 2008-2010.

Acronym referring to Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, expanded to several countries since 2024. This grouping embodies multipolarity: powers that reject the Western liberal order without necessarily forming a coherent alternative bloc.
Charles Krauthammer (1950-2018), American intellectual and journalist, famous for theorizing the end of the Cold War as a period of total domination by the United States.
North Atlantic Treaty Organization, intergovernmental military alliance created in 1949, a pillar of Western power during and after the Cold War.
Vast infrastructure and investment project launched by China in 2013 to link Asia, Europe, and Africa, strengthening its global geopolitical weight.
Term designating developing or emerging countries (often from Africa, Latin America, and Asia) seeking to emancipate themselves from Western influence.
American political scientist, leader of the neorealist school, known for his thesis on the inevitability of conflict between rising powers and established powers.
A commercial practice consisting of prioritizing supply chains and trade with allied countries or those sharing the same political values to reduce strategic risks.

Krauthammer described (1990) the post-Cold War era as a "unipolar moment" with the United States as the sole superpower. He predicted it would last 30 to 40 years - an accurate prediction, as the "unipolar moment" ended around 2008-2010.
A vast infrastructure and investment project launched by China in 2013 to link Asia, Europe, and Africa, strengthening its global geopolitical weight.
A vast infrastructure and investment project launched by China in 2013 to link Asia, Europe, and Africa, strengthening its global geopolitical weight.

course_205_le_petrole_comme_source_de_co.explanation: Economic paradox: countries rich in natural resources (oil, diamonds) often experience lower growth and more frequent conflicts. The oil "rent" creates predatory states and discourages economic diversification.

Hubbert's theory (1956) predicting that global oil production would reach a summit and then decline. The American shale oil revolution pushed back this limit, but the debate over resource depletion remains central.
Pioneer of the American oil industry, known for having drilled the first mechanized oil well in 1859 in Titusville.
Iranian Prime Minister who nationalized his country's oil industry in 1951 before being overthrown by a coup supported by the CIA and MI6.
A 1973 conflict between Israel and a coalition led by Egypt and Syria, serving as the trigger for the first oil crisis.
Oil trapped in sedimentary rocks with low permeability, whose industrial extraction via hydraulic fracturing disrupted the global market as of 2010.

Economic paradox: countries rich in natural resources (oil, diamonds) often experience slower growth and more frequent conflicts. The oil "rent" creates predatory states and discourages economic diversification.

course_206_le_canal_de_suez_pourquoi_il_.explanation: When Nasser nationalized the canal, France, Great Britain, and Israel invaded Egypt. Under American pressure (Eisenhower threatened to collapse the pound sterling), they had to withdraw - marking the end of Franco-British colonial power.

A 400 m container ship that ran aground across the canal for 6 days, blocking 400 ships. It cost the global economy 400 million dollars per hour, perfectly illustrating the strategic importance of the canal in global chains.
A point located at the southern tip of Africa. Before the Suez Canal, ships had to bypass it to travel between Europe and Asia.
Title held by the rulers of Egypt between 1867 and 1914, while the country was officially under Ottoman suzerainty but increasingly influenced by European powers.
Political movement aiming for the unification of Arab peoples, of which Nasser was the main leader in the 1950s and 1960s.
Shia rebel group in Yemen which, from 2023, disrupted maritime traffic in the Red Sea to protest against regional conflicts.
Strait located at the south of the Red Sea, between Yemen and Djibouti, constituting the mandatory crossing point to access the Suez Canal from the Indian Ocean.

A 400m container ship that ran aground across the canal for 6 days, blocking 400 ships. It cost the world economy 400 million dollars per hour, perfectly illustrating the strategic importance of the canal in global chains.

course_207_l_otan_a_quoi_ca_sert_encore|.displayTerm: Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty
course_207_l_otan_a_quoi_ca_sert_encore|.explanation: Collective defense clause: an attack on one member counts as an attack on all of them. It has been invoked only once in NATO's history, on September 12, 2001, the day after the September 11 attacks. Its exact scope is left deliberately vague.
Since 1991, NATO has welcomed 14 new members, including former Soviet republics. Russia considers this enlargement an existential threat - an argument used to justify the invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Also called the Washington Treaty, it is the founding act signed on April 4, 1949, which defines the goals of NATO and the principle of solidarity among its members.
Military alliance created in 1955 by the USSR in reaction to NATO, bringing together the communist countries of Eastern Europe. It disappeared in 1991.
Geographical group composed of Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania. Former Soviet republics, they are now members of NATO and the EU.
President of the Russian Federation since 1999 (with an interruption as Prime Minister), he considers the extension of NATO as an aggression against Russian influence.
Process by which military tension intensifies until the use of atomic weapons. This is the major fear that hinders a direct NATO intervention in Ukraine.
Immaterial domain of digital and computer networks, now considered by NATO as a full-fledged battlefield in the same way as land, air, and sea.

course_208_l_onu_puissante_ou_impuissant.explanation: Principle adopted by the UN in 2005: the international community can intervene in a sovereign state to protect civilians in danger. Developed in the 1990s after the inaction in Rwanda and Bosnia, its application remains very selective.

The UN includes agencies with specific mandates: WHO (global health), UNICEF (children), FAO (food), UNESCO (culture), UNHCR (refugees). These agencies often achieve concrete results where the Security Council is blocked by a veto.
Founding treaty of the UN signed on June 26, 1945, by 50 states, defining the goals and principles of the organization.
Main organ of the UN responsible for maintaining peace. It includes 15 members, 5 of whom are permanent and hold the power of veto.
Main deliberative organ of the UN where each member state has an equal vote. Its resolutions are not legally binding.
Constitutional text of the organization that defines the rights and obligations of member states and the structures of the institution.

course_209_la_russie_de_poutine|The KGB.explanation: The Soviet KGB was dissolved in 1991 and replaced by the FSB (domestic) and the SVR (foreign). Putin, a former KGB officer in Dresden, has extensively promoted former KGB members (the “siloviki”) to key positions of power in Russia.

course_209_la_russie_de_poutine|“Soverei.explanation: Concept developed by the ideologue Vladislav Surkov: Russia has its own form of democracy adapted to its history, not subject to Western liberal standards. Criticism: this concept actually justifies authoritarianism by rebranding it as “cultural sovereignty”.

course_209_la_russie_de_poutine|Gazprom.explanation: Russian state-owned gas giant, used by the Kremlin as an instrument of economic and diplomatic power (the energy weapon) as well as a tool for media control.

course_209_la_russie_de_poutine|oligarch.explanation: Businessman who acquired immense wealth and considerable politics influence during the privatizations of the 1990s in Russia.

course_209_la_russie_de_poutine|siloviki.explanation: A term designating politics officials coming from the security services (KGB/FSB), the military, or the police, who form the inner circle of power under Putin.

course_209_la_russie_de_poutine|civil so.explanation: A set of non-governmental organizations (NGOs) and citizens acting independently of the state. Under Putin, it is increasingly repressed.

course_209_la_russie_de_poutine|KGB and.explanation: The Soviet KGB was dissolved in 1991 and replaced by the FSB (domestic) and the SVR (foreign). Putin, a former KGB officer in Dresden, has extensively promoted former members of the KGB (the "siloviki") to key positions in Russian power.

course_210_la_guerre_en_ukraine_explique.explanation: Agreement by which Ukraine gave up the 1,900 inherited Soviet nuclear warheads in exchange for security guarantees from Russia, the United States, and the United Kingdom. Russia violated it as early as 2014, which haunts Ukrainian security discussions.

course_210_la_guerre_en_ukraine_explique.displayTerm: The Donbas and the separatist republics
course_210_la_guerre_en_ukraine_explique.explanation: An industrial region in eastern Ukraine where pro-Russian separatists proclaimed “republics” with Russian military support in 2014. This “low-intensity” conflict (14,000 deaths) preceded the full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022.
A cooperative society under Belgian law that manages the international financial messaging network allowing secure cross-border payments.
North Atlantic Treaty Organization, an intergovernmental military alliance created in 1949 to ensure the collective defense of its members.
Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, a former federal state in Eurasia with a communist regime born in 1922 and dissolved in 1991.

An industrial region in eastern Ukraine where pro-Russian separatists proclaimed "republics" with Russian military support in 2014. This "low intensity" conflict (14,000 deaths) preceded the full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022.

course_211_comment_fonctionne_le_prix_du.explanation: Contracts by which buyers and sellers commit to a future transaction at a price fixed today. Speculators with no intention of physical delivery represent the vast majority of transactions, amplifying price fluctuations.
Massive boom in American production in the 21st century thanks to hydraulic fracturing, altering the global geopolitical energy balance.
Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries, a cartel founded in 1960 aimed at coordinating the oil politics of its members to stabilize prices.
Light oil from North Sea fields, serving as a major price benchmark for international markets, particularly in Europe and Africa.
West Texas Intermediate, high-quality oil extracted in the United States serving as the main benchmark for the American market.
In economics, a situation where the demand for a good varies little despite a strong variation in its price, because consumers cannot easily do without it.

A seahorse-shaped brain structure in the temporal lobe, essential for forming new conscious memories. Its surgical removal (case H.M.) leads to a total inability to form new memories without erasing old ones.

A cognitive system that temporarily maintains a small amount of information (7±2 items) available for ongoing processing. Managed by the prefrontal cortex, it is limited in capacity and duration (a few seconds without rehearsal).

An all-or-nothing electrical signal triggered when the depolarization of a neuron exceeds a threshold. It propagates along the axon at 1 to 100 m/s depending on myelination. It is the "click" of information that the neuron sends.

Chemical molecules released in the synapse that transmit signals between neurons. The main ones: glutamate (excitatory), GABA (inhibitory), dopamine, serotonin. Psychoactive drugs act on these systems.

course_212_les_paradis_fiscaux_expliques.explanation: Switzerland maintained absolute banking secrecy for decades, criminally protecting bankers who refused to disclose their clients' identities. This secrecy, eroded since 2010 under international pressure, had made Switzerland the world's leading tax haven.

Tax optimization mechanism: a subsidiary in a normal country "buys" services from a subsidiary in a tax haven at overvalued prices. Profits are thus transferred to the low-tax jurisdiction, reducing the overall tax bill.
A term designating financial activities or capital investments carried out outside the country of residence, generally in jurisdictions with advantageous taxation.
The natural person who ultimately owns or controls a legal entity or for whom a transaction is carried out, as opposed to nominees.
A practice by which a tax administration confirms in advance to a company how it will be taxed, often allowing for the negotiation of very low rates.
A massive leak of 11.5 million documents in 2016 revealing the offshore assets of global figures managed by the law firm Mossack Fonseca.
An Anglo-Saxon legal structure allowing for the transfer of ownership of assets to a third party who manages them for the benefit of a beneficiary, often ensuring anonymity.
A set of technologies allowing for the analysis of immense volumes of data, used by tax authorities to detect sophisticated evasion patterns.

course_213_l_evasion_fiscale_des_multina.explanation: Tax structure using Irish and Dutch subsidiaries to transfer intellectual property rights to Bermuda. Apple, Google, and Facebook used it until its phase-out (2020), paying effective rates of less than 2%.

Agreement signed by 136 countries to impose a minimum rate of 15% on the profits of multinationals, regardless of their country of filing. The first major international tax agreement in history, it aims to end the tax "race to the bottom."

Prices at which a company transfers tangible goods, intangible assets or provides services to associated companies (subsidiaries). Manipulating these prices allows profits to be shifted to lower-taxed areas.
Advance agreements between a national tax administration and a multinational, fixing in advance how tax will be calculated. They are often criticized for being disguised tax advantages.

Current of thought and activism (led by NGOs such as Oxfam) advocating for a fair distribution of the tax burden, where multinationals and the wealthiest contribute proportionally to their actual capacity.
Legal notion defining the minimum physical presence (office, branch) required for a state to have the right to tax the profits of a foreign company.

An agreement signed by 136 countries to tax the profits of multinationals at a minimum rate of 15%, whatever country they file in. It is the first major international tax agreement, and it aims to end the "race to the bottom".

course_214_la_crise_de_l_etat_providence.explanation: Document by British economist Beveridge laying the foundations of the Welfare state: universal protection against the "five giants" (poverty, disease, ignorance, squalor, idleness). It inspired the creation of the NHS and post-war social systems.

By pay-as-you-go: the active workforce finances current retirees. With aging, fewer active workers finance more retirees. By capitalization (funded): individual savings subject to market fluctuations. The debate on the "right" reform is universal in developed countries.
The body that led the various movements of the French Resistance during the Second World War and developed the social reform program of 1944.
Small job or digital platform economy (like Uber), characterized by short-term contracts and independent contractor status rather than employment.
Social model combining ease of dismissal for companies (flexibility) and strong protections for workers in transition (security), typical of the Danish model.
Contribution Sociale Généralisée. French tax intended to diversify the financing of social protection beyond salary contributions alone.
The phenomenon of challenging the traditional economic model through digital platforms that connect providers and clients directly, often to the detriment of classic employment.

course_215_les_inegalites_nord_sud|The \.explanation: Graph by economist Milanovic: between 1988 and 2008, the Asian middle class and the global ultra-rich progressed the most, while the working class in rich countries stagnated. This curve partly explains the rise of Western populism.

course_215_les_inegalites_nord_sud|Unequ.explanation: Poor countries export raw materials at low prices and import expensive manufactured goods. This structure inherited from colonialism perpetuates economic dependence: when commodity prices drop, these countries become even poorer.

course_215_les_inegalites_nord_sud|“elep.explanation: Graph by economist Milanovic: between 1988 and 2008, the Asian middle class and the global very rich progressed the most, while the working class in rich countries stagnated. This curve partly explains the rise of Western populism.

course_215_les_inegalites_nord_sud|terms.explanation: Ratio between the prices of a country's exports and the prices of its imports. When it deteriorates (raw materials sold for less against manufactured goods bought for more), the country becomes structurally poorer.

course_215_les_inegalites_nord_sud|deter.displayTerm: deterioration of the terms of trade
course_215_les_inegalites_nord_sud|deter.explanation: Economic phenomenon where the prices of primary products decrease relative to the prices of manufactured products over the long term, penalizing raw material exporting countries.

course_215_les_inegalites_nord_sud|offic.explanation: All financial flows transferred by developed states to developing countries to promote the improvement of living conditions and economic growth.

course_216_la_dette_mondiale|Keynesian d.explanation: For Keynes (1936), the state must borrow to spend during recessions. Public debt is an economic management tool, not a moral issue. This theory justifies stimulus plans like the New Deal or post-COVID stimulus.

course_216_la_dette_mondiale|Modern Mone.explanation: The view that a state borrowing in its own currency, such as the United States or Japan, cannot technically go bankrupt, because it can always create money. The only risk is inflation, so large deficits are acceptable as long as inflation stays under control.

course_216_la_dette_mondiale|IMF.explanation: The International Monetary Fund is an international organization overseeing global financial stability and lending to countries in difficulty, often in exchange for structural reforms.

course_216_la_dette_mondiale|Maastricht.explanation: Signed in 1992, it sets convergence criteria for the European Union, including public debt limited to 60% of GDP and a deficit of 3%.

course_216_la_dette_mondiale|Keynesian t.explanation: For Keynes (1936), the state must borrow to spend during recessions. Public debt is an economic management tool, not a moral issue. This theory justifies recovery plans such as the New Deal or post-COVID stimulus.

course_217_l_economie_de_plateforme_uber.explanation: A platform becomes more valuable as the number of users increases. Facebook, Uber, Amazon: the more users there are, the better the service, which attracts even more users - creating almost insurmountable natural monopolies.

An economy of "gig work" where individuals offer their services via platforms without permanent contracts. It weakens traditional social protections (retirement, unemployment) while offering flexibility for workers.
The process of efficiently connecting a supplier and a requester on a digital marketplace.
A situation where a worker, although legally independent, is subject to the control, monitoring, and instructions of an algorithm (rating, pricing, disconnection).
A legal decision transforming a service provision contract (independent) into an employment contract (salaried) after establishing a subordinate relationship.
A legal decision transforming a service provision contract (independent) into an employment contract (salaried) after establishing a subordinate relationship.
A fiscal mechanism (such as the GAFA tax) aimed at taxing the income of digital platforms in the place where they create value, and not only where they are domiciled.

A platform becomes more valuable as the number of users increases. Facebook, Uber, Amazon: the more users there are, the better the service, which attracts even more users - creating virtually insurmountable natural monopolies.

An economy of "piecework" where individuals offer their services via platforms without permanent contracts. It weakens traditional social protections (retirement, unemployment) while offering flexibility for workers.
Circular building, used here to designate the underground chamber where Danae was imprisoned.
Magic wallet (kibisis) capable of containing Medusa's head without her blood or power affecting the wearer.

course_218_le_role_des_donnees_le_petrol.explanation: General Data Protection Regulation - the most ambitious personal data protection law. It gives European citizens the right to access their data, correct them and delete them. Global companies are subject to its rules.
Concept by Shoshana Zuboff: GAFAM created a model based on capturing human behaviors to sell them as predictions to advertisers. Humans become the "raw material" of an invisible economic market.
A field of study within artificial intelligence that uses statistical methods to enable computers to learn from data without being explicitly programmed for each task.
Acronym for the five American giants of technology: Google, Apple, Facebook (Meta), Amazon and Microsoft.
Chinese equivalent of GAFAM, grouping Baidu, Alibaba, Tencent and Xiaomi.
The capacity of a state or an organization to control its digital infrastructures, its data and its technologies in order not to depend on foreign powers.

course_219_la_fracture_numerique_mondial.explanation: Mobile payment service (2007) allowing money to be sent via SMS without a bank account. Having become the dominant payment system in Kenya and several African countries, it shows that developing countries can "leapfrog" certain technological stages.

A constellation of satellites offering high-speed Internet in areas without terrestrial infrastructure. It can transform Internet access in rural areas of developing countries but remains expensive. Also used by Ukraine in its war against Russia.
Intelligent telephone equipped with an operating system allowing access to the Internet and the installation of applications.
Professional activity carried out remotely thanks to digital tools.
(Massive Open Online Course) Educational course broadcast on the Internet and accessible to everyone for free or at a low cost.
Sets of data so large that they require specific computer tools to be analyzed and exploited.

course_220_la_desinformation_et_les_fake.explanation: Social media algorithms personalize content based on past preferences, creating "bubbles" where each user only sees what confirms their beliefs. This polarizes debates and promotes large-scale disinformation.

A Saint Petersburg troll farm funded by Prigozhin, employing hundreds of people to create fake accounts and manipulate American and European public opinion. Brought to light during the Mueller investigation into the 2016 election.
The Massachusetts Institute of Technology, a prestigious research university that conducts numerous studies on the impact of digital technologies on society.
Agence France-Presse, a leading global news agency that has developed one of the largest fact-checking networks in the world.
Ultra-realistic audio or video recordings generated by artificial intelligence, allowing the face or voice of one person to be substituted by another to attribute imaginary words to them.
Ultra-realistic audio or video recordings generated by artificial intelligence, allowing the face or voice of one person to be substituted by another to attribute imaginary words to them.

Saint Petersburg troll factory funded by Prigozhin, employing hundreds of people to create fake accounts and manipulate American and European public opinion. Highlighted during the Mueller investigation into the 2016 election.

course_221_le_trou_de_la_couche_d_ozone_.explanation: Synthetic chemical compounds invented in the 1920s, used as refrigerants and as propellants in spray cans. Because they are chemically stable, they drift up into the stratosphere, where they destroy ozone. Nobody noticed that effect for decades.

International treaty that phases out CFCs, ratified by 197 countries. It is the only treaty in history ratified by every UN member state, and it is considered the greatest success of environmental diplomacy.
Continent located at the South Pole, where extreme weather conditions in the stratosphere in spring promote the massive destruction of ozone by CFCs.
Second layer of the Earth's atmosphere, located between approximately 10 and 50 km in altitude, housing most of the ozone layer.
Gas naturally present in the atmosphere, but whose excess linked to human activities is the main driver of current global warming.

course_222_la_crise_de_la_biodiversite|E.explanation: Benefits that ecosystems provide for free: pollination, water purification, climate regulation, flood prevention. The Dasgupta Review (2021) values them at 125 trillion dollars a year, far more than global GDP.

Thresholds in natural systems beyond which rapid and irreversible changes occur: Arctic ice melt, death of coral reefs, forest dieback. Once these points are passed, returning to the previous state becomes impossible.

course_222_la_crise_de_la_biodiversite|W.explanation: World Wide Fund for Nature, one of the largest international non-governmental environmental protection organizations.

course_222_la_crise_de_la_biodiversite|I.explanation: Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem services, often described as the 'IPCC of biodiversity'.

course_222_la_crise_de_la_biodiversite|D.explanation: Major economic report (2021) commissioned by the British Treasury, which theorizes the integration of nature into global economic indicators.

course_222_la_crise_de_la_biodiversite|p.explanation: Quantified thresholds that humanity should not exceed in order to avoid compromising the Earth's habitable conditions.

course_222_la_crise_de_la_biodiversite|C.explanation: United Nations Biodiversity Conference held in 2022, which resulted in the historic '30 by 30' agreement for nature protection.

course_222_la_crise_de_la_biodiversite|r.explanation: Capacity of an ecosystem to return to its normal functioning after undergoing a major disturbance.

course_223_l_economie_circulaire|The 3Rs.explanation: Waste management hierarchy in order of priority. First reduce consumption, then reuse existing products, and finally recycle as a last resort. The order is crucial: recycling consumes a lot of energy and does not solve overconsumption.

course_223_l_economie_circulaire|Planned.explanation: Industrial strategy consisting of designing products intended to be replaced quickly. Apple, Samsung and many electronic manufacturers are accused of this practice - non-replaceable parts, non-removable batteries, updates forcing the purchase of new devices.

course_223_l_economie_circulaire|planned.explanation: Industrial strategy consisting of designing products intended to be replaced quickly. Apple, Samsung and many electronic manufacturers are accused of this practice - non-replaceable parts, non-removable batteries, updates forcing the purchase of new devices.

course_223_l_economie_circulaire|Bauxite.explanation: The main ore allowing the production of aluminum.

course_223_l_economie_circulaire|Industr.explanation: Organizational model where companies within the same territory exchange their flows (energy, water, materials) so that the waste of some becomes the resources of others.

course_223_l_economie_circulaire|Lithium.explanation: Alkali metal essential for the manufacturing of rechargeable batteries for electric vehicles and mobile devices.

course_223_l_economie_circulaire|Extende.explanation: Legal principle according to which manufacturers and importers must take responsibility, financially or technically, for the end-of-life management of the products they put on the market.

course_223_l_economie_circulaire|Product.explanation: Economic model built on using a good, by renting a service, rather than owning it by buying the object.

course_223_l_economie_circulaire|Digital.explanation: Information tool storing the technical characteristics and composition of a product to facilitate its repair and future recycling.

course_224_pourquoi_les_abeilles_sont_el.explanation: Phenomenon documented since 2006: entire hives disappear without explanation, bees leaving the hive and not returning. The causes are multifactorial: neonicotinoids pesticides, Varroa destructor, loss of habitat, combined pathogens.

Pesticides absorbed by the entire plant, including nectar and pollen, paralyzing the nervous system of insects. Banned for certain crops in Europe since 2018, despite resistance from the agro-industry, they remain authorized in many countries.
A pollination trick used by some insects, such as bumblebees, which vibrate their wing muscles to shake pollen loose from the anthers of certain flowers.
Process of transporting pollen grains from the male organs (stamens) to the female organs (pistil) of a flower, allowing fertilization and the production of seeds and fruits.
All insect species living in a given environment.
Sequence of feeding relationships between living beings that eat one another (food chain).
Non-productive elements of a farm (hedges, ponds, low walls, flowered strips) that provide shelter and resources for biodiversity.
A building with a circular plan, here used to designate the underground chamber where Danaë was imprisoned.
Magic sac (kibisis) capable of containing Medusa's head without her blood or power affecting the wearer.

course_225_la_montee_des_eaux|Arctic sea.displayTerm: Arctic sea ice and the albedo effect
course_225_la_montee_des_eaux|Arctic sea.explanation: Unlike sea ice (the melting of which does not raise water levels), the melting of ice from Greenland and Antarctica makes the oceans rise directly. Furthermore, the dark water replacing the white ice absorbs more heat, accelerating warming.

course_225_la_montee_des_eaux|Storm surg.explanation: Storms combined with rising sea levels create temporary "surges" well above the average level. A 50 cm rise in sea levels can multiply the frequency of floods previously described as "hundred-year floods" by 10 - Rare events become common.

course_225_la_montee_des_eaux|Ice sheet.explanation: An immense glacier of vast extent, which can reach several kilometers in thickness, covering a continental landmass (such as in Greenland or Antarctica).

course_225_la_montee_des_eaux|IPCC.explanation: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, an UN body responsible for assessing the scientific knowledge on climate change.

course_225_la_montee_des_eaux|Thermal ex.explanation: Physical phenomenon by which a substance (in this case water) increases in volume due to a rise in its temperature.

course_225_la_montee_des_eaux|Mangrove.explanation: A maritime marsh ecosystem including specific trees (mangroves) that stabilize coasts and protect against erosion and storm surges.

course_225_la_montee_des_eaux|Arctic sea.displayTerm: Arctic sea ice and albedo effect
course_225_la_montee_des_eaux|Arctic sea.explanation: Unlike sea ice (the melting of which does not raise water levels), the melting of ice in Greenland and Antarctica raises the oceans directly. Furthermore, dark water replacing white ice absorbs more heat, accelerating warming.

course_226_l_ia_et_l_emploi|The Luddites.explanation: English weaving workers who destroyed mechanical weaving machines. Often caricatured as anti-progress, they were actually protesting against the degradation of their working conditions and wages caused by mechanization without social protections.

course_226_l_ia_et_l_emploi|Universal Ba.explanation: Regular payment of a fixed sum to all citizens, without conditions. Seen as a response to automation. Experiments in Finland, Kenya and California give encouraging results but their generalization remains highly debated economically.

course_226_l_ia_et_l_emploi|Generative A.explanation: A type of artificial intelligence capable of creating new content (text, images, code, sound) from learned examples, rather than simply analyzing existing data.

course_226_l_ia_et_l_emploi|white-collar.explanation: A term referring to office workers, managers, and professional roles, as opposed to 'blue-collar workers' who work in industry or manual labor.

course_226_l_ia_et_l_emploi|Prompt engin.explanation: A profession consisting of designing and refining the textual instructions given to a generative AI to obtain the most relevant and effective result possible.

course_226_l_ia_et_l_emploi|Generative A.explanation: Type of artificial intelligence capable of creating new content (text, images, code, sound) from learned examples, rather than simply analyzing existing data.

course_227_le_populisme_pourquoi_ca_mont.explanation: Inglehart and Norris show that populism is as much cultural as economic: the "losers" of globalization and the cultural revolution find themselves in parties that defend their traditional values against a cosmopolitan elite perceived as contemptuous.

A concept claimed by Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán (2014): a democratically elected regime that restricts checks and balances (press, justice, NGOs). This model, also practiced by Erdogan and Modi, challenges the notion of liberal democracy.
Political scientist and professor at Princeton, author of 'What is Populism?', who defines the phenomenon by its anti-pluralism and its claim to exclusivity of representation.
Serbian-American economist specializing in inequality, famous for his 'elephant curve' showing the distribution of global income gains.
Process of opening economic borders and accelerating global trade, whose unequal effects are a driver of the populist vote.
Political movement associated with Donald Trump, mixing populism, economic nationalism, and direct communication shaking up institutional norms.
Political conception rejecting the diversity of opinions within the people, asserting that the popular will is one, indivisible, and embodied by a single leader.
Violent reaction or resistance of a social group to rapid cultural or political changes perceived as a threat to its values.
Major traditional press outlets (TV, newspapers), often described as 'media elites' by populists to discredit them.
Political strategy aimed at making a radical party more acceptable to the moderate electorate by smoothing its image and discourse.
